arXiv:2611.10965v1 [stat.ML] 07 Nov 2026

Bayesian transfer for offline Q-learning with multi-task Gaussian processes

Wenxing Guo Affiliation: School of Mathematics, Statistics and Actuarial Science Affiliation: University of Essex Affiliation: Colchester, United Kingdom
Abstract

Offline reinforcement learning can benefit from data collected in related tasks, yet indiscriminate knowledge transfer may lead to negative transfer under task mismatch and limited target-data coverage. We propose a target-aware Bayesian transfer framework for offline Q-learning based on multi-task Gaussian processes that jointly model task-specific Q-functions. Source tasks are assessed using target predictive evidence and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), while posterior uncertainty and behavior-supported action sets guide conservative Bellman updates and policy extraction. To account for the dependence induced by Bellman bootstrapping, we distinguish Bellman innovations from bootstrap errors and establish stability and predictive source-selection results under explicit regularity conditions. We further derive selection-adaptive posterior contraction and offline policy-performance bounds, identifying the structural conditions under which source information can be pooled to achieve minimax-optimal rates in a shared-function Gaussian sequence experiment. Simulation studies with heterogeneous source tasks demonstrate improved target Q-function estimation and reduced material negative transfer compared with indiscriminate source pooling. An application to human decision-making data further shows higher average expected immediate payoff than both target-only learning and matched-size random source selection. These results highlight the benefits of combining target-aware source selection with uncertainty-aware conservative learning for reliable and sample-efficient offline reinforcement learning.

Keywords: Offline reinforcement learning; Bayesian transfer learning; Multi-task Gaussian processes; Target-aware source selection; Posterior contraction; Negative transfer.

1 Introduction

Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to accelerate learning in a target task by leveraging knowledge acquired from related source tasks. Rather than learning each decision-making problem in isolation, an agent may reuse experience, value functions, policies, or representations across tasks. This is particularly attractive when collecting target-task interactions is expensive or only a limited offline dataset is available. However, the usefulness of transferred knowledge depends on the relationship between the source and target tasks. Differences in rewards, transition dynamics, and state–action coverage can make apparently relevant experience misleading, resulting in negative transfer (Taylor and Stone, 2009; Lazaric et al., 2008). The central question is therefore not merely how to transfer knowledge, but how to identify which sources are useful for a particular target and how to account for uncertainty in that decision. This question becomes especially important in offline RL. A learner operating on a fixed dataset cannot freely collect additional interactions to correct errors caused by inappropriate transfer. Moreover, increasing the amount of training data does not necessarily improve decision quality when the additional data change the distribution on which value estimates are fitted. Extrapolation beyond dataset support can undermine offline value learning (Fujimoto et al., 2019), while indiscriminate sharing across tasks can further amplify distributional shift (Yu et al., 2021). These observations motivate a transfer mechanism that considers task relevance, predictive uncertainty, and the target decision problem jointly. Existing research studies several complementary forms of knowledge reuse. Lazaric et al. (2008) transfer experience samples according to source-task compliance and sample relevance, explicitly considering differences between task models. Tirinzoni et al. (2018) develop an importance-weighted sample-transfer approach and provide a finite-sample analysis of the resulting batch RL procedure. Another line of work transfers structured value representations: successor features separate reward-dependent components from shared dynamics and support generalized policy improvement across tasks with common transition dynamics (Barreto et al., 2017). More recently, Chen et al. (2026) developed a transfer fitted Q-iteration framework for batch reinforcement learning and established statistical error bounds that account for task discrepancies and source and target sample sizes. Luo et al. (2026) proposed a joint estimation approach that incorporates source information into target Q-function learning through an ℓ1\ell_{1}-penalized objective, with theoretical guarantees for target estimation and policy learning under homogeneous or heterogeneous transition dynamics. These approaches study knowledge transfer through regression-based estimation and task-specific discrepancy correction. Our framework instead models cross-task dependence probabilistically through a multi-task Gaussian process and investigates target-aware source selection under Bellman-generated regression responses. These methods illustrate different ways of exploiting task relationships. Our focus is instead on representing cross-task dependence probabilistically at the level of Q-functions and using target-specific predictive evidence to guide source selection.

Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a nonparametric framework for specifying distributions over functions and obtaining posterior predictions under an explicit observation model (Rasmussen and Williams, 2006). GP-based RL methods have used this machinery for value estimation and control (Engel et al., 2005). Grande et al. (2014) further analyze sample-efficient model-based and model-free GP algorithms, demonstrating that learning guarantees depend on the algorithmic treatment of uncertainty rather than on the use of a GP alone. For multiple related outputs, Bonilla et al. (2007) combine an input covariance function with a learned task covariance matrix, while Alvarez et al. (2012) describe the broader connection between multi-output GPs and vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). Chowdhary et al. (2014) developed an off-policy Gaussian-process Q-learning framework and established convergence conditions for batch learning. Wang et al. (2025) proposed a nonstationary multi-output Gaussian process with dynamic spike-and-slab priors on task correlations to identify informative sources and mitigate negative transfer, including an application to reinforcement learning. These studies demonstrate the usefulness of Gaussian processes for value-function learning and adaptive information sharing. Our focus is on target-specific predictive source selection within offline Q-learning, together with statistical analysis of the dependence and errors introduced by Bellman bootstrapping. These constructions offer a natural language for modeling similarities among task-specific value functions. A particularly close predecessor is the Bayesian multi-task RL framework of Lazaric and Ghavamzadeh (2010). Their approach combines Gaussian-process temporal-difference modeling with hierarchical Bayesian priors, sharing information among related value functions and transferring the learned structure to a newly observed task. Building on this foundation, the present work focuses on target-aware source-subset selection within iterative Q-learning. In particular, we study source usefulness through target prediction risk and explicitly account for the fact that the regression responses are constructed through Bellman updates rather than supplied as independent observations of the true Q-function.

Our approach also relates to methods that control the consequences of uncertainty in offline RL. Batch-constrained learning restricts action selection to reduce extrapolation error (Fujimoto et al., 2019), whereas conservative Q-learning regularizes value estimates to mitigate overestimation under distribution shift (Kumar et al., 2020). Jin et al. (2021) provide a theoretical treatment of pessimistic value iteration using uncertainty-dependent penalties. In the multi-task setting, conservative data sharing routes experience according to its usefulness for individual tasks instead of pooling all datasets indiscriminately (Yu et al., 2021). Bai et al. (2024) developed an uncertainty-based multi-task data-sharing framework that applies pessimistic value iteration to pooled offline datasets without explicit data selection. Their analysis highlights the role of data coverage and uncertainty in controlling policy suboptimality. In contrast, our approach explicitly evaluates candidate source tasks using target-predictive evidence and combines source selection with Gaussian-process uncertainty penalties and behavior-supported action maximization. More recent model-based work relates uncertainty penalties to disagreement in Bellman estimates across learned dynamics models (Sun et al., 2023). Our method follows the conservative-learning motivation but uses posterior GP uncertainty together with task selection and behavior-supported action maximization. The resulting pessimistic score is a decision rule; its interpretation as a valid lower confidence bound requires the corresponding statistical assumptions.

Domain-adaptation theory distinguishes distributional similarity from compatibility of the prediction tasks themselves. For example, Ben-David et al. (2010) relate target generalization to source performance, domain divergence, and a joint approximation term. In kernel methods, maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) compares distributions through differences between their RKHS mean embeddings (Gretton et al., 2012). This provides a useful way to quantify mismatch between source and target state–action distributions. Nevertheless, a small discrepancy between these marginals does not by itself establish that two MDPs have compatible rewards or transition dynamics: the same state–action distribution can accompany different Bellman operators. Motivated by this distinction, we treat MMD-based penalties as complementary distributional information for source assessment, rather than as a stand-alone certificate of beneficial transfer. The statistical analysis of transfer Q-learning must also address the recursive nature of its training targets. Finite-time analyses of fitted value iteration connect regression error, function-class approximation, and error propagation through Bellman updates (Munos and Szepesvári, 2008). Separately, GP posterior contraction theory relates convergence to RKHS approximation and small-ball probabilities of the prior (van der Vaart and van Zanten, 2008). These results provide useful foundations, but applying regression contraction arguments to Q-learning requires additional control of trajectory dependence and bootstrap error.

We investigate these issues in a Bayesian transfer framework that models the target and source Q-functions jointly. For task indices i,ji,j and shared state–action representations x,x′x,x^{\prime}, we use the separable covariance structure K⁡((i,x),(j,x′))=Ktask​(i,j)​kin​(x,x′).K\bigl((i,x),(j,x^{\prime})\bigr)=K_{\mathrm{task}}(i,j)\,k_{\mathrm{in}}(x,x^{\prime}). The input kernel describes within-task regularity, while the task kernel represents cross-task dependence. We consider both source datasets with Q-function labels and source transition datasets whose labels are constructed iteratively. Bayesian source-subset selection is formulated around target predictive performance, with sparsity-inducing inclusion indicators allowing sources to be excluded. The selection objective is target-specific: it concerns the usefulness of a source subset for the target, rather than recovery of every relationship among all tasks. For offline policy learning, posterior predictions are combined through a pessimistic score Q−​(s,a)=μpost​(s,a)−αpess​σpost​(s,a),Q^{-}(s,a)=\mu_{\mathrm{post}}(s,a)-\alpha_{\mathrm{pess}}\sigma_{\mathrm{post}}(s,a), and actions are optimized over a behavior-supported set. This combines two distinct safeguards: source selection addresses potentially misleading cross-task information, while pessimism and action restrictions address uncertainty in the resulting target estimates. On the theoretical side, Bellman-generated responses are decomposed into the optimal Q-function, Bellman innovation noise, and a bootstrap remainder. This decomposition organizes our investigation of how one-step regression accuracy, source selection, and target posterior concentration interact. Here, safe transfer refers to comparison with a target-only learning strategy under the stated assumptions, not to an unconditional guarantee of improvement for every finite dataset.

This paper makes four main contributions. First, we develop a target-aware Bayesian transfer framework for offline Q-learning based on multi-task Gaussian processes. By jointly modeling task-specific Q-functions through a separable covariance structure, the proposed framework accommodates both directly labeled source data and transition-only source data. It integrates target-predictive source-subset selection, posterior uncertainty quantification, and conservative policy extraction through uncertainty penalties and behavior-supported action sets. Second, we establish a theoretical foundation for source selection under Bellman bootstrapping. By decomposing Bellman-generated responses into conditionally centered innovations and bootstrap errors, we derive uniform Bellman residual bounds and establish bootstrap consistency under explicit regularity conditions. We further analyze how bootstrap perturbations affect target-predictive scores and derive posterior concentration results for predictively near-optimal source subsets. Under an additional calibration condition linking predictive scores to target risk, these results also imply target-risk near-oracle selection. Third, we investigate transfer-adaptive posterior contraction and the statistical benefits of source information. We establish conditions under which predictive source selection and control of Bellman errors yield contraction of the model-averaged target posterior. Our analysis distinguishes the target-information bottleneck associated with full-rank task covariance from the precision pooling available under a rank-one shared-function model. In the latter Gaussian sequence experiment, we establish minimax-optimal contraction and estimation rates. We also derive offline policy-performance bounds that explicitly account for Q-function estimation error, action coverage, and uncertainty-aware pessimism. Fourth, we evaluate the proposed method through controlled simulations and an application to real human decision-making data. The simulations examine heterogeneous source tasks, target-aware selection, negative-transfer behavior, Q-function estimation accuracy, and the contribution of pessimistic policy extraction. The real-data analysis further evaluates cross-participant transfer and source selection against target-only learning and matched-size random source selection. Across these settings, the results demonstrate improved average estimation or decision performance while highlighting the conditions and limitations of safe knowledge transfer. Together, these contributions provide a unified statistical framework for understanding when source information can improve offline Q-learning, how transferable sources can be identified, and how uncertainty and task mismatch affect the reliability of transfer.

Section 2 introduces the problem setup, multi-task GP model, and learning algorithms. Section 3 studies Bellman bootstrap stability and target-aware source selection. Section 4 investigates posterior contraction and its connections to transfer gains and offline policy performance. Section 5 presents the simulation design and experimental results. Finally, Section 6 provides a real-data analysis to evaluate cross-participant transfer and target-aware source selection in human decision-making tasks.

2.2 Reinforcement learning

We consider an infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision process (MDP) (Sutton and Barto, 1998),

ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,P,R,γ),\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,R,\gamma), (1)

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a measurable state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a nonempty finite action space, P(⋅∣s,a)P(\cdot\mid s,a) denotes the conditional probability distribution of the next state given the current state–action pair, and γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) is the discount factor. The conditional mean reward is defined by

R(s,a)=𝔼[rt∣St=s,At=a].R(s,a)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[r_{t}\mid S_{t}=s,\ A_{t}=a\right].

We assume the uniform moment condition

sup(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜𝔼[|rt|∣St=s,At=a]<∞.\sup_{(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[|r_{t}|\mid S_{t}=s,\ A_{t}=a\right]<\infty.

This condition, together with γ<1\gamma<1, guarantees integrability of the infinite-horizon discounted return. The finiteness of 𝒜\mathcal{A} ensures that the action maxima in the Bellman operators are attained.

A stationary Markov policy π(⋅∣s)\pi(\cdot\mid s) assigns a probability distribution over actions at each state. Its action-value function is

Qπ(s,a)=𝔼π[∑t=0∞γtrt|S0=s,A0=a],Q^{\pi}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}r_{t}\;\middle|\;S_{0}=s,\ A_{0}=a\right], (2)

where the initial action is fixed to aa and subsequent actions follow π\pi. The learning objective is to recover the optimal action-value function

Q∗​(s,a)=supπQπ​(s,a),Q_{*}(s,a)=\sup_{\pi}Q^{\pi}(s,a), (3)

and an optimal deterministic policy can then be chosen as

π∗​(s)=arg⁡maxa∈𝒜​Q∗​(s,a),s∈𝒮.\pi_{*}(s)=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{*}(s,a),\qquad s\in\mathcal{S}.

The optimal Q-function satisfies the Bellman optimality equation

Q∗​(s,a)=R⁡(s,a)+γ​∫𝒮maxa′∈𝒜⁡Q∗​(s′,a′)​P​(d​s′∣s,a).Q_{*}(s,a)=R(s,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{S}}\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q_{*}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\,P(\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\mid s,a). (4)

For a bounded measurable function QQ, define the Bellman optimality operator by

(𝒯Q)(s,a)=R(s,a)+γ𝔼S′∼P(⋅∣s,a)[maxa′∈𝒜Q(S′,a′)].(\mathcal{T}Q)(s,a)=R(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{S^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)}\!\left[\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}Q(S^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right].

The contraction property of the Bellman optimality operator is central to the subsequent analysis, as it controls the propagation of approximation errors across successive Q-learning iterations. Specifically, for any two bounded Q-functions QQ and Q~\widetilde{Q},

‖𝒯​Q−𝒯​Q~‖∞≤γ​‖Q−Q~‖∞.\|\mathcal{T}Q-\mathcal{T}\widetilde{Q}\|_{\infty}\leq\gamma\|Q-\widetilde{Q}\|_{\infty}. (5)

Hence, 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a γ\gamma-contraction on the space of bounded Q-functions equipped with the supremum norm. Since γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), the contraction mapping theorem implies that 𝒯\mathcal{T} admits a unique bounded fixed point, namely Q∗Q_{*}, and that repeated exact Bellman updates converge geometrically to Q∗Q_{*}. In fitted Q-learning, however, the exact Bellman update is replaced by a regression estimate constructed from sampled Bellman targets. This replacement introduces regression and sampling errors at each iteration. The contraction property in (5) provides the basic mechanism for controlling the accumulation of these one-step errors and for establishing convergence of the fitted iterates to Q∗Q_{*} (Munos and Szepesvári, 2008).

In the multi-task setting, task 00 is the target and tasks k∈[J]k\in[J] are sources. Unless otherwise stated, they share 𝒮\mathcal{S}, 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and γ\gamma, but may have different transition kernels P(k)P^{(k)} and reward functions R(k)R^{(k)}. We denote their Bellman operators and optimal Q-functions by 𝒯(k)\mathcal{T}^{(k)} and Q∗(k)Q_{*}^{(k)}, respectively.

2.3 Gaussian process regression

Gaussian process regression (GPR) provides a nonparametric Bayesian framework for modeling unknown functions and quantifying predictive uncertainty (Rasmussen and Williams, 2006). To model statistical dependence across tasks, we place a joint Gaussian process prior on the collection of task-specific Q-functions. Specifically, define

Q⁡(k,x)=Q(k)​(x),(k,x)∈{0,…,J}×𝒳,Q(k,x)=Q^{(k)}(x),\qquad(k,x)\in\{0,\ldots,J\}\times\mathcal{X},

and assume Q∼𝒢​𝒫​(m,K),Q\sim\mathcal{GP}(m,K), with task-specific mean functions m⁡(k,x)=m(k)​(x).m(k,x)=m^{(k)}(x). In the common-state–action setting, x=(s,a)x=(s,a). For heterogeneous tasks, we instead use a task-specific representation x=ϕ(k)​(s,a)∈𝒳,x=\phi^{(k)}(s,a)\in\mathcal{X}, where ϕ(k)\phi^{(k)} maps the original state–action space of task kk to a shared representation space 𝒳\mathcal{X}. In this case, the GP model assumes that the modeled Q-function factors through the representation ϕ(k)\phi^{(k)}, whereas the Bellman operator remains defined on the original state and action spaces. Using the notation introduced in Section 2.1, we adopt the separable multi-task covariance structure

K⁡((i,x),(j,x′))=Ktask​(i,j)​kin​(x,x′),K\bigl((i,x),(j,x^{\prime})\bigr)=K_{\mathrm{task}}(i,j)\,k_{\mathrm{in}}(x,x^{\prime}),

which decomposes the covariance into a task-level component and an input-level component. Specifically, Ktask​(i,j)K_{\mathrm{task}}(i,j) governs the prior dependence between tasks ii and jj, whereas kin​(x,x′)k_{\mathrm{in}}(x,x^{\prime}) characterizes similarity between state–action inputs (Bonilla et al., 2007; Alvarez et al., 2012). The off-diagonal entries of 𝐊task\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{task}} characterize prior dependence across tasks. Any structural prior on 𝐊task\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{task}} is restricted to the cone of positive-semidefinite matrices.

For fixed task indices i,ji,j and inputs x,x′x,x^{\prime}, define

vi=K⁡((i,x),(i,x)),vj=K⁡((j,x′),(j,x′)),ci​j=K⁡((i,x),(j,x′)).v_{i}=K\bigl((i,x),(i,x)\bigr),\quad v_{j}=K\bigl((j,x^{\prime}),(j,x^{\prime})\bigr),\quad c_{ij}=K\bigl((i,x),(j,x^{\prime})\bigr).

The finite-dimensional marginal distribution induced by the GP prior is then

[Q(i)​(x)Q(j)​(x′)]∼𝒩⁡([m(i)​(x)m(j)​(x′)],[vici​jci​jvj]).\begin{bmatrix}Q^{(i)}(x)\\ Q^{(j)}(x^{\prime})\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\begin{bmatrix}m^{(i)}(x)\\ m^{(j)}(x^{\prime})\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}v_{i}&c_{ij}\\ c_{ij}&v_{j}\end{bmatrix}\right).

If vi>0v_{i}>0, conditioning on an exact latent evaluation Q(i)​(x)=qQ^{(i)}(x)=q gives

Q(j)​(x′)|Q(i)​(x)=q∼𝒩⁡(m(j)​(x′)+ci​jvi​(q−m(i)​(x)),vj−ci​j2vi).Q^{(j)}(x^{\prime})\mid Q^{(i)}(x)=q\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(m^{(j)}(x^{\prime})+\frac{c_{ij}}{v_{i}}\bigl(q-m^{(i)}(x)\bigr),\;v_{j}-\frac{c_{ij}^{2}}{v_{i}}\right).

Thus, information from task ii affects predictions for task jj through the cross-task covariance ci​jc_{ij}. More generally, suppose that task ii is observed with Gaussian noise,

y=Q(i)​(x)+ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σi2),y=Q^{(i)}(x)+\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{i}^{2}),

where ϵ\epsilon is independent of the latent GP. Then

Q(j)​(x′)|y∼𝒩⁡(m(j)​(x′)+ci​jvi+σi2​(y−m(i)​(x)),vj−ci​j2vi+σi2).Q^{(j)}(x^{\prime})\mid y\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(m^{(j)}(x^{\prime})+\frac{c_{ij}}{v_{i}+\sigma_{i}^{2}}\bigl(y-m^{(i)}(x)\bigr),\;v_{j}-\frac{c_{ij}^{2}}{v_{i}+\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right).

This expression makes explicit that cross-task information sharing depends jointly on the cross-covariance ci​jc_{ij}, the marginal uncertainty viv_{i}, and the observation noise σi2\sigma_{i}^{2}. A large task covariance alone therefore does not imply beneficial transfer; whether source information improves target prediction also depends on the observation model and the compatibility of the corresponding tasks.

Throughout this section, GP conditioning is understood conditional on the kernel and noise hyperparameters, whose dependence is suppressed from the notation. If these hyperparameters are assigned priors and integrated out, the resulting predictive distribution is generally a mixture of Gaussian distributions rather than a single Gaussian. We use m(k)m^{(k)} to denote prior mean functions and μ(k)\mu^{(k)} to denote posterior mean functions. Finally, the GP prior specifies statistical regularity and dependence among the task-specific Q-functions, but does not by itself impose the Bellman fixed-point equations. The reinforcement-learning structure enters through the Bellman-generated responses and the iterative Q-learning updates developed in the subsequent section.

2.4 Multi-task transfer Q-learning

The target task is observed through an offline transition dataset

𝒟off(0)={(st(0),at(0),rt(0),st′(0))}t=1n0.\mathcal{D}^{(0)}_{\mathrm{off}}=\bigl\{(s_{t}^{(0)},a_{t}^{(0)},r_{t}^{(0)},s_{t}^{\prime(0)})\bigr\}_{t=1}^{n_{0}}.

We first describe transfer from labeled source data, for which Gaussian conditioning is exact under the stated observation model, and then extend the construction to Bellman-generated responses. For each k∈[J]k\in[J], let 𝒟(k)={(xt(k),yt(k))}t=1nk\mathcal{D}^{(k)}=\{(x_{t}^{(k)},y_{t}^{(k)})\}_{t=1}^{n_{k}}. The labeled-source model is

yt(k)=Q(k)​(xt(k))+ϵt(k),ϵt(k)∼𝒩⁡(0,σk2),y_{t}^{(k)}=Q^{(k)}(x_{t}^{(k)})+\epsilon_{t}^{(k)},\qquad\epsilon_{t}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{k}^{2}), (6)

where σk2>0\sigma_{k}^{2}>0. Conditional on the inputs, the noises are independent across observations and tasks and independent of the latent functions. Define 𝐗(k)=[x1(k),…,xnk(k)]⊤\mathbf{X}^{(k)}=[x_{1}^{(k)},\ldots,x_{n_{k}}^{(k)}]^{\top} and 𝐲(k)=(y1(k),…,ynk(k))⊤,\mathbf{y}^{(k)}=(y_{1}^{(k)},\ldots,y_{n_{k}}^{(k)})^{\top}, and let 𝐐(k)=Q(k)​(𝐗(k))\mathbf{Q}^{(k)}=Q^{(k)}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)}) denote the vector of latent evaluations. Then

𝐲(k)=𝐐(k)+ϵ(k),ϵ(k)∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,σk2​𝐈nk).\mathbf{y}^{(k)}=\mathbf{Q}^{(k)}+\bm{\epsilon}^{(k)},\qquad\bm{\epsilon}^{(k)}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{n_{k}}). (7)

Let 𝐗(0)\mathbf{X}^{(0)} denote the target inputs and set 𝐐(0)=Q(0)​(𝐗(0))\mathbf{Q}^{(0)}=Q^{(0)}(\mathbf{X}^{(0)}). For i,j∈{0,…,J}i,j\in\{0,\ldots,J\}, define

𝐊(i,j)=Ktask​(i,j)​𝐊in​(𝐗(i),𝐗(j)),[𝐊in​(𝐗,𝐗′)]a​b=kin​(xa,xb′).\mathbf{K}^{(i,j)}=K_{\mathrm{task}}(i,j)\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{X}^{(i)},\mathbf{X}^{(j)}),\qquad[\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{in}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X}^{\prime})]_{ab}=k_{\mathrm{in}}(x_{a},x_{b}^{\prime}).

To condition on all sources simultaneously, stack their responses and prior means in a fixed task order:

𝐲s=((𝐲(1))⊤,…,(𝐲(J))⊤)⊤,𝐦s=((𝐦(1))⊤,…,(𝐦(J))⊤)⊤,𝚺s=diag⁡(σ12​𝐈n1,…,σJ2​𝐈nJ),\mathbf{y}_{s}=\bigl((\mathbf{y}^{(1)})^{\top},\ldots,(\mathbf{y}^{(J)})^{\top}\bigr)^{\top},\quad\mathbf{m}_{s}=\bigl((\mathbf{m}^{(1)})^{\top},\ldots,(\mathbf{m}^{(J)})^{\top}\bigr)^{\top},\quad\bm{\Sigma}_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{n_{1}},\ldots,\sigma_{J}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{n_{J}}),

where 𝐦(k)=m(k)​(𝐗(k))\mathbf{m}^{(k)}=m^{(k)}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)}). Set

𝐊(s,s)=[𝐊(i,j)]i,j=1J,𝐊(0,s)=[𝐊(0,1),…,𝐊(0,J)],𝐊(s,0)=(𝐊(0,s))⊤.\mathbf{K}^{(s,s)}=[\mathbf{K}^{(i,j)}]_{i,j=1}^{J},\quad\mathbf{K}^{(0,s)}=[\mathbf{K}^{(0,1)},\ldots,\mathbf{K}^{(0,J)}],\quad\mathbf{K}^{(s,0)}=(\mathbf{K}^{(0,s)})^{\top}.

Writing XX for the collection of all input locations, we have

[𝐲s𝐐(0)]|X∼𝒩⁡([𝐦s𝐦(0)],[𝐊(s,s)+𝚺s𝐊(s,0)𝐊(0,s)𝐊(0,0)]).\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{y}_{s}\\ \mathbf{Q}^{(0)}\end{bmatrix}\Bigm|X\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{m}_{s}\\ \mathbf{m}^{(0)}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{K}^{(s,s)}+\bm{\Sigma}_{s}&\mathbf{K}^{(s,0)}\\ \mathbf{K}^{(0,s)}&\mathbf{K}^{(0,0)}\end{bmatrix}\right). (8)

Consequently, 𝐐(0)|X,𝐲s∼𝒩⁡(𝝁0|s,𝚺0|s)\mathbf{Q}^{(0)}\mid X,\mathbf{y}_{s}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_{0\mid s},\bm{\Sigma}_{0\mid s}), where

𝝁0|s=𝐦(0)+𝐊(0,s)​(𝐊(s,s)+𝚺s)−1​(𝐲s−𝐦s),\bm{\mu}_{0\mid s}=\mathbf{m}^{(0)}+\mathbf{K}^{(0,s)}\bigl(\mathbf{K}^{(s,s)}+\bm{\Sigma}_{s}\bigr)^{-1}(\mathbf{y}_{s}-\mathbf{m}_{s}),

and

𝚺0|s=𝐊(0,0)−𝐊(0,s)​(𝐊(s,s)+𝚺s)−1​𝐊(s,0).\bm{\Sigma}_{0\mid s}=\mathbf{K}^{(0,0)}-\mathbf{K}^{(0,s)}\bigl(\mathbf{K}^{(s,s)}+\bm{\Sigma}_{s}\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{K}^{(s,0)}.

Positive observation-noise variances ensure that the inverted matrix is positive definite. These expressions retain the cross-source covariance blocks; conditioning separately on each source does not, in general, yield the joint posterior. For a selected source subset S⊆[J]S\subseteq[J], the same construction uses only the corresponding source blocks, while target observations are retained in the subsequent update. The choice S=∅S=\varnothing gives target-only learning. Source selection is developed in Section 3.

When direct source Q-labels are unavailable, the source information is provided through transition data. At iteration ee, we construct the Bellman pseudo-response for task kk as

yt,e(k)=rt(k)+γ​maxa′∈𝒜(k)​Q^e−1(k)​(st′(k),a′),y_{t,e}^{(k)}=r_{t}^{(k)}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}\bigl(s_{t}^{\prime(k)},a^{\prime}\bigr),

and use the same construction for the target task before introducing the conservative modification described below. This corresponds to a fitted Q-iteration step in which the Bellman targets are regressed through the multi-task GP model (Munos and Szepesvári, 2008). To characterize the statistical error introduced by the Bellman update, decompose the pseudo-response as

yt,e(k)=Q∗(k)​(xt(k))+ϵt(k)+bt,e(k),y_{t,e}^{(k)}=Q_{*}^{(k)}\bigl(x_{t}^{(k)}\bigr)+\epsilon_{t}^{(k)}+b_{t,e}^{(k)},

where

ϵt(k)\displaystyle\epsilon_{t}^{(k)} =rt(k)+γ​maxa′∈𝒜(k)​Q∗(k)​(st′(k),a′)−Q∗(k)​(xt(k)),\displaystyle=r_{t}^{(k)}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}Q_{*}^{(k)}\bigl(s_{t}^{\prime(k)},a^{\prime}\bigr)-Q_{*}^{(k)}\bigl(x_{t}^{(k)}\bigr),
bt,e(k)\displaystyle b_{t,e}^{(k)} =γ⁡[maxa′∈𝒜(k)⁡Q^e−1(k)​(st′(k),a′)−maxa′∈𝒜(k)⁡Q∗(k)​(st′(k),a′)].\displaystyle=\gamma\left[\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}\bigl(s_{t}^{\prime(k)},a^{\prime}\bigr)-\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}Q_{*}^{(k)}\bigl(s_{t}^{\prime(k)},a^{\prime}\bigr)\right].

The term ϵt(k)\epsilon_{t}^{(k)} represents the Bellman innovation at the optimal Q-function, whereas bt,e(k)b_{t,e}^{(k)} captures the additional error arising from replacing Q∗(k)Q_{*}^{(k)} by the previous fitted iterate Q^e−1(k)\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}.
By the Bellman optimality equation, 𝔼[ϵt(k)|St(k),At(k)]=0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\epsilon_{t}^{(k)}\,\middle|\,S_{t}^{(k)},A_{t}^{(k)}\right]=0. Moreover, using the elementary inequality

|maxa⁡f⁡(a)−maxa⁡g⁡(a)|≤maxa⁡|f⁡(a)−g⁡(a)|,\left|\max_{a}f(a)-\max_{a}g(a)\right|\leq\max_{a}|f(a)-g(a)|,

the bootstrap error satisfies

|bt,e(k)|≤γ​maxa′∈𝒜(k)​|Q^e−1(k)​(st′(k),a′)−Q∗(k)​(st′(k),a′)|≤γ​‖Q^e−1(k)−Q∗(k)‖∞.\displaystyle|b_{t,e}^{(k)}|\leq\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}\left|\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}\bigl(s_{t}^{\prime(k)},a^{\prime}\bigr)-Q_{*}^{(k)}\bigl(s_{t}^{\prime(k)},a^{\prime}\bigr)\right|\leq\gamma\left\|\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}-Q_{*}^{(k)}\right\|_{\infty}.

Hence, the Bellman decomposition separates a conditionally centered innovation term from a bootstrap error whose magnitude is controlled by the estimation error of the preceding Q-function iterate. This distinction is important for the GP update. Unlike the labeled-source model, the Bellman-generated responses are generally neither conditionally Gaussian nor independent across observations, and the bootstrap term may depend on the same data used to construct Q^e−1(k)\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}. Accordingly, the Gaussian regression model applied to these pseudo-responses is viewed as a working posterior, rather than as the exact Bayesian posterior under the trajectory-generating mechanism. The dependence structure and the stability of the bootstrap error are analyzed in Section 3.

To avoid relying on actions with insufficient support in the target offline data, define the behavior-supported action set

𝒞β​(s)={a∈𝒜:β^​(a∣s)≥τβ},\mathcal{C}_{\beta}(s)=\left\{a\in\mathcal{A}:\widehat{\beta}(a\mid s)\geq\tau_{\beta}\right\},

where β^​(a∣s)\widehat{\beta}(a\mid s) is the estimated target behavior policy and τβ>0\tau_{\beta}>0 is a support threshold. We assume that 𝒞β​(s)\mathcal{C}_{\beta}(s) is nonempty for every state encountered by the learning procedure. Restricting Bellman maximization to 𝒞β​(s)\mathcal{C}_{\beta}(s) limits the use of poorly supported actions, while posterior uncertainty is incorporated through a pessimistic value adjustment, following the general principle of conservative offline reinforcement learning (Fujimoto et al., 2019; Jin et al., 2021). At iteration e−1e-1, define the pessimistic target score

Qe−1−​(s,a)=μe−1(0)​(s,a)−αpess​σe−1(0)​(s,a),Q_{e-1}^{-}(s,a)=\mu_{e-1}^{(0)}(s,a)-\alpha_{\mathrm{pess}}\sigma_{e-1}^{(0)}(s,a), (9)

where αpess≥0\alpha_{\mathrm{pess}}\geq 0 controls the strength of the uncertainty penalty. Here σe−1(0)​(s,a)\sigma_{e-1}^{(0)}(s,a) denotes the posterior standard deviation of the latent target Q-function, rather than the predictive standard deviation of a noisy observation. The corresponding conservative Bellman pseudo-response is

yt,e(0),cons=rt(0)+γ​maxa′∈𝒞β​(st′(0))​Qe−1−​(st′(0),a′).y_{t,e}^{(0),\mathrm{cons}}=r_{t}^{(0)}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta}(s_{t}^{\prime(0)})}Q_{e-1}^{-}\bigl(s_{t}^{\prime(0)},a^{\prime}\bigr). (10)

Thus, the target update combines two forms of regularization: action restriction controls extrapolation outside the empirical support of the target behavior policy, whereas the pessimistic term penalizes state–action pairs with large posterior uncertainty.

At iteration ee, let 𝐲~e\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}_{e} denote the vector obtained by stacking the source responses and the current target pseudo-responses. Each observation is paired with its task index, so we write the augmented input as ze,u=(ku,xu),u=1,…,Ne,z_{e,u}=(k_{u},x_{u}),~u=1,\ldots,N_{e}, where ku∈{0,…,J}k_{u}\in\{0,\ldots,J\} denotes the task associated with the uuth observation. Define the corresponding prior-mean vector and joint Gram matrix by

𝐦~e=(m(ku)​(xu))u=1Neand𝐊e=[K⁡(ze,u,ze,v)]u,v=1Ne.\widetilde{\mathbf{m}}_{e}=\bigl(m^{(k_{u})}(x_{u})\bigr)_{u=1}^{N_{e}}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf{K}_{e}=\bigl[K(z_{e,u},z_{e,v})\bigr]_{u,v=1}^{N_{e}}.

Let 𝚲e=diag⁡(νe,12,…,νe,Ne2)≻0\bm{\Lambda}_{e}=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\nu_{e,1}^{2},\ldots,\nu_{e,N_{e}}^{2}\bigr)\succ 0 denote the diagonal working-noise covariance matrix. For directly observed source labels, the corresponding entries are given by their observation-noise variances. For a target pseudo-response constructed at input xx, we set νe2​(x)=λ+[σe−1(0)​(x)]2,λ>0.\nu_{e}^{2}(x)=\lambda+\bigl[\sigma_{e-1}^{(0)}(x)\bigr]^{2},~\lambda>0. Source pseudo-responses in the transition-only setting are assigned analogous positive working variances. These quantities are used for regularization in the GP update and are not identified with the true conditional variances of the Bellman innovations. For a target query xx, define the covariance vector 𝐤0,e​(x)=(K⁡(ze,u,(0,x)))u=1Ne.\mathbf{k}_{0,e}(x)=\bigl(K(z_{e,u},(0,x))\bigr)_{u=1}^{N_{e}}. Conditioning the multi-task GP on the stacked observations gives

μe(0)​(x)\displaystyle\mu_{e}^{(0)}(x) =m(0)​(x)+𝐤0,e​(x)⊤​(𝐊e+𝚲e)−1​(𝐲~e−𝐦~e),\displaystyle=m^{(0)}(x)+\mathbf{k}_{0,e}(x)^{\top}(\mathbf{K}_{e}+\bm{\Lambda}_{e})^{-1}\bigl(\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}_{e}-\widetilde{\mathbf{m}}_{e}\bigr), (11)
[σe(0)​(x)]2\displaystyle\bigl[\sigma_{e}^{(0)}(x)\bigr]^{2} =K⁡((0,x),(0,x))−𝐤0,e​(x)⊤​(𝐊e+𝚲e)−1​𝐤0,e​(x).\displaystyle=K\bigl((0,x),(0,x)\bigr)-\mathbf{k}_{0,e}(x)^{\top}(\mathbf{K}_{e}+\bm{\Lambda}_{e})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_{0,e}(x).

The same conditioning formulas apply to a source task kk after replacing the query index 00 by kk, and we set Q^e(k)=μe(k).\widehat{Q}_{e}^{(k)}=\mu_{e}^{(k)}. In the transition-only setting, source pseudo-responses are updated at each Bellman iteration. For a given transition, the newly computed pseudo-response replaces its previous value rather than being treated as an additional independent observation.

After EE iterations, the target policy is defined by

πoff​(s)=arg⁡maxa∈𝒞β​(s)​{μE(0)​(s,a)−αpess​σE(0)​(s,a)}.\pi_{\mathrm{off}}(s)=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta}(s)}\left\{\mu_{E}^{(0)}(s,a)-\alpha_{\mathrm{pess}}\sigma_{E}^{(0)}(s,a)\right\}. (12)

The quantity μe(0)−αpess​σe(0)\mu_{e}^{(0)}-\alpha_{\mathrm{pess}}\sigma_{e}^{(0)} serves as a pessimistic value score. Its interpretation as a formal lower confidence bound requires additional calibration conditions. Action restriction, posterior pessimism, and source selection play distinct roles: they control target-data support, predictive uncertainty, and potentially harmful cross-task transfer, respectively. The theoretical analysis therefore treats coverage, regression accuracy, bootstrap stability, and transfer selection as separate components.

3 Selection consistency

3.1 Target-aware transfer selection consistency

In this section, we study the consistency of target-aware source selection under Bellman bootstrapping. Candidate source subsets are evaluated according to their predictive contribution to the target task, and the primary question is whether the resulting selection rule asymptotically eliminates target-risk-suboptimal subsets. Accordingly, the theoretical objective is concentration on a target-risk oracle class rather than, in general, recovery of a predetermined source subset. The analysis requires both control of Bellman-bootstrap perturbations and sufficient predictive-score separation between oracle and suboptimal subsets. Exact recovery of a unique source subset additionally requires an identifying target-risk gap. For heterogeneous tasks, we assume that the shared representations preserve the optimal values,

Q∗(k)(s,a)=q∗(k)(ϕ(k)(s,a)),k=0,…,J,Q_{*}^{(k)}(s,a)=q_{*}^{(k)}\bigl(\phi^{(k)}(s,a)\bigr),\qquad k=0,\ldots,J,

and retain the convention Q∗(k)​(x)=q∗(k)​(x)Q_{*}^{(k)}(x)=q_{*}^{(k)}(x) on the represented domain. Bellman maximization remains defined on the native action spaces, and we write V∗(k)​(s)=maxa∈𝒜(k)⁡Q∗(k)​(s,a)V_{*}^{(k)}(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}Q_{*}^{(k)}(s,a). All sampling statements below are with respect to the true joint trajectory law ℙ⋆\mathbb{P}_{\star}.

At iteration ee, every candidate S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J} is evaluated against the same target response vector 𝐘e(0)\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)} from Section 2.4. The response-construction rule and the target working-noise matrix 𝚲0,e≻0\bm{\Lambda}_{0,e}\succ 0 are held common across candidates. Let 𝒞e\mathscr{C}_{e} contain all input locations, source pseudo-responses, and fitting information treated as fixed at this selection step. For fixed GP hyperparameters, let 𝝁0,S,e\bm{\mu}_{0,S,e} and 𝚺0,S,e\bm{\Sigma}_{0,S,e} be the source-conditioned moments of the target latent evaluations. These moments are obtained by jointly conditioning on the source blocks indexed by SS, retaining the cross-source covariances (Bonilla et al., 2007). The corresponding target predictive density is

pS,e(⋅∣𝒞e)=𝒩n0(𝝁0,S,e,𝚺0,S,e+𝚲0,e).p_{S,e}(\,\cdot\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})=\mathcal{N}_{n_{0}}\!\left(\bm{\mu}_{0,S,e},\bm{\Sigma}_{0,S,e}+\bm{\Lambda}_{0,e}\right).

Given a subset prior Π⁡(S)>0\Pi(S)>0, define

Πe​(S∣Ye,X)=Π⁡(S)​pS,e​(𝐘e(0)∣𝒞e)∑U∈𝒮JΠ⁡(U)​pU,e​(𝐘e(0)∣𝒞e).\Pi_{e}(S\mid Y_{e},X)=\frac{\Pi(S)\,p_{S,e}(\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)}\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})}{\displaystyle\sum_{U\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\Pi(U)\,p_{U,e}(\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)}\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})}. (13)

This predictive-score update defines a working subset posterior; it need not coincide with the posterior under the full trajectory likelihood. Let Q^S,eMT\widehat{Q}_{S,e}^{\mathrm{MT}} denote the target posterior mean after additionally conditioning on 𝐘e(0)\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)}. Selection is assessed through the target risk R0R_{0} defined in Section 2.1, applied to this fitted estimator rather than to the source-conditioned predictive mean. The comparator Q^eST\widehat{Q}_{e}^{\mathrm{ST}} is a separately specified target-only fit with source-free response construction and tuning. It coincides with the empty-subset fit only when these components also coincide. The oracle class introduced below is defined by target risk, not by task-covariance magnitude or marginal input similarity.

For an oracle reference S⋆S^{\star} and a candidate SS, define

KL0,e​(S⋆,S∣𝒞e)=∫ℝn0pS⋆,e​(𝐲∣𝒞e)​log⁡pS⋆,e​(𝐲∣𝒞e)pS,e​(𝐲∣𝒞e)​𝑑𝐲.\mathrm{KL}_{0,e}(S^{\star},S\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n_{0}}}p_{S^{\star},e}(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})\log\frac{p_{S^{\star},e}(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})}{p_{S,e}(\mathbf{y}\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{y}. (14)

This quantity measures the separation between the two working predictive distributions under the reference predictive model. To characterize the corresponding predictive-score separation under the actual trajectory law ℙ⋆\mathbb{P}_{\star}, define, whenever the conditional expectation exists,

Δ0,e​(S⋆,S∣𝒞e)=𝔼⋆​[log⁡pS⋆,e​(𝐘e(0)∣𝒞e)pS,e​(𝐘e(0)∣𝒞e)|𝒞e].\Delta_{0,e}(S^{\star},S\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})=\mathbb{E}_{\star}\!\left[\log\frac{p_{S^{\star},e}(\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)}\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})}{p_{S,e}(\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)}\mid\mathscr{C}_{e})}\,\middle|\,\mathscr{C}_{e}\right]. (15)

By construction, −Δ0,e-\Delta_{0,e} is the conditional expected log predictive odds of SS relative to S⋆S^{\star}. If pS⋆,e(⋅∣𝒞e)p_{S^{\star},e}(\,\cdot\mid\mathscr{C}_{e}) coincides with the true conditional law of 𝐘e(0)\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)}, then Δ0,e=KL0,e\Delta_{0,e}=\mathrm{KL}_{0,e} and is therefore nonnegative. Under model misspecification, this identity no longer holds, and Δ0,e\Delta_{0,e} need not be nonnegative. Establishing selection consistency therefore requires separation in expected predictive score under ℙ⋆\mathbb{P}_{\star}, together with uniform control of stochastic score fluctuations on the same scale. Predictive KL separation alone is insufficient unless a valid link to the corresponding expected-score separation under the true data-generating law is established. Related likelihood-ratio theory for dependent and misspecified models provides a useful framework (Shalizi, 2009), but the required conditions and concentration bounds must be verified for the predictive update in (13).

Write Zt(k)=(St(k),At(k),Rt(k),St+1(k))Z_{t}^{(k)}=(S_{t}^{(k)},A_{t}^{(k)},R_{t}^{(k)},S_{t+1}^{(k)}), and let ϵt(k)\epsilon_{t}^{(k)} and bt,e(k)b_{t,e}^{(k)} denote the Bellman innovation and bootstrap remainder of Section 2.4, respectively. We impose the following sampling conditions.

Assumption 1 (Geometric absolute regularity).

For each k∈{0,…,J}k\in\{0,\ldots,J\}, the transition process {Zt(k)}t≥1\{Z_{t}^{(k)}\}_{t\geq 1} is stationary. For sigma-fields 𝒰\mathcal{U} and 𝒱\mathcal{V}, define

β⁡(𝒰,𝒱)=12​sup{Ai},{Bj}∑i=1I∑j=1L|ℙ⋆​(Ai∩Bj)−ℙ⋆​(Ai)​ℙ⋆​(Bj)|,\beta(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V})=\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\{A_{i}\},\{B_{j}\}}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\left|\mathbb{P}_{\star}(A_{i}\cap B_{j})-\mathbb{P}_{\star}(A_{i})\mathbb{P}_{\star}(B_{j})\right|,

where the supremum is over finite measurable partitions of the probability space with Ai∈𝒰A_{i}\in\mathcal{U} and Bj∈𝒱B_{j}\in\mathcal{V}. With ℱab,(k)=σ(Zt(k):a≤t≤b)\mathcal{F}_{a}^{b,(k)}=\sigma(Z_{t}^{(k)}:a\leq t\leq b), set

βk​(ℓ)=supt≥1β⁡(ℱ1t,(k),ℱt+ℓ∞,(k)).\beta_{k}(\ell)=\sup_{t\geq 1}\beta\!\left(\mathcal{F}_{1}^{t,(k)},\mathcal{F}_{t+\ell}^{\infty,(k)}\right).

There exist task-uniform constants Cmix<∞C_{\mathrm{mix}}<\infty and ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) such that βk​(ℓ)≤Cmix​ρℓ\beta_{k}(\ell)\leq C_{\mathrm{mix}}\rho^{\ell} for every ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1.

Assumption 2 (Conditionally sub-Gaussian Bellman innovations).

For each task kk, let the pre-transition filtration be

ℱt(k)=σ⁡(S1(k),A1(k),(Ru(k),Su+1(k),Au+1(k))1≤u<t).\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}=\sigma\!\left(S_{1}^{(k)},A_{1}^{(k)},(R_{u}^{(k)},S_{u+1}^{(k)},A_{u+1}^{(k)})_{1\leq u<t}\right).

The innovation ϵt(k)\epsilon_{t}^{(k)} is ℱt+1(k)\mathscr{F}_{t+1}^{(k)}-measurable and, for a finite variance proxy σk2>0\sigma_{k}^{2}>0, satisfies

𝔼⋆[ϵt(k)∣ℱt(k)]=0,𝔼⋆[exp(uϵt(k))∣ℱt(k)]≤exp(u2​σk22),u∈ℝ.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\star}[\epsilon_{t}^{(k)}\mid\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}]=0,\quad\mathbb{E}_{\star}\!\left[\exp(u\epsilon_{t}^{(k)})\mid\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}\right]\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{u^{2}\sigma_{k}^{2}}{2}\right),\quad u\in\mathbb{R}.

Assumption 1 uses the absolute-regularity coefficient (Bradley, 2005) for the full transition process, including rewards and successor states. Neither assumption imposes cross-task independence or state–action coverage. The proxy σk2\sigma_{k}^{2} concerns the innovation at the Bellman fixed point and is distinct from the GP working-noise variance. In particular, Assumption 2 does not extend the same centering or sub-Gaussian condition to ϵt(k)+bt,e(k)\epsilon_{t}^{(k)}+b_{t,e}^{(k)}.

For the conservative target response introduced in Section 2.4, write

Yt,e(0),cons=Q∗(0)​(Xt(0))+ϵt(0)+b~t,e(0),Y_{t,e}^{(0),\mathrm{cons}}=Q_{*}^{(0)}(X_{t}^{(0)})+\epsilon_{t}^{(0)}+\widetilde{b}_{t,e}^{(0)},

where b~t,e(0)\widetilde{b}_{t,e}^{(0)} collects the discrepancy induced by using the behavior-supported action set and the pessimistic value estimate in place of the optimal continuation value. Let 𝒞β(0)​(s)\mathcal{C}_{\beta}^{(0)}(s) denote the nonempty behavior-supported action set for the target task, and define the corresponding coverage gap by

cβ(0)​(s)=V∗(0)​(s)−maxa∈𝒞β(0)​(s)⁡Q∗(0)​(s,a).c_{\beta}^{(0)}(s)=V_{*}^{(0)}(s)-\max_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta}^{(0)}(s)}Q_{*}^{(0)}(s,a).

Since 𝒞β(0)​(s)⊆𝒜(0)\mathcal{C}_{\beta}^{(0)}(s)\subseteq\mathcal{A}^{(0)}, we have cβ(0)​(s)≥0c_{\beta}^{(0)}(s)\geq 0. The conservative bootstrap remainder then satisfies the pathwise bound

|b~t,e(0)|≤γ⁡{‖μe−1(0)−Q∗(0)‖∞+cβ(0)​(St+1(0))+αpess​supa′∈𝒞β(0)​(St+1(0))σe−1(0)​(St+1(0),a′)}.|\widetilde{b}_{t,e}^{(0)}|\leq\gamma\Bigl\{\|\mu_{e-1}^{(0)}-Q_{*}^{(0)}\|_{\infty}+c_{\beta}^{(0)}(S_{t+1}^{(0)})+\alpha_{\mathrm{pess}}\sup_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta}^{(0)}(S_{t+1}^{(0)})}\sigma_{e-1}^{(0)}(S_{t+1}^{(0)},a^{\prime})\Bigr\}.

This decomposition shows that the conservative update introduces two additional sources of error beyond the fitted-value approximation: loss due to restricted action coverage and the uncertainty penalty induced by pessimism. Consequently, extending the bootstrap-stability analysis from the unconstrained Bellman response to the conservative response requires both terms to be controlled at the relevant asymptotic scale.

Fix a task kk. Let wt(k)​(s,a)w_{t}^{(k)}(s,a) denote state–action-specific nonnegative weights satisfying

wt(k)​(s,a)≥0,∑t=1nkwt(k)​(s,a)=1.w_{t}^{(k)}(s,a)\geq 0,\qquad\sum_{t=1}^{n_{k}}w_{t}^{(k)}(s,a)=1.

Given a fixed measurable function gk:𝒮(k)→ℝg_{k}:\mathcal{S}^{(k)}\to\mathbb{R} with ‖gk‖∞≤B\|g_{k}\|_{\infty}\leq B, define the conditional transition estimator

𝔼^nk(k)[gk(S′)∣s,a]=∑t=1nkwt(k)(s,a)gk(St+1(k)).\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{k}}^{(k)}[g_{k}(S^{\prime})\mid s,a]=\sum_{t=1}^{n_{k}}w_{t}^{(k)}(s,a)\,g_{k}(S_{t+1}^{(k)}).

In discrete state–action spaces, a natural choice is to use normalized visit indicators associated with observations satisfying (St(k),At(k))=(s,a)(S_{t}^{(k)},A_{t}^{(k)})=(s,a). In continuous settings, the weights may instead be induced by a conditional regression or smoothing procedure, whose approximation and coverage properties must be specified. Conditioning on (s,a)(s,a) is essential, since an unweighted trajectory average generally estimates a marginal successor-state expectation rather than the transition expectation conditional on the current state–action pair. Using the same weighting scheme, define the empirical Bellman operator by

(𝒯^nk(k)​Q)​(s,a)=∑t=1nkwt(k)​(s,a)​[Rt(k)+γ​maxa′∈𝒜(k)⁡Q⁡(St+1(k),a′)].(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{n_{k}}^{(k)}Q)(s,a)=\sum_{t=1}^{n_{k}}w_{t}^{(k)}(s,a)\left[R_{t}^{(k)}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}Q(S_{t+1}^{(k)},a^{\prime})\right].

This operator is used to isolate the sampling component of a Bellman update from the error introduced by the regression fit. It is therefore an analytical device and need not coincide with the GP regression estimator. Using the population Bellman operator 𝒯(k)\mathcal{T}^{(k)} defined in Section 2.2, the one-step Bellman residual admits the decomposition

Q^e(k)−𝒯(k)​Q^e−1(k)=(Q^e(k)−𝒯^nk(k)​Q^e−1(k))+(𝒯^nk(k)​Q^e−1(k)−𝒯(k)​Q^e−1(k)).\widehat{Q}_{e}^{(k)}-\mathcal{T}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}={}\left(\widehat{Q}_{e}^{(k)}-\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{n_{k}}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}\right)+\left(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{n_{k}}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}-\mathcal{T}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}\right). (16)

The first term represents the regression and function-approximation error of the fitted Bellman update, whereas the second measures the conditional sampling error arising from estimation of the Bellman expectation using the observed trajectory (Munos and Szepesvári, 2008). An additional difficulty arises when the same trajectory is reused across Bellman iterations. In this setting, the continuation function gk,e​(s′)=maxa′∈𝒜(k)⁡Q^e−1(k)​(s′,a′)g_{k,e}(s^{\prime})=\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}) depends on the data used to construct the empirical Bellman operator. Consequently, a concentration result established only for a fixed function gkg_{k} cannot be applied directly to the fitted iterate. Uniform concentration over a suitably controlled function class, a valid sample-splitting construction, or another explicit treatment of this dependence is therefore required. Any effective sample size nk,effn_{k,\mathrm{eff}} used below is understood to arise from the particular concentration argument being applied and does not replace the state–action coverage conditions required for conditional estimation.

The following results establish control of the two error components in (16). We first derive concentration bounds for dependent Markov observations and then obtain a uniform finite-rank GP regression bound that remains valid for data-dependent Bellman iterates. Combining these results yields uniform control of the one-step Bellman residual. This bound is subsequently propagated through the Bellman contraction to establish bootstrap stability. The finite-rank analysis requires additional Markov-contraction and nondegenerate feature-design conditions beyond geometric β\beta-mixing and does not imply a dimension-free parametric rate for a general GP kernel.

Lemma 1 (Concentration for bounded Markov averages).

Let U1,…,UNU_{1},\ldots,U_{N} be a possibly inhomogeneous Markov chain on a standard Borel space, with an arbitrary initial distribution. Let PiP_{i} denote the transition kernel from UiU_{i} to Ui+1U_{i+1}, and define

θi=supu,v∥Pi(⋅∣u)−Pi(⋅∣v)∥TV,i=1,…,N−1,\theta_{i}=\sup_{u,v}\bigl\|P_{i}(\cdot\mid u)-P_{i}(\cdot\mid v)\bigr\|_{\mathrm{TV}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,N-1,

where ‖μ−ν‖TV:=supA|μ⁡(A)−ν⁡(A)|\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|. Set

ci,N=1+∑j=i+1N∏ℓ=ij−1θℓ,MN=max1≤i≤N⁡ci,N,c_{i,N}=1+\sum_{j=i+1}^{N}\prod_{\ell=i}^{j-1}\theta_{\ell},\qquad M_{N}=\max_{1\leq i\leq N}c_{i,N},

with cN,N=1c_{N,N}=1. Let h1,…,hNh_{1},\ldots,h_{N} be deterministic measurable functions satisfying max1≤i≤N⁡‖hi‖∞≤B\max_{1\leq i\leq N}\|h_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq B for some B>0B>0, and define

FN=1N​∑i=1Nhi​(Ui).F_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}h_{i}(U_{i}).

Then, for every u>0u>0,

ℙ⁡(|FN−𝔼​FN|≥u)≤2​exp⁡{−N2​u28​B2​∑i=1Nci,N2}≤2​exp⁡{−N​u28​B2​MN2}.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigl(|F_{N}-\mathbb{E}F_{N}|\geq u\bigr)\leq 2\exp\!\left\{-\frac{N^{2}u^{2}}{8B^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i,N}^{2}}\right\}\leq 2\exp\!\left\{-\frac{Nu^{2}}{8B^{2}M_{N}^{2}}\right\}. (17)

If θi≤θ\theta_{i}\leq\theta for all ii, with θ∈[0,1)\theta\in[0,1), then

MN≤11−θ.M_{N}\leq\frac{1}{1-\theta}.

The concentration bound does not require stationarity. When the chain is stationary and hi=hh_{i}=h for every ii, the centering simplifies to 𝔼​FN=𝔼⁡[h⁡(U1)]\mathbb{E}F_{N}=\mathbb{E}[h(U_{1})].

The proof is provided in Appendix A.1. The proof uses a direct Doob-martingale argument related to the Markov concentration framework of Kontorovich and Ramanan (2008). To apply the lemma to task kk, suppose that the shifted state–action process Ut=(St+1(k),At+1(k)),t=1,…,N,U_{t}=(S_{t+1}^{(k)},A_{t+1}^{(k)}),~t=1,\ldots,N, is Markov, and define its transition coefficients as in Lemma 1. For a deterministic measurable function gg with ‖g‖∞≤B\|g\|_{\infty}\leq B, taking ht​(s,a)=g​(s)h_{t}(s,a)=g(s) gives

FN=1N​∑t=1Ng⁡(St+1(k)),𝔼​FN=1N​∑t=1N𝔼⁡[g⁡(St+1(k))].F_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}g(S_{t+1}^{(k)}),\qquad\mathbb{E}F_{N}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}[g(S_{t+1}^{(k)})].

The underlying process is taken to be defined through time N+1N+1, although evaluating FNF_{N} does not require observing AN+1(k)A_{N+1}^{(k)}. Under stationarity, the centering reduces to the marginal expectation 𝔼⁡[g⁡(S1(k))]\mathbb{E}[g(S_{1}^{(k)})]. The lemma therefore controls a marginal sampling average rather than the conditional transition estimator at a specified state–action pair. The uniform bound on MNM_{N} applies when the shifted transition kernels satisfy the stated contraction condition, which is not implied by geometric β\beta-mixing alone. Furthermore, the deterministic-function requirement excludes direct substitution of a continuation function fitted to the same trajectory. Lemma 3 addresses this dependence through a uniform argument over the prescribed function classes.

Consider J+1J+1 tasks, each providing NN observations. Let Wt(k)=(St(k),At(k))W_{t}^{(k)}=(S_{t}^{(k)},A_{t}^{(k)}) denote the native state–action process and let Xt(k)=ϕ(k)​(Wt(k))X_{t}^{(k)}=\phi^{(k)}(W_{t}^{(k)}) be its shared representation. The Markov assumption is imposed on Wt(k)W_{t}^{(k)}, not on the represented process Xt(k)X_{t}^{(k)}. A fixed measurable feature map ψ:𝒳→ℝm\psi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} defines the finite-rank input kernel and taskwise design matrices by

kin(x,x′)=ψ(x)⊤ψ(x′),Φk=[ψ(X1(k)),…,ψ(XN(k))]⊤,Ak=Φk⊤Φk.\displaystyle k_{\mathrm{in}}(x,x^{\prime})=\psi(x)^{\top}\psi(x^{\prime}),\quad\Phi_{k}=[\psi(X_{1}^{(k)}),\ldots,\psi(X_{N}^{(k)})]^{\top},\quad A_{k}=\Phi_{k}^{\top}\Phi_{k}.

The feature map ψ\psi is distinct from the task-specific representation maps ϕ(k)\phi^{(k)}. Set

Φ=diag⁡(Φ0,…,ΦJ),A=Φ⊤​Φ=diag⁡(A0,…,AJ),\Phi=\operatorname{diag}(\Phi_{0},\ldots,\Phi_{J}),\quad A=\Phi^{\top}\Phi=\operatorname{diag}(A_{0},\ldots,A_{J}),

and stack the taskwise responses as Y=(Y0⊤,…,YJ⊤)⊤Y=(Y_{0}^{\top},\ldots,Y_{J}^{\top})^{\top}, where Yk=(Y1(k),…,YN(k))⊤Y_{k}=(Y_{1}^{(k)},\ldots,Y_{N}^{(k)})^{\top}. For a block vector v=(v0⊤,…,vJ⊤)⊤v=(v_{0}^{\top},\ldots,v_{J}^{\top})^{\top} and a conformably partitioned matrix H=[Hk​ℓ]H=[H_{k\ell}], define

‖v‖2,∞=maxk⁡‖vk‖2,‖H‖b=max⁡∑ℓ=0Jk⁡‖Hk​ℓ‖op.\|v\|_{2,\infty}=\max_{k}\|v_{k}\|_{2},\quad\|H\|_{\mathrm{b}}=\max_{k}\sum_{\ell=0}^{J}\|H_{k\ell}\|_{\mathrm{op}}.

The matrix norm is submultiplicative and satisfies ‖H​v‖2,∞≤‖H‖b​‖v‖2,∞\|Hv\|_{2,\infty}\leq\|H\|_{\mathrm{b}}\|v\|_{2,\infty}. Under a zero-mean Gaussian coefficient prior with precision Ω=Ktask−1⊗Im\Omega=K_{\mathrm{task}}^{-1}\otimes I_{m}, where Ktask≻0K_{\mathrm{task}}\succ 0, and a common Gaussian working-noise variance λN>0\lambda_{N}>0, the joint posterior mean is

ϑ^=(A+λNΩ)−1Φ⊤Y,f^(k)(x)=ψ(x)⊤ϑ^k.\displaystyle\widehat{\vartheta}=(A+\lambda_{N}\Omega)^{-1}\Phi^{\top}Y,\quad\widehat{f}^{(k)}(x)=\psi(x)^{\top}\widehat{\vartheta}_{k}. (18)

This is the weight-space representation of finite-rank multi-task GP regression (Rasmussen and Williams, 2006; Bonilla et al., 2007). The working variance λN\lambda_{N} is a regularization parameter and need not equal the variance proxy of the actual observation noise. The choice Ω=I(J+1)​m\Omega=I_{(J+1)m} gives independent task fits.

Lemma 2 (Uniform finite-rank GP regression under Markov designs).

Suppose that each native design process {Wt(k)}t=1N\{W_{t}^{(k)}\}_{t=1}^{N} is stationary and satisfies the conditions of Lemma 1, with MN(k)≤MNM_{N}^{(k)}\leq M_{N} for a deterministic bound MNM_{N}. Assume that

supx∈𝒳‖ψ⁡(x)‖2≤κ,Σk=𝔼⁡[ψ⁡(Xt(k))​ψ​(Xt(k))⊤],λmin​(Σk)≥ν>0.\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\|\psi(x)\|_{2}\leq\kappa,\quad\Sigma_{k}=\mathbb{E}[\psi(X_{t}^{(k)})\psi(X_{t}^{(k)})^{\top}],\quad\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{k})\geq\nu>0.

Let the responses satisfy

Yt(k)=ψ​(Xt(k))⊤​ϑk+ξt(k),maxk⁡‖ϑk‖2≤R,Y_{t}^{(k)}=\psi(X_{t}^{(k)})^{\top}\vartheta_{k}+\xi_{t}^{(k)},\quad\max_{k}\|\vartheta_{k}\|_{2}\leq R,

for deterministic coefficients ϑk\vartheta_{k}. For each task, let {ℱt(k)}\{\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}\} be a filtration such that Xt(k)X_{t}^{(k)} is ℱt(k)\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}-measurable, ξt(k)\xi_{t}^{(k)} is ℱt+1(k)\mathscr{F}_{t+1}^{(k)}-measurable, and

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(u​ξt(k))∣ℱt(k)]≤exp⁡(u2​σ22),u∈ℝ.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp(u\xi_{t}^{(k)})\mid\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}\right]\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{u^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}\right),\qquad u\in\mathbb{R}.

Suppose that ‖Ω‖b≤ΛN\|\Omega\|_{\mathrm{b}}\leq\Lambda_{N} and λN​ΛN≤N​ν/4\lambda_{N}\Lambda_{N}\leq N\nu/4. Given δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), assume

N≥128​κ4​MN2ν2​{m​log⁡9+log⁡4​(J+1)δ}.N\geq\frac{128\kappa^{4}M_{N}^{2}}{\nu^{2}}\left\{m\log 9+\log\frac{4(J+1)}{\delta}\right\}. (19)

Define

LN​(δ)=m​log⁡5+log⁡4​(J+1)δ,sN​(δ)=2​σ​κ​2​LN​(δ)N.L_{N}(\delta)=m\log 5+\log\frac{4(J+1)}{\delta},\quad s_{N}(\delta)=2\sigma\kappa\sqrt{\frac{2L_{N}(\delta)}{N}}.

Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

max0≤k≤J⁡‖f^(k)−f(k)‖∞≤4​κν​{sN​(δ)+λN​ΛN​RN},f(k)​(x)=ψ​(x)⊤​ϑk.\max_{0\leq k\leq J}\|\widehat{f}^{(k)}-f^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{4\kappa}{\nu}\left\{s_{N}(\delta)+\frac{\lambda_{N}\Lambda_{N}R}{N}\right\},\quad f^{(k)}(x)=\psi(x)^{\top}\vartheta_{k}. (20)

On the same event, let f^d(k)\widehat{f}_{d}^{(k)} be the fit obtained by replacing YY with Y+dY+d while keeping Φ\Phi, Ω\Omega, and λN\lambda_{N} fixed. Every perturbation satisfying maxk,t⁡|dt(k)|≤a\max_{k,t}|d_{t}^{(k)}|\leq a obeys

maxk⁡‖f^d(k)−f^(k)‖∞≤4​κ2​aν.\max_{k}\|\widehat{f}_{d}^{(k)}-\widehat{f}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{4\kappa^{2}a}{\nu}.

Thus (20) remains valid for the perturbed fit after adding 4​κ2​a/ν4\kappa^{2}a/\nu to its right-hand side. The perturbations may depend on the full dataset.

The proof is provided in Appendix A.2.

Lemma 2 is uniform over tasks and input locations for the stated regression model. Its stochastic term and regularization bias are explicit. In particular, m​ν≤tr⁡(Σk)≤κ2,m\nu\leq\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{k})\leq\kappa^{2}, so a growing feature dimension requires tracking the dependence of κ\kappa and ν\nu on mm. The condition m/N→0m/N\to 0 alone does not remove the dimension dependence from the error bound. The same argument applies to a symmetric positive-semidefinite, possibly data-dependent penalty Ω\Omega when its norm bound holds pathwise. In this extension, the inverse in (18) exists on ℰD\mathcal{E}_{D}. If it is singular on other realizations, the estimator may be defined there as zero without changing the high-probability conclusion. This convention is unnecessary for a positive-definite GP precision. A singular task covariance, learned features, or observation-specific adaptive working variances requires a separate analysis.

Lemma 3 (Uniform Bellman residual control under trajectory reuse).

Retain the design, feature, and regularization conditions of Lemma 2, including (19). For each task kk, let 𝒬k\mathcal{Q}_{k} be a nonempty deterministic class of measurable functions on 𝒮(k)×𝒜(k)\mathcal{S}^{(k)}\times\mathcal{A}^{(k)} that is totally bounded in the supremum norm. Suppose

supq∈𝒬k‖q‖∞≤B,‖Q∗(k)‖∞≤B.\sup_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{k}}\|q\|_{\infty}\leq B,\quad\|Q_{*}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq B.

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(u​ϵt(k))∣ℱt(k)]≤exp⁡(u2​σ22),u∈ℝ,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp(u\epsilon_{t}^{(k)})\mid\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}\right]\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{u^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2}\right),\quad u\in\mathbb{R},

where ℱt(k)\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)} is the pre-transition filtration. For every q∈𝒬kq\in\mathcal{Q}_{k}, suppose that a coefficient vector ϑk​(q)∈ℝm\vartheta_{k}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{m} satisfies

∥ϑk(q)∥2≤RN,sups,a|(𝒯(k)q)(s,a)−ψ(ϕ(k)(s,a))⊤ϑk(q)|≤aN.\displaystyle\|\vartheta_{k}(q)\|_{2}\leq R_{N},\quad\sup_{s,a}\left|(\mathcal{T}^{(k)}q)(s,a)-\psi(\phi^{(k)}(s,a))^{\top}\vartheta_{k}(q)\right|\leq a_{N}. (21)

Yt(k)​(qk)=Rt(k)+γ​maxa∈𝒜(k)​qk​(St+1(k),a).Y_{t}^{(k)}(q_{k})=R_{t}^{(k)}+\gamma\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}q_{k}(S_{t+1}^{(k)},a).

Let ϑ^​(𝐪)\widehat{\vartheta}(\bm{q}) be the coefficient estimate in (18) for these stacked responses, and set

𝔉N(k)​(𝒒)​(s,a)=ψ​(ϕ(k)​(s,a))⊤​ϑ^k​(𝒒).\mathfrak{F}_{N}^{(k)}(\bm{q})(s,a)=\psi(\phi^{(k)}(s,a))^{\top}\widehat{\vartheta}_{k}(\bm{q}).

Given a deterministic ε>0\varepsilon>0, define

HN(ε)=maxklog𝒩(ε,𝒬k,∥⋅∥∞),σB2=2σ2+8γ2B2,ℓN=mlog5+HN(ε)+log4​(J+1)δ,\displaystyle H_{N}(\varepsilon)=\max_{k}\log\mathcal{N}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{Q}_{k},\|\cdot\|_{\infty}),\quad\sigma_{B}^{2}=2\sigma^{2}+8\gamma^{2}B^{2},\quad\ell_{N}=m\log 5+H_{N}(\varepsilon)+\log\frac{4(J+1)}{\delta},
