sup𝒒∈𝒬maxk⁡‖𝔉N(k)​(𝒒)−𝒯(k)​qk‖∞≤η¯N​(δ,ε),\sup_{\bm{q}\in\mathcal{Q}}\max_{k}\|\mathfrak{F}_{N}^{(k)}(\bm{q})-\mathcal{T}^{(k)}q_{k}\|_{\infty}\leq\overline{\eta}_{N}(\delta,\varepsilon), (22)

where

η¯N​(δ,ε)=(1+4​κ2ν)​aN+4​κν​{2​σB​κ​2​ℓNN+2​γ​κ​ε+λN​ΛN​RNN}.\displaystyle\overline{\eta}_{N}(\delta,\varepsilon)={}\left(1+\frac{4\kappa^{2}}{\nu}\right)a_{N}+\frac{4\kappa}{\nu}\left\{2\sigma_{B}\kappa\sqrt{\frac{2\ell_{N}}{N}}+2\gamma\kappa\varepsilon+\frac{\lambda_{N}\Lambda_{N}R_{N}}{N}\right\}.

On this same event, every fitted iteration satisfying 𝐐^e−1∈𝒬\widehat{\bm{Q}}_{e-1}\in\mathcal{Q} and 𝐐^e=𝔉N​(𝐐^e−1)\widehat{\bm{Q}}_{e}=\mathfrak{F}_{N}(\widehat{\bm{Q}}_{e-1}) obeys

maxk⁡‖Q^e(k)−𝒯(k)​Q^e−1(k)‖∞≤η¯N​(δ,ε).\max_{k}\|\widehat{Q}_{e}^{(k)}-\mathcal{T}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq\overline{\eta}_{N}(\delta,\varepsilon).

The event is common to all such iterations, even when the iterates are constructed from the same trajectories used in the regression.

The proof is provided in Appendix A.3.

Condition (21) requires the finite-rank feature space to approximate the Bellman image of every candidate continuation function. It is an approximate Bellman-completeness condition, with exact completeness when aN=0a_{N}=0. Neither this property nor membership of the fitted iterates in the prescribed classes follows from bounded rewards alone. For example, the clipped feature class

𝒬k={(s,a)⟼clip[−B,B]⁡(ψ​(ϕ(k)​(s,a))⊤​θ):‖θ‖2≤L}\mathcal{Q}_{k}=\left\{(s,a)\longmapsto\operatorname{clip}_{[-B,B]}\bigl(\psi(\phi^{(k)}(s,a))^{\top}\theta\bigr):\|\theta\|_{2}\leq L\right\}

satisfies

HN​(ε)≤m​log⁡(1+2​κ​Lε).H_{N}(\varepsilon)\leq m\log\!\left(1+\frac{2\kappa L}{\varepsilon}\right).

This follows by covering the coefficient ball at radius ε/κ\varepsilon/\kappa and using the nonexpansiveness of clipping. Applying the lemma with this class requires verifying the coefficient constraint for the actual iterates or accounting explicitly for a projection step. Clipping alone ensures bounded output values but does not establish the coefficient constraint. If ‖𝒯(k)​q‖∞≤B\|\mathcal{T}^{(k)}q\|_{\infty}\leq B, clipping a fitted output to [−B,B][-B,B] cannot increase its distance from 𝒯(k)​q\mathcal{T}^{(k)}q, so it preserves the residual bound. A sufficient condition is |R(k)​(s,a)|≤Rmax|R^{(k)}(s,a)|\leq R_{\max} and B≥Rmax/(1−γ)B\geq R_{\max}/(1-\gamma), because ‖𝒯(k)​q‖∞≤Rmax+γ​B≤B\|\mathcal{T}^{(k)}q\|_{\infty}\leq R_{\max}+\gamma B\leq B. Here the bound is on the conditional mean reward and does not require bounded realized rewards. With fixed mm and uniformly bounded κ\kappa, ν−1\nu^{-1}, σB\sigma_{B}, RNR_{N}, ΛN\Lambda_{N}, and LL, setting aN=0a_{N}=0, λN=O⁡(1)\lambda_{N}=O(1), and ε=N−1\varepsilon=N^{-1} gives

η¯N​(δ,N−1)=O⁡(m​log⁡N+log⁡((J+1)/δ)N),\overline{\eta}_{N}(\delta,N^{-1})=O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{m\log N+\log((J+1)/\delta)}{N}}\right),

subject to (19) and the preceding entropy bound. When mm grows, the dependence on κ\kappa, ν\nu, RNR_{N}, and ΛN\Lambda_{N} must also be retained. The high-probability event is simultaneous over all iterations whose inputs remain in the prescribed classes. Trajectory reuse therefore requires uniformity over the continuation functions rather than an interpretation of successive Bellman responses as independent observations (Munos and Szepesvári, 2008).

The next theorem converts the uniform residual control of Lemma 3 into consistency of the fitted Q-iterates. The error-propagation argument is deterministic, while the statistical guarantee uses the common high-probability event established in that lemma.

Theorem 1 (Bootstrap consistency).

For each task kk, let 𝒯(k)\mathcal{T}^{(k)} be a γ\gamma-contraction in the supremum norm, with fixed point Q∗(k)Q_{*}^{(k)}, where γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Define

De,N=maxk⁡‖Q^e(k)−Q∗(k)‖∞,ηe,N=maxk⁡‖Q^e(k)−𝒯(k)​Q^e−1(k)‖∞.D_{e,N}=\max_{k}\|\widehat{Q}_{e}^{(k)}-Q_{*}^{(k)}\|_{\infty},\quad\eta_{e,N}=\max_{k}\|\widehat{Q}_{e}^{(k)}-\mathcal{T}^{(k)}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}.

Then, for every e≥1e\geq 1,

De,N≤γe​D0,N+∑j=1eγe−j​ηj,N.D_{e,N}\leq\gamma^{e}D_{0,N}+\sum_{j=1}^{e}\gamma^{e-j}\eta_{j,N}. (23)

Suppose further that the conditions of Lemma 3 hold up to iteration ENE_{N} and that D0,N≤D0D_{0,N}\leq D_{0} almost surely. Then, with probability at least 1−δN1-\delta_{N},

De,N≤γe​D0+1−γe1−γ​η¯N,1≤e≤EN,D_{e,N}\leq\gamma^{e}D_{0}+\frac{1-\gamma^{e}}{1-\gamma}\,\overline{\eta}_{N},\qquad 1\leq e\leq E_{N}, (24)

where η¯N\overline{\eta}_{N} is the uniform one-step residual bound from Lemma 3. If

δN→0,η¯N→0,γEN​D0→0,\delta_{N}\to 0,\qquad\overline{\eta}_{N}\to 0,\qquad\gamma^{E_{N}}D_{0}\to 0,

then

DEN,N→ℙ0.D_{E_{N},N}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0.

The proof is provided in Appendix A.4.

Corollary 1 (Stability of the Bellman bootstrap remainder).

Under Theorem 1, define, for e≥1e\geq 1,

bt,e(k)=γ⁡{maxa∈𝒜(k)⁡Q^e−1(k)​(St+1(k),a)−maxa∈𝒜(k)⁡Q∗(k)​(St+1(k),a)}.b_{t,e}^{(k)}=\gamma\left\{\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}(S_{t+1}^{(k)},a)-\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}Q_{*}^{(k)}(S_{t+1}^{(k)},a)\right\}.

Then, for every k,t,ek,t,e,

|bt,e(k)|≤γ​De−1,N.|b_{t,e}^{(k)}|\leq\gamma D_{e-1,N}. (25)

Hence, on the event ℰN\mathcal{E}_{N} of Theorem 1,

supk,t|bt,e(k)|≤γ​re−1,N,1≤e≤EN.\sup_{k,t}|b_{t,e}^{(k)}|\leq\gamma r_{e-1,N},\quad 1\leq e\leq E_{N}. (26)

Consequently, for any deterministic sequence eN≤ENe_{N}\leq E_{N},

reN−1,N→0,δN→0r_{e_{N}-1,N}\to 0,\quad\delta_{N}\to 0

imply

supk,t|bt,eN(k)|→ℙ0.\sup_{k,t}|b_{t,e_{N}}^{(k)}|\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0.

Suppose additionally that the fitted update is deterministically restricted to the supremum-norm ball of radius BB, for example by clipping or projection, and that ‖Q∗(k)‖∞≤B\|Q_{*}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq B for every task. Then

supk,t𝔼⁡[(bt,e(k))2]≤γ2​{re−1,N2+4​B2​δN},1≤e≤EN.\sup_{k,t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(b_{t,e}^{(k)})^{2}\right]\leq\gamma^{2}\left\{r_{e-1,N}^{2}+4B^{2}\delta_{N}\right\},\quad 1\leq e\leq E_{N}. (27)

Therefore, reN−1,N→0r_{e_{N}-1,N}\to 0 and δN→0\delta_{N}\to 0 also imply

supk,t𝔼⁡[(bt,eN(k))2]⟶0.\sup_{k,t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(b_{t,e_{N}}^{(k)})^{2}\right]\longrightarrow 0.

The proof is provided in Appendix A.5. The preceding results concern the Bellman remainder associated with the unconstrained update. For a conservative target update, the same pathwise error-propagation argument remains valid, but the corresponding one-step residual must also account for the coverage gap and the pessimism penalty identified in (3.1). Lemma 1 suggests the quantity N/(MN(k))2N/(M_{N}^{(k)})^{2} as a concentration scale for bounded marginal averages. It should not, however, be interpreted automatically as the effective sample size of a conditional Bellman regression problem. Whenever a task-specific quantity nk,effn_{k,\mathrm{eff}} has been justified by the relevant concentration analysis, one may introduce Neff=n0,eff+∑k=1Jnk,effN_{\mathrm{eff}}=n_{0,\mathrm{eff}}+\sum_{k=1}^{J}n_{k,\mathrm{eff}} as a bookkeeping quantity. Additional transfer and coverage conditions are required before this sum can be interpreted as target information available for learning. The results above therefore establish control of Bellman bootstrapping, but do not by themselves imply consistent source selection. The latter additionally requires alignment between target risk and predictive scores, together with uniform control of the corresponding score fluctuations.

The preceding results establish control of the Bellman bootstrap remainder under dependent trajectory sampling. We next turn to source selection and study whether the resulting predictive scores consistently favor population-optimal source subsets.

3.2 Predictive selection consistency and target-risk implications

The preceding analysis establishes control of Bellman-generated responses under dependent trajectory sampling. We now study source selection through the target predictive scores. To distinguish the criterion used for selection from the criterion used for evaluation, predictive optimality and target-risk optimality are treated separately. For each S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J}, let 𝒬S\mathcal{Q}_{S} be a nonempty deterministic class of target predictors. Suppose that the minimum target risk over 𝒬S\mathcal{Q}_{S} is finite and attained, and define

QS†=arg⁡minQ∈𝒬S​R0​(Q),R0†​(S)=R0​(QS†),Q_{S}^{\dagger}=\arg\min_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{S}}R_{0}(Q),\quad R_{0}^{\dagger}(S)=R_{0}(Q_{S}^{\dagger}),

where arg⁡min\arg\min denotes a fixed deterministic choice when the minimizer is not unique. The oracle target risk and the corresponding oracle subset class are

R0∗=minS∈𝒮J⁡R0†​(S),𝒮risk={S∈𝒮J:R0†​(S)=R0∗}.R_{0}^{*}=\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}R_{0}^{\dagger}(S),\quad\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{risk}}=\left\{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}:R_{0}^{\dagger}(S)=R_{0}^{*}\right\}.

For a deterministic tolerance ϵN>0\epsilon_{N}>0, define the target-risk near-oracle class

𝒢Nrisk​(ϵN)={S∈𝒮J:R0†​(S)<R0∗+ϵN}.\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{risk}}(\epsilon_{N})=\left\{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}:R_{0}^{\dagger}(S)<R_{0}^{*}+\epsilon_{N}\right\}.

These quantities specify the population target of transfer and are not themselves used to construct the predictive selection rule.

Using the Bellman decomposition from Section 3.1, write

𝐘e=𝐘¯+𝐛e,Y¯t(k)=Q∗(k)​(Xt(k))+ϵt(k).\mathbf{Y}_{e}=\overline{\mathbf{Y}}+\mathbf{b}_{e},\quad\overline{Y}_{t}^{(k)}=Q_{*}^{(k)}(X_{t}^{(k)})+\epsilon_{t}^{(k)}.

The vector 𝐘¯\overline{\mathbf{Y}} removes the Bellman bootstrap remainder and serves only as an analytical reference. For each S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J}, define the predictive score based on the actual Bellman responses and its oracle-response counterpart by

ℓe,N​(S)=log⁡pS,N​(𝐘e(0)∣X,𝐘e(S)),ℓN∘​(S)=log⁡pS,N​(𝐘¯(0)∣X,𝐘¯(S)).\ell_{e,N}(S)=\log p_{S,N}\!\left(\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)}\mid X,\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(S)}\right),\qquad\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S)=\log p_{S,N}\!\left(\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(0)}\mid X,\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(S)}\right).

All candidate subsets are evaluated using the same target-response vector and the same predictive construction. The comparison between ℓe,N\ell_{e,N} and ℓN∘\ell_{N}^{\circ} is made with the predictive hyperparameters held fixed. If hyperparameters are refitted after perturbing the responses, the resulting change must be included in the score perturbation considered below. Let ΠN\Pi_{N} be a deterministic prior satisfying ΠN​(S)>0\Pi_{N}(S)>0 for every S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J}. Define the working subset posterior by

Πe,N​(S∣𝐘e,X)=ΠN​(S)​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(S)}∑U∈𝒮JΠN​(U)​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(U)}.\Pi_{e,N}(S\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X)=\frac{\Pi_{N}(S)\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(S)\}}{\displaystyle\sum_{U\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\Pi_{N}(U)\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(U)\}}.

This is a predictive-score weighting rule and need not coincide with the Bayesian posterior under the full trajectory likelihood (Bissiri et al., 2016). Assume that ℓN∘​(S)\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S) is integrable under the true trajectory law ℙ⋆\mathbb{P}_{\star} for every S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J}, and define ℒN∘​(S)=𝔼⋆​[ℓN∘​(S)].\mathcal{L}_{N}^{\circ}(S)=\mathbb{E}_{\star}[\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S)]. The optimal population predictive score and its oracle subset class are

ℒN∗=maxS∈𝒮J⁡ℒN∘​(S),𝒮Npred={S∈𝒮J:ℒN∘​(S)=ℒN∗}.\mathcal{L}_{N}^{*}=\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\mathcal{L}_{N}^{\circ}(S),\quad\mathcal{S}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}=\left\{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}:\mathcal{L}_{N}^{\circ}(S)=\mathcal{L}_{N}^{*}\right\}.

Choose the predictive oracle reference

SN⋆=arg⁡maxS∈𝒮Npred​ΠN​(S),πN⋆=ΠN​(SN⋆),S_{N}^{\star}=\arg\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}}\Pi_{N}(S),\quad\pi_{N}^{\star}=\Pi_{N}(S_{N}^{\star}),

where arg⁡max\arg\max denotes a fixed deterministic choice when the maximizer is not unique. For a deterministic predictive tolerance dN>0d_{N}>0, define

ℬNpred​(dN)={S∈𝒮J:ℒN∗−ℒN∘​(S)≥dN}.\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d_{N})=\left\{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}:\mathcal{L}_{N}^{*}-\mathcal{L}_{N}^{\circ}(S)\geq d_{N}\right\}.

Thus, 𝒮J∖ℬNpred​(dN)\mathcal{S}_{J}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d_{N}) is the corresponding predictive near-oracle class. For each candidate subset, define the centered oracle-score contrast

ZN​(S)=ℓN∘​(S)−ℓN∘​(SN⋆)−{ℒN∘​(S)−ℒN∗}.Z_{N}(S)=\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S)-\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S_{N}^{\star})-\left\{\mathcal{L}_{N}^{\circ}(S)-\mathcal{L}_{N}^{*}\right\}.

By construction, 𝔼⋆​[ZN​(S)]=0.\mathbb{E}_{\star}[Z_{N}(S)]=0. Define the perturbation of the relative predictive score by

ue,N​(S)={ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)}−{ℓN∘​(S)−ℓN∘​(SN⋆)},\displaystyle u_{e,N}(S)=\bigl\{\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\bigr\}-\bigl\{\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S)-\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S_{N}^{\star})\bigr\},

and set 𝔅e,N=maxS∈𝒮J⁡|ue,N​(S)|.\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}|u_{e,N}(S)|. The actual relative predictive score then admits the exact decomposition

ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)=−{ℒN∗−ℒN∘​(S)}+ZN​(S)+ue,N​(S).\displaystyle\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})={}-\left\{\mathcal{L}_{N}^{*}-\mathcal{L}_{N}^{\circ}(S)\right\}+Z_{N}(S)+u_{e,N}(S).

Hence, selection is governed by three components: population predictive separation, stochastic fluctuation of the oracle-response score, and perturbation caused by Bellman bootstrapping. Define the population tail envelope

ΨN​(x)=supS∈𝒮Jℙ⋆​(|ZN​(S)|>x),x>0.\Psi_{N}(x)=\sup_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(|Z_{N}(S)|>x\right),\quad x>0.

This is a property of the population distribution of the oracle-response scores and involves no fitted quantity. For every deterministic aN>0a_{N}>0, the union bound gives

ℙ⋆​(maxS∈𝒮J⁡|ZN​(S)|>aN)≤|𝒮J|​ΨN​(aN).\mathbb{P}_{\star}\!\left(\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}|Z_{N}(S)|>a_{N}\right)\leq|\mathcal{S}_{J}|\Psi_{N}(a_{N}).

Specific models may be used to obtain an explicit form for ΨN\Psi_{N}, but the selection result below only requires the resulting uniform tail bound. The prior enters through the deterministic quantity qN=maxS∈𝒮J⁡log⁡ΠN​(S)πN⋆.q_{N}=\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\log\frac{\Pi_{N}(S)}{\pi_{N}^{\star}}.

The following result transfers the Bellman-bootstrap control obtained in Section 3.1 to the predictive scores.

Lemma 4 (Pathwise predictive-score perturbation under Bellman bootstrapping).

For each S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J}, suppose that, conditional on the input locations XX, the working target predictive density has the Gaussian form

pS,N​(𝐲(0)∣X,𝐲(S))=𝒩⁡(𝐚S+AS​𝐲(S),VS).p_{S,N}\bigl(\mathbf{y}^{(0)}\mid X,\mathbf{y}^{(S)}\bigr)=\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{a}_{S}+A_{S}\mathbf{y}^{(S)},V_{S}\right).

Conditional on XX, the quantities 𝐚S\mathbf{a}_{S}, ASA_{S}, and VSV_{S} are determined by a fixed predictive specification and do not depend on the response values. In particular, no response-dependent hyperparameter refitting is performed when passing from the oracle-response score to the actual score. Suppose there exist deterministic sequences v¯N>0\underline{v}_{N}>0 and LA,N<∞L_{A,N}<\infty such that, almost surely,

infS∈𝒮Jλmin​(VS)≥v¯N,supS∈𝒮J‖AS‖op≤LA,N.\inf_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\lambda_{\min}(V_{S})\geq\underline{v}_{N},\quad\sup_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\|A_{S}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L_{A,N}.

Define

𝐫S∘=𝐘¯(0)−𝐚S−AS𝐘¯(S),𝐝S,e=𝐛e(0)−AS𝐛e(S),ℛN=maxS∈𝒮J∥𝐫S∘∥2,𝒟e,N=maxS∈𝒮J∥𝐝S,e∥2.\displaystyle\mathbf{r}_{S}^{\circ}=\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(0)}-\mathbf{a}_{S}-A_{S}\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(S)},\quad\mathbf{d}_{S,e}=\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(0)}-A_{S}\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(S)},\quad\mathcal{R}_{N}=\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\|\mathbf{r}_{S}^{\circ}\|_{2},\quad\mathcal{D}_{e,N}=\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\|\mathbf{d}_{S,e}\|_{2}.

Then

𝔅e,N≤2​ℛN​𝒟e,N+𝒟e,N2v¯N.\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}\leq\frac{2\mathcal{R}_{N}\mathcal{D}_{e,N}+\mathcal{D}_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{v}_{N}}. (28)

Moreover, if 𝐛e\mathbf{b}_{e} denotes the vector obtained by stacking the Bellman bootstrap remainders from all tasks, then

𝒟e,N≤(1+LA,N)​‖𝐛e‖2,\mathcal{D}_{e,N}\leq(1+L_{A,N})\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}, (29)

and hence

𝔅e,N≤1v¯N​{2​(1+LA,N)​ℛN​‖𝐛e‖2+(1+LA,N)2​‖𝐛e‖22}.\displaystyle\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}\leq\frac{1}{\underline{v}_{N}}\Bigl\{2(1+L_{A,N})\mathcal{R}_{N}\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}+(1+L_{A,N})^{2}\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr\}. (30)

The proof is provided in Appendix A.6.

Corollary 2 (Rate of the bootstrap predictive-score perturbation).

Let ntot=∑k=0Jnk,n_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{k=0}^{J}n_{k}, and define βe,N2=γ2​{re−1,N2+4​B2​δN},\beta_{e,N}^{2}=\gamma^{2}\left\{r_{e-1,N}^{2}+4B^{2}\delta_{N}\right\}, where re−1,Nr_{e-1,N} and δN\delta_{N} are the deterministic quantities appearing in Corollary 1. Suppose there exist deterministic sequences sN>0s_{N}>0 and ηR,N↓0\eta_{R,N}\downarrow 0 such that ℙ⋆​(ℛN>sN)≤ηR,N.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathcal{R}_{N}>s_{N}\right)\leq\eta_{R,N}. Then

𝔅e,N=Oℙ⋆​[(1+LA,N)​sN​ntot​βe,N+(1+LA,N)2​ntot​βe,N2v¯N].\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=O_{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}\left[\frac{(1+L_{A,N})s_{N}\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{tot}}}\,\beta_{e,N}+(1+L_{A,N})^{2}n_{\mathrm{tot}}\beta_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{v}_{N}}\right]. (31)

The proof is provided in Appendix A.7.

For later use, define

ρe,Nbt=(1+LA,N)​sN​ntot​βe,N+(1+LA,N)2​ntot​βe,N2v¯N.\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}=\frac{(1+L_{A,N})s_{N}\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{tot}}}\,\beta_{e,N}+(1+L_{A,N})^{2}n_{\mathrm{tot}}\beta_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{v}_{N}}. (32)

Then Corollary 2 gives 𝔅e,N=Oℙ⋆​(ρe,Nbt).\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=O_{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}\bigl(\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\bigr). In addition, if sN=O⁡(n0),LA,N=O⁡(1)s_{N}=O(\sqrt{n_{0}}),~L_{A,N}=O(1) and v¯N−1=O⁡(1),\underline{v}_{N}^{-1}=O(1), then ρe,Nbt=O⁡(n0​ntot​βe,N+ntot​βe,N2).\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}=O\!\left(\sqrt{n_{0}n_{\mathrm{tot}}}\,\beta_{e,N}+n_{\mathrm{tot}}\beta_{e,N}^{2}\right).

Lemma 5 (Deterministic posterior comparison).

Let ∅≠ℬ⊆𝒮J\varnothing\neq\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{J}. Then

Πe,N​(ℬ∣𝐘e,X)≤min⁡{1,exp⁡(log⁡|ℬ|+qN+maxS∈ℬ⁡{ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)})}.\displaystyle\Pi_{e,N}(\mathcal{B}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X)\leq\min\Bigg\{1,\,\exp\Bigg(\log|\mathcal{B}|+q_{N}+\max_{S\in\mathcal{B}}\bigl\{\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\bigr\}\Bigg)\Bigg\}. (33)

Moreover,

maxS∈ℬ⁡Πe,N​(S∣𝐘e,X)Πe,N​(SN⋆∣𝐘e,X)≤exp⁡(qN+maxS∈ℬ⁡{ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)}).\max_{S\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{\Pi_{e,N}(S\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X)}{\Pi_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X)}\leq\exp\Bigg(q_{N}+\max_{S\in\mathcal{B}}\bigl\{\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\bigr\}\Bigg). (34)

For ℬ=∅\mathcal{B}=\varnothing, the posterior-mass conclusion is immediate.

The proof is provided in Appendix A.8.

Theorem 2 (Predictive near-oracle posterior concentration and selection).

Let dN>0d_{N}>0 be deterministic, and let e=eNe=e_{N} be a deterministic iteration index for which Corollary 2 applies. Write ℬN=ℬNpred​(dN).\mathcal{B}_{N}=\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d_{N}). For a>0a>0, define the upper-tail fluctuation probability ΞN+​(a,dN)=ℙ⋆​(maxS∈ℬN⁡ZN​(S)>a),\Xi_{N}^{+}(a;d_{N})=\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\max_{S\in\mathcal{B}_{N}}Z_{N}(S)>a\right), with the convention that ΞN+​(a,dN)=0\Xi_{N}^{+}(a;d_{N})=0 when ℬN=∅\mathcal{B}_{N}=\varnothing. Suppose there exists a deterministic sequence aN>0a_{N}>0 such that

ΞN+​(aN,dN)⟶0.\Xi_{N}^{+}(a_{N};d_{N})\longrightarrow 0. (35)

Define the prior-mass penalty ΛN​(dN)=log⁡(1∨ΠN​(ℬN)πN⋆),\Lambda_{N}(d_{N})=\log\left(1\vee\frac{\Pi_{N}(\mathcal{B}_{N})}{\pi_{N}^{\star}}\right), and the effective predictive margin κN=dN−aN−ΛN​(dN).\kappa_{N}=d_{N}-a_{N}-\Lambda_{N}(d_{N}). Assume κN⟶∞,ρe,Nbt=o⁡(κN),\kappa_{N}\longrightarrow\infty,~\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}=o(\kappa_{N}), where ρe,Nbt\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}} is the deterministic rate in Corollary 2.
Then

Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)→ℙ⋆0.\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}0. (36)

Moreover,

𝔼⋆​[Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)]⟶0.\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\right]\longrightarrow 0. (37)

If S^\widehat{S} is drawn from the working subset posterior, with the auxiliary sampling randomness included in the probability, then

ℙ⋆​(S^∈ℬN)⟶0.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\widehat{S}\in\mathcal{B}_{N}\right)\longrightarrow 0. (38)

The same conclusion holds for any maximum-a-posteriori selection.

The proof is provided in Appendix A.9. Theorem 2 establishes concentration with respect to the population predictive criterion. Predictive optimality, however, need not coincide with target-risk optimality. To quantify their population-level discrepancy, define the calibration radius

ωN​(d)=maxS∈𝒮J∖ℬNpred​(d)⁡{R0†​(S)−R0∗},d>0.\omega_{N}(d)=\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d)}\left\{R_{0}^{\dagger}(S)-R_{0}^{*}\right\},\qquad d>0.

The maximum is well defined because 𝒮J\mathcal{S}_{J} is finite and 𝒮J∖ℬNpred​(d)\mathcal{S}_{J}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d) contains the population predictive oracle class. By construction,

S∉ℬNpred​(d)⟹R0†​(S)−R0∗≤ωN​(d).S\notin\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R_{0}^{\dagger}(S)-R_{0}^{*}\leq\omega_{N}(d).

Thus, ωN​(d)\omega_{N}(d) measures the largest target-risk excess among subsets that are within dd of the optimal population predictive score. It is a deterministic population quantity and does not involve a fitted estimator.

Corollary 3 (Target-risk implication of predictive selection).

Under the conditions of Theorem 2,

Πe,N​({S∈𝒮J:R0†​(S)−R0∗≤ωN​(dN)}|𝐘e,X)→ℙ⋆1.\displaystyle\Pi_{e,N}\Bigl(\bigl\{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}:R_{0}^{\dagger}(S)-R_{0}^{*}\leq\omega_{N}(d_{N})\bigr\}\,\Bigm|\,\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\Bigr)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}1. (39)

Moreover,

𝔼⋆​[Πe,N​({S:R0†​(S)−R0∗≤ωN​(dN)}|𝐘e,X)]⟶1.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\star}\Bigg[\Pi_{e,N}\Bigl(\bigl\{S:R_{0}^{\dagger}(S)-R_{0}^{*}\leq\omega_{N}(d_{N})\bigr\}\,\Bigm|\,\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\Bigr)\Bigg]\longrightarrow 1. (40)

For either a posterior draw or a maximum-a-posteriori selection,

ℙ⋆{R0†(S^)−R0∗≤ωN(dN)}⟶1.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left\{R_{0}^{\dagger}(\widehat{S})-R_{0}^{*}\leq\omega_{N}(d_{N})\right\}\longrightarrow 1. (41)

Consequently, if ωN​(dN)⟶0,\omega_{N}(d_{N})\longrightarrow 0, then the selected subset is target-risk near-oracle:

R0†​(S^)−R0∗→ℙ⋆0.R_{0}^{\dagger}(\widehat{S})-R_{0}^{*}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}0. (42)

More generally, for any deterministic sequence ϵN>ωN​(dN)\epsilon_{N}>\omega_{N}(d_{N}),

Πe,N​(𝒢Nrisk​(ϵN)∣𝐘e,X)→ℙ⋆1,\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{risk}}(\epsilon_{N})\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}1, (43)

and

ℙ⋆{R0†(S^)<R0∗+ϵN}⟶1.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left\{R_{0}^{\dagger}(\widehat{S})<R_{0}^{*}+\epsilon_{N}\right\}\longrightarrow 1. (44)

The proof is provided in Appendix A.10.

Theorem 2 establishes concentration on subsets that are near-optimal under the population predictive criterion. Corollary 3 quantifies the target-risk consequence through the population calibration radius ωN​(dN)\omega_{N}(d_{N}). This quantity measures the largest target-risk excess within the predictive near-oracle class. The predictive selection result therefore does not require predictive and target-risk optimality to coincide. Target-risk consistency follows when the discrepancy between the two criteria vanishes at the selected predictive tolerance, namely when ωN​(dN)→0\omega_{N}(d_{N})\to 0. All quantities entering this calibration statement are defined at the population level and do not involve fitted estimators.

4 Transfer-adaptive posterior contraction under predictive source selection

The preceding analysis establishes two ingredients needed for transfer: control of Bellman-generated responses and concentration of the source-subset weights under the population predictive criterion. Neither result, however, determines how much statistical information the selected source observations provide about the target Q-function. Posterior contraction requires an additional analysis of the target marginal posterior conditional on a source subset. This section therefore separates three questions: contraction of the target working posterior, frequentist accuracy of its posterior mean, and decision quality of the policy induced by that posterior. We first identify the information available to the target under the separable multi-task GP model and show why generic full-rank task covariance does not justify additive pooling of source and target sample sizes. We then derive finite-design perturbation bounds and a selection-to-contraction result. Finally, an explicit shared-function experiment is used to establish a pooled contraction rate and its corresponding minimax lower bound.

Throughout this section, source relevance is distinguished from source information. Predictive selection determines which subsets receive asymptotically nonnegligible weight, whereas the amount of transferable information is determined by the conditional covariance structure of the working GP model. In particular, an additive effective sample size is not assumed merely because a subset is predictively near-oracle. The rank-one shared-function model considered below is an additional structural specialization of the separable GP model and is not implied by bounded eigenvalues of a general task covariance matrix. Unless stated otherwise, all probability statements are under the true trajectory distribution ℙ⋆\mathbb{P}_{\star}.

4.1 Setup, selection weights and transferable information

Let f0=Q∗(0)f_{0}=Q_{*}^{(0)} and ℍ=L2​(PX(0))\mathbb{H}=L^{2}(P_{X}^{(0)}) with norm ∥⋅∥ℍ\|\cdot\|_{\mathbb{H}}. For S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J}, define the active task set ℐ⁡(S)={0}∪S.\mathcal{I}(S)=\{0\}\cup S. The source-subset weights are those obtained from the predictive selection step:

ωe,N​(S)=Πe,N​(S∣𝐘e,X),S∈𝒮J.\omega_{e,N}(S)=\Pi_{e,N}\left(S\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right),\quad S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}.

For a fixed subset SS, let ΠS,e,N(0)\Pi_{S,e,N}^{(0)} denote the corresponding target marginal working posterior on ℍ\mathbb{H}. To avoid confusing this function-space posterior with the subset posterior Πe,N​(S∣𝐘e,X)\Pi_{e,N}(S\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X), define the model-averaged target working posterior by

Π~e,N(0)​(A)=∑S∈𝒮Jωe,N​(S)​ΠS,e,N(0)​(A),A⊆ℍ,\widetilde{\Pi}_{e,N}^{(0)}(A)=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\omega_{e,N}(S)\Pi_{S,e,N}^{(0)}(A),\quad A\subseteq\mathbb{H},

where ∑S∈𝒮Jωe,N​(S)=1.\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\omega_{e,N}(S)=1. Let 𝒢Nctr⊆𝒮J\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{J} be a nonempty deterministic family of subsets for which the contraction conditions introduced below hold uniformly, and define the posterior weight assigned outside this family by

ΩNctr=∑S∉𝒢Nctrωe,N​(S).\Omega_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}=\sum_{S\notin\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}}\omega_{e,N}(S).

To transfer subsetwise contraction to Π~e,N(0)\widetilde{\Pi}_{e,N}^{(0)}, it is sufficient that ΩNctr→ℙ⋆0.\Omega_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}0. This condition can be linked directly to the predictive selection result. In particular, if for some deterministic dN>0d_{N}>0,

𝒮J∖ℬNpred​(dN)⊆𝒢Nctr,\mathcal{S}_{J}\setminus\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d_{N})\subseteq\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}, (45)

then

ΩNctr\displaystyle\Omega_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}} ≤Πe,N​(ℬNpred​(dN)∣𝐘e,X)→ℙ⋆0\displaystyle\leq\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d_{N})\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}0

by Theorem 2. If (45) does not hold, concentration on 𝒢Nctr\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}} requires a separate argument. Thus, predictive near-oracle selection and posterior contraction are related but logically distinct. For every active task, retain the Bellman decomposition

𝐘e(k)=𝐘¯(k)+𝐛e(k),Y¯t(k)=Q∗(k)​(Xt(k))+ϵt(k).\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(k)}=\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(k)}+\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(k)},\quad\overline{Y}_{t}^{(k)}=Q_{*}^{(k)}(X_{t}^{(k)})+\epsilon_{t}^{(k)}.

The oracle response 𝐘¯(k)\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(k)} is an analytical device and is not an additional observed sample. The Bellman remainder 𝐛e(k)\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(k)} need not be centered, Gaussian, or independent of the oracle response. For conservative Bellman targets it may also contain the coverage and pessimism terms identified in Section 3.1. Consequently, its effect cannot in general be represented by simply increasing a Gaussian observation-noise variance.

Proposition 1 (Frequency-wise target information and the obstruction to generic pooling).

Fix S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J} and let BS=Ktask​(ℐ⁡(S),ℐ⁡(S)).B_{S}=K_{\mathrm{task}}\bigl(\mathcal{I}(S),\mathcal{I}(S)\bigr). For a fixed input-kernel eigenvalue λj>0\lambda_{j}>0, consider the Gaussian sequence working experiment

𝜽j∼𝒩(0,λjBS),𝐙j=𝜽j+DS−1/2𝝃j,\bm{\theta}_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\lambda_{j}B_{S}\right),\quad\mathbf{Z}_{j}=\bm{\theta}_{j}+D_{S}^{-1/2}\bm{\xi}_{j}, (46)

where DS=diag(τk:k∈ℐ(S)),τk>0,D_{S}=\operatorname{diag}\left(\tau_{k}:k\in\mathcal{I}(S)\right),~\tau_{k}>0, and 𝛏j∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\bm{\xi}_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) is independent of 𝛉j\bm{\theta}_{j}.

BS=(B00B0​SBS​0BS​S),B_{S}=\begin{pmatrix}B_{00}&B_{0S}\\ B_{S0}&B_{SS}\end{pmatrix},

and let DS,src=diag(τk:k∈S).D_{S,\mathrm{src}}=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_{k}:k\in S). For S≠∅S\neq\varnothing, define

v0​j​(S)=Var⁡(θ0​j∣𝐙j)=(τ0+cj,S−1)−1.v_{0j}(S)=\operatorname{Var}\left(\theta_{0j}\mid\mathbf{Z}_{j}\right)=\left(\tau_{0}+c_{j,S}^{-1}\right)^{-1}. (48)

cj,S≥λj​χS.c_{j,S}\geq\lambda_{j}\chi_{S}. (49)

v0​j​(S)≥{τ0+(λj​χS)−1}−1.v_{0j}(S)\geq\left\{\tau_{0}+(\lambda_{j}\chi_{S})^{-1}\right\}^{-1}. (50)

cj,S⟶λj​χS,v0​j​(S)⟶{τ0+(λj​χS)−1}−1.c_{j,S}\longrightarrow\lambda_{j}\chi_{S},\quad v_{0j}(S)\longrightarrow\left\{\tau_{0}+(\lambda_{j}\chi_{S})^{-1}\right\}^{-1}. (51)

BS=(1ϱϱ1),0<|ϱ|<1,B_{S}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\varrho\\ \varrho&1\end{pmatrix},\quad 0<|\varrho|<1,

we have χS=1−ϱ2\chi_{S}=1-\varrho^{2}, therefore complete knowledge of the source function leaves

v0​joracle​source={τ0+[(1−ϱ2)​λj]−1}−1.v_{0j}^{\mathrm{oracle\ source}}=\left\{\tau_{0}+\bigl[(1-\varrho^{2})\lambda_{j}\bigr]^{-1}\right\}^{-1}. (52)

Hence, with fixed target precision τ0\tau_{0}, arbitrarily precise source observations alone cannot force the target posterior to contract to a point. By contrast, suppose the task covariance is rank one,

BS=𝐠ℐ⁡(S)​𝐠ℐ⁡(S)⊤,g0=1.B_{S}=\mathbf{g}_{\mathcal{I}(S)}\mathbf{g}_{\mathcal{I}(S)}^{\top},\quad g_{0}=1. (53)

Equivalently,

θk​j=gk​θj,θj∼𝒩⁡(0,λj).\theta_{kj}=g_{k}\theta_{j},\quad\theta_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda_{j}).

Then

Var⁡(θ0​j∣𝐙j)=(λj−1+𝔫S)−1,𝔫S=∑k∈ℐ⁡(S)τk​gk2.\operatorname{Var}\left(\theta_{0j}\mid\mathbf{Z}_{j}\right)=\left(\lambda_{j}^{-1}+\mathfrak{n}_{S}\right)^{-1},\quad\mathfrak{n}_{S}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)}\tau_{k}g_{k}^{2}. (54)

Thus 𝔫S\mathfrak{n}_{S} is an additive pooled precision in the rank-one experiment. It should not be interpreted as an effective sample size for the original trajectory data unless such an identification is established separately.

The proof is provided in Appendix B.1.

Proposition 1 distinguishes two fundamentally different transfer regimes. Under a full-rank task covariance, conditioning on arbitrarily precise source observations leaves a positive task-specific innovation variance λj​χS\lambda_{j}\chi_{S} for the target. Source observations can reduce uncertainty, but they cannot replace increasing target information. Under the rank-one shared-function model, this innovation component vanishes and the taskwise precisions combine additively through 𝔫S\mathfrak{n}_{S}. The quantity 𝔫S\mathfrak{n}_{S} is therefore justified as a pooled precision only within the stated shared-function experiment. An identification such as τk≍nk,effσk2\tau_{k}\asymp\frac{n_{k,\mathrm{eff}}}{\sigma_{k}^{2}} for dependent reinforcement-learning trajectories requires a separate concentration or experiment-reduction argument. It does not follow from source selection, task-kernel correlation, or the raw observation counts alone.

4.2 Spectral regularity, RKHS geometry and posterior perturbation

Posterior contraction requires two distinct forms of control. The first concerns approximation of the target truth by the GP prior and the amount of prior mass assigned to small neighborhoods of that truth. The second concerns the perturbation introduced when oracle responses are replaced by Bellman-generated responses. We develop these two ingredients in a common notation and keep them separate from the source-selection argument of the preceding section. Let

Tin​g​(x)=∫kin​(x,x′)​g​(x′)​PX(0)​(d​x′)T_{\mathrm{in}}g(x)=\int k_{\mathrm{in}}(x,x^{\prime})g(x^{\prime})P_{X}^{(0)}(\mathrm{d}x^{\prime})

denote the covariance operator induced by the input kernel on ℍ=L2​(PX(0)).\mathbb{H}=L^{2}(P_{X}^{(0)}). Let {(λj,φj)}j≥1\{(\lambda_{j},\varphi_{j})\}_{j\geq 1} be its eigenpairs, with {φj}j≥1\{\varphi_{j}\}_{j\geq 1} orthonormal in ℍ\mathbb{H}. Assume

cλ​j−1−2​α/d≤λj≤Cλ​j−1−2​α/d,α>0,c_{\lambda}j^{-1-2\alpha/d}\leq\lambda_{j}\leq C_{\lambda}j^{-1-2\alpha/d},\quad\alpha>0, (55)

and let θ0​j=⟨f0,φj⟩ℍ,f0=Q∗(0).\theta_{0j}=\langle f_{0},\varphi_{j}\rangle_{\mathbb{H}},~f_{0}=Q_{*}^{(0)}. We impose the spectral smoothness condition

∑j≥1j2​α/d​θ0​j2≤L2.\sum_{j\geq 1}j^{2\alpha/d}\theta_{0j}^{2}\leq L^{2}. (56)

The corresponding spectral smoothness class is denoted by

Θα​(L):={f∈ℍ:∑j≥1j2​α/d​⟨f,φj⟩ℍ2≤L2}.\Theta_{\alpha}(L):=\left\{f\in\mathbb{H}:\sum_{j\geq 1}j^{2\alpha/d}\langle f,\varphi_{j}\rangle_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\leq L^{2}\right\}.

Let ℋin\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}} denote the RKHS associated with kink_{\mathrm{in}}. In the above spectral representation, ‖h‖ℋin2=∑j≥1⟨h,φj⟩ℍ2λj\|h\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}}}^{2}=\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{\langle h,\varphi_{j}\rangle_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}}{\lambda_{j}} whenever the series is finite. Condition (56) describes regularity of the truth relative to the eigenbasis of the covariance operator. It should not be identified automatically with membership in the native RKHS. For example, under the standard Matérn parameterization on a regular dd-dimensional domain, Matérn smoothness α\alpha corresponds to a native Sobolev order α+d/2\alpha+d/2 rather than α\alpha (Kanagawa et al., 2018).

Lemma 6 (Separable multi-task RKHS geometry).

Fix S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J}, let ℐ⁡(S)={0}∪S,\mathcal{I}(S)=\{0\}\cup S, and define BS=Ktask​(ℐ⁡(S),ℐ⁡(S)).B_{S}=K_{\mathrm{task}}\bigl(\mathcal{I}(S),\mathcal{I}(S)\bigr). Consider the separable kernel

KS​((k,x),(ℓ,x′))=(BS)k​ℓ​kin​(x,x′),k,ℓ∈ℐ⁡(S).K_{S}\bigl((k,x),(\ell,x^{\prime})\bigr)=(B_{S})_{k\ell}k_{\mathrm{in}}(x,x^{\prime}),\quad k,\ell\in\mathcal{I}(S).

If BS≻0B_{S}\succ 0, the associated vector-valued RKHS ℋBS\mathcal{H}_{B_{S}} consists of vectors 𝐟S=(f(k))k∈ℐ⁡(S)\mathbf{f}_{S}=\bigl(f^{(k)}\bigr)_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)} with components in ℋin\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}}, and its squared norm is

‖𝐟S‖ℋBS2=∑k,ℓ∈ℐ⁡(S)(BS−1)k​ℓ​⟨f(k),f(ℓ)⟩ℋin.\|\mathbf{f}_{S}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{B_{S}}}^{2}=\sum_{k,\ell\in\mathcal{I}(S)}(B_{S}^{-1})_{k\ell}\left\langle f^{(k)},f^{(\ell)}\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}}}. (57)

If, for deterministic constants 0<b−≤b+<∞0<b_{-}\leq b_{+}<\infty, b−​I⪯BS⪯b+​I,b_{-}I\preceq B_{S}\preceq b_{+}I, then

b+−1​∑k∈ℐ⁡(S)‖f(k)‖ℋin2≤‖𝐟S‖ℋBS2≤b−−1​∑k∈ℐ⁡(S)‖f(k)‖ℋin2.b_{+}^{-1}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)}\|f^{(k)}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}}}^{2}\leq\|\mathbf{f}_{S}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{B_{S}}}^{2}\leq b_{-}^{-1}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)}\|f^{(k)}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}}}^{2}. (58)

If BSB_{S} is positive semidefinite but singular, the same expression holds with BS†B_{S}^{\dagger} in place of BS−1B_{S}^{-1}, provided 𝐟S\mathbf{f}_{S} belongs to the range of BSB_{S} in the task coordinate.

The proof is provided in Appendix B.2. The preceding lemma describes the geometry induced by the task covariance. Norm equivalence controls the cost of approximating a vector of task functions, but it does not imply that source observations act as independent target observations. In particular, the full-rank and rank-one information structures identified in Proposition 1 remain fundamentally different.

Lemma 7 (Spectral approximation and GP prior concentration).

Suppose (55) and (56) hold. Then there exists C<∞C<\infty such that, for all sufficiently large RR,

infh∈ℋin:‖h‖ℋin≤R∥h−f0∥ℍ≤CR−2α/d.\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}}:\|h\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{in}}}\leq R}\|h-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}\leq CR^{-2\alpha/d}. (59)

Let W=∑j≥1λj​Zj​φj,Zj∼iid𝒩⁡(0,1),W=\sum_{j\geq 1}\sqrt{\lambda_{j}}\,Z_{j}\varphi_{j},~Z_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,1), be the centered ℍ\mathbb{H}-valued GP induced by the input covariance operator. Then there exist constants C1,C2<∞C_{1},C_{2}<\infty such that, for all sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0,

−log⁡ℙ⁡(‖W‖ℍ≤ε)\displaystyle-\log\mathbb{P}\left(\|W\|_{\mathbb{H}}\leq\varepsilon\right) ≤C1ε−d/α,\displaystyle\leq C_{1}\varepsilon^{-d/\alpha}, (60)
−log⁡ℙ⁡(‖W−f0‖ℍ≤ε)\displaystyle-\log\mathbb{P}\left(\|W-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}\leq\varepsilon\right) ≤C2ε−d/α.\displaystyle\leq C_{2}\varepsilon^{-d/\alpha}. (61)

The constants may depend on L,α,d,cλL,\alpha,d,c_{\lambda}, and CλC_{\lambda}.

The proof is provided in Appendix B.3. Lemma 7 provides approximation and prior-mass bounds for the target component. These are ingredients for posterior contraction, but they do not by themselves establish contraction under Bellman-generated responses. We next quantify the perturbation induced by replacing the analytical oracle responses with the actual responses used by the learning algorithm.

Fix S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J} and stack the active-task responses as 𝐘e,S=(𝐘e(k))k∈ℐ⁡(S),𝐘¯S=(𝐘¯(k))k∈ℐ⁡(S),\mathbf{Y}_{e,S}=\bigl(\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(k)}\bigr)_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)},~\overline{\mathbf{Y}}_{S}=\bigl(\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(k)}\bigr)_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)}, and 𝐛e,S=(𝐛e(k))k∈ℐ⁡(S).\mathbf{b}_{e,S}=\bigl(\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(k)}\bigr)_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)}. Then

𝐘e,S=𝐘¯S+𝐛e,S.\mathbf{Y}_{e,S}=\overline{\mathbf{Y}}_{S}+\mathbf{b}_{e,S}.

Let 𝐊S,N\mathbf{K}_{S,N} denote the GP Gram matrix associated with the active task-tagged inputs and let ΛS,N≻0\Lambda_{S,N}\succ 0 be the corresponding working-noise covariance. Throughout this comparison, the kernel, prior mean, and working-noise specification are held fixed. In particular, no response-dependent hyperparameter refitting is performed between the oracle and actual response fits. For a target query xx, let 𝐤0,S,N​(x)\mathbf{k}_{0,S,N}(x) denote the covariance vector between (0,x)(0,x) and the active task-tagged inputs. Define the target smoothing operator 𝒫S,N:ℝn⁡(S)⟶ℍ\mathcal{P}_{S,N}:\mathbb{R}^{n(S)}\longrightarrow\mathbb{H} by

(𝒫S,N​v)​(x)=𝐤0,S,N​(x)⊤​(𝐊S,N+ΛS,N)−1​v,(\mathcal{P}_{S,N}v)(x)=\mathbf{k}_{0,S,N}(x)^{\top}(\mathbf{K}_{S,N}+\Lambda_{S,N})^{-1}v, (62)

where n⁡(S)=∑k∈ℐ⁡(S)nk.n(S)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)}n_{k}. Let 𝐦S,N\mathbf{m}_{S,N} be the stacked prior-mean vector at the active inputs. The subset-specific target marginal working posterior introduced in Section 4.1 is

ΠS,e,N(0)=𝒩ℍ​(μS,e,N(0),CS,N(0)),\Pi_{S,e,N}^{(0)}=\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{H}}\left(\mu_{S,e,N}^{(0)},C_{S,N}^{(0)}\right),

where

μS,e,N(0)=m(0)+𝒫S,N​(𝐘e,S−𝐦S,N),\mu_{S,e,N}^{(0)}=m^{(0)}+\mathcal{P}_{S,N}\left(\mathbf{Y}_{e,S}-\mathbf{m}_{S,N}\right), (63)

and

CS,N(0)​(x,x′)=K⁡((0,x),(0,x′))−𝐤0,S,N​(x)⊤​(𝐊S,N+ΛS,N)−1​𝐤0,S,N​(x′).\displaystyle C_{S,N}^{(0)}(x,x^{\prime})=K\bigl((0,x),(0,x^{\prime})\bigr)-\mathbf{k}_{0,S,N}(x)^{\top}(\mathbf{K}_{S,N}+\Lambda_{S,N})^{-1}\mathbf{k}_{0,S,N}(x^{\prime}).

Assume that CS,N(0)C_{S,N}^{(0)} defines a positive trace-class covariance operator on ℍ\mathbb{H}. Define the analytical oracle posterior mean by

μ¯S,N(0)=m(0)+𝒫S,N​(𝐘¯S−𝐦S,N).\overline{\mu}_{S,N}^{(0)}=m^{(0)}+\mathcal{P}_{S,N}\left(\overline{\mathbf{Y}}_{S}-\mathbf{m}_{S,N}\right). (64)

The actual and oracle fits use the same covariance operator CS,N(0)C_{S,N}^{(0)}.

Lemma 8 (Pathwise target-posterior perturbation by Bellman errors).

For every S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J},

μS,e,N(0)−μ¯S,N(0)=𝒫S,N​𝐛e,S.\mu_{S,e,N}^{(0)}-\overline{\mu}_{S,N}^{(0)}=\mathcal{P}_{S,N}\mathbf{b}_{e,S}. (65)

Consequently,

‖μS,e,N(0)−f0‖ℍ≤‖μ¯S,N(0)−f0‖ℍ+dS,e,Nbt,\|\mu_{S,e,N}^{(0)}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}\leq\|\overline{\mu}_{S,N}^{(0)}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}+d_{S,e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}, (66)

where dS,e,Nbt=‖𝒫S,N​𝐛e,S‖ℍ.d_{S,e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}=\|\mathcal{P}_{S,N}\mathbf{b}_{e,S}\|_{\mathbb{H}}. Moreover,

dS,e,Nbt≤∥𝒫S,NΛS,N1/2∥op∥ΛS,N−1/2𝐛e,S∥2.d_{S,e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\leq\|\mathcal{P}_{S,N}\Lambda_{S,N}^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\Lambda_{S,N}^{-1/2}\mathbf{b}_{e,S}\|_{2}. (67)

The proof is provided in Appendix B.4.

Corollary 4 (Deterministic-rate control of the posterior perturbation).

Let 𝒢Nctr\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}} be the deterministic contraction family introduced in Section 4.1. Suppose there exist deterministic sequences ν¯N>0\underline{\nu}_{N}>0 and L𝒫,N<∞L_{\mathcal{P},N}<\infty such that, almost surely,

ΛS,N⪰ν¯N​I,‖𝒫S,N​ΛS,N1/2‖op≤L𝒫,N\Lambda_{S,N}\succeq\underline{\nu}_{N}I,\quad\|\mathcal{P}_{S,N}\Lambda_{S,N}^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq L_{\mathcal{P},N} (68)

for every S∈𝒢NctrS\in\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}. Let βe,N\beta_{e,N} denote the deterministic Bellman-bootstrap scale obtained in Corollary 1, so that

supk,t𝔼⋆​[(bt,e(k))2]≤βe,N2.\sup_{k,t}\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[(b_{t,e}^{(k)})^{2}\right]\leq\beta_{e,N}^{2}.

Then, for every S∈𝒢NctrS\in\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}},

𝔼⋆​[(dS,e,Nbt)2]≤L𝒫,N2​ν¯N−1​n​(S)​βe,N2.\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\bigl(d_{S,e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\bigr)^{2}\right]\leq L_{\mathcal{P},N}^{2}\underline{\nu}_{N}^{-1}n(S)\beta_{e,N}^{2}. (69)

Moreover, for every deterministic uN>0u_{N}>0,

ℙ⋆​(maxS∈𝒢Nctr⁡dS,e,Nbt>uN)≤L𝒫,N2​βe,N2ν¯N​uN2​∑S∈𝒢Nctrn⁡(S).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\max_{S\in\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}}d_{S,e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}>u_{N}\right)\leq\frac{L_{\mathcal{P},N}^{2}\beta_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{\nu}_{N}u_{N}^{2}}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}}n(S). (70)

The proof is provided in Appendix B.5.

Lemma 9 (Gaussian concentration for the target working posterior).

Let G∼𝒩ℍ​(0,C),G\sim\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{H}}(0,C), where CC is a positive trace-class covariance operator on ℍ\mathbb{H}. Then, for every t>0t>0,

ℙ{∥G∥ℍ>tr⁡(C)+2​‖C‖op​t}≤e−t.\mathbb{P}\left\{\|G\|_{\mathbb{H}}>\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(C)}+\sqrt{2\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}t}\right\}\leq e^{-t}. (71)

Consequently, if Π=𝒩ℍ​(μ,C),\Pi=\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{H}}(\mu,C), then, for every f0∈ℍf_{0}\in\mathbb{H} and t>0t>0,

Π⁡(‖f−f0‖ℍ>‖μ−f0‖ℍ+tr⁡(C)+2​‖C‖op​t)≤e−t.\displaystyle\Pi\Bigl(\|f-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}>\|\mu-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}+\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(C)}+\sqrt{2\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}t}\Bigr)\leq e^{-t}. (72)

Moreover,

∫‖f−f0‖ℍ2​Π​(𝑑f)=‖μ−f0‖ℍ2+tr⁡(C).\int\|f-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\,\Pi(\mathrm{d}f)=\|\mu-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}+\operatorname{tr}(C). (73)

The proof is provided in Appendix B.6. The results above isolate the ingredients required by the contraction analysis. Lemma 7 controls approximation and prior mass around the target truth. Lemma 8 and Corollary 4 quantify the additional displacement caused by Bellman-generated responses. Lemma 9 converts bounds on the posterior mean and covariance into posterior concentration in the target prediction norm. None of these results alone implies a contraction rate. Their role is to provide verifiable inputs for the selection-adaptive contraction theorem that follows.

4.3 Main posterior contraction results

We now combine the subset-selection weights, the oracle posterior approximation, and the Bellman perturbation bounds developed above. The first result is a lifting theorem: it converts uniform contraction of the subset-specific target posteriors into contraction of the model-averaged target posterior. The subsequent results identify the rate in two explicitly specified Gaussian sequence experiments. The full-rank task model exhibits a target-information bottleneck, whereas the rank-one shared-function model permits genuine precision pooling.

For deterministic sequences εN>0\varepsilon_{N}>0 and 𝔦N>0\mathfrak{i}_{N}>0, define

ℛNorc=maxS∈𝒢Nctr⁡max⁡{‖μ¯S,N(0)−f0‖ℍεN,tr⁡(CS,N(0))εN,𝔦N​‖CS,N(0)‖op}.\mathcal{R}_{N}^{\mathrm{orc}}=\max_{S\in\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}}\max\left\{\frac{\|\overline{\mu}_{S,N}^{(0)}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}}{\varepsilon_{N}},\frac{\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(C_{S,N}^{(0)})}}{\varepsilon_{N}},\sqrt{\mathfrak{i}_{N}\|C_{S,N}^{(0)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\right\}.

For a fixed constant C0<∞C_{0}<\infty, let ζNorc​(C0)=ℙ⋆​(ℛNorc>C0).\zeta_{N}^{\mathrm{orc}}(C_{0})=\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathcal{R}_{N}^{\mathrm{orc}}>C_{0}\right). This is a population failure probability associated with the oracle-response experiment. For u>0u>0, let ζNbt​(u)=L𝒫,N2​βe,N2ν¯N​u2​∑S∈𝒢Nctrn⁡(S),\zeta_{N}^{\mathrm{bt}}(u)=\frac{L_{\mathcal{P},N}^{2}\beta_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{\nu}_{N}u^{2}}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{G}_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}}n(S), which is the deterministic upper bound supplied by Corollary 4.

4.4 Posterior mean risk, minimax optimality and transfer gains

Posterior contraction and frequentist prediction risk are related but distinct. Contraction in probability does not by itself imply a second-moment risk bound for the unmodified posterior mean. We first derive a risk bound for an explicitly projected posterior mean. We then establish the minimax rate in the exact shared-function sequence experiment and clarify the distinction between improvement in contraction scale and strict frequentist risk improvement. Finally, we give an exact prior-averaged transfer-gain identity under correct specification.

Corollary 7 (Risk of the projected posterior mean).

Suppose the conditions of Theorem 3 hold and ‖f0‖ℍ≤L\|f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}\leq L for some fixed L<∞L<\infty. Let 𝔹L={f∈ℍ:‖f‖ℍ≤L},\mathbb{B}_{L}=\left\{f\in\mathbb{H}:\|f\|_{\mathbb{H}}\leq L\right\}, and let TL:ℍ→𝔹LT_{L}:\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{B}_{L} be the metric projection onto 𝔹L\mathbb{B}_{L}. Define the projected model-averaged posterior by

Π~e,N(0),L=Π~e,N(0)∘TL−1\widetilde{\Pi}_{e,N}^{(0),L}=\widetilde{\Pi}_{e,N}^{(0)}\circ T_{L}^{-1}

and its posterior mean by

f^e,NL=∫ℍf​Π~e,N(0),L​(𝑑f).\widehat{f}_{e,N}^{L}=\int_{\mathbb{H}}f\,\widetilde{\Pi}_{e,N}^{(0),L}(\mathrm{d}f).

Let rN=εN+uN,r_{N}=\varepsilon_{N}+u_{N}, and define the deterministic population error bounds

δNctr=ζNorc​(C0)+ζNbt​(uN)\delta_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}=\zeta_{N}^{\mathrm{orc}}(C_{0})+\zeta_{N}^{\mathrm{bt}}(u_{N})

and

δNsel=𝔼⋆​[Πe,N​(ℬNpred​(dN)∣𝐘e,X)].\delta_{N}^{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d_{N})\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\right].

Then, for some constant C<∞C<\infty independent of NN,

𝔼⋆​[‖f^e,NL−f0‖ℍ2]≤C​rN2+4​L2​(δNctr+δNsel).\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\|\widehat{f}_{e,N}^{L}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]\leq Cr_{N}^{2}+4L^{2}\left(\delta_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}+\delta_{N}^{\mathrm{sel}}\right). (93)

Consequently, if rN→0,δNctr→0,δNsel→0,r_{N}\to 0,~\delta_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}\to 0,~\delta_{N}^{\mathrm{sel}}\to 0, then

𝔼⋆​[‖f^e,NL−f0‖ℍ2]⟶0.\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\|\widehat{f}_{e,N}^{L}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]\longrightarrow 0.

If, in addition, δNctr+δNsel=O⁡(rN2),\delta_{N}^{\mathrm{ctr}}+\delta_{N}^{\mathrm{sel}}=O(r_{N}^{2}), then

𝔼⋆​[‖f^e,NL−f0‖ℍ2]=O⁡(rN2).\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\|\widehat{f}_{e,N}^{L}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]=O(r_{N}^{2}).

The proof is provided in Appendix B.13. The projection in Corollary 7 is an explicit modification of the posterior mean. No corresponding risk rate is asserted here for the unprojected posterior mean. Such a result requires additional uniform-integrability or posterior moment control.

Theorem 6 (Minimax optimality in the exact shared-function experiment).

Fix a deterministic subset SS and consider the exact shared-function sequence experiment (84) with

hk​j=0,k∈ℐ⁡(S),j≥1.h_{kj}=0,\quad k\in\mathcal{I}(S),\quad j\geq 1.

Let

n=𝔫S=∑k∈ℐ⁡(S)τk​gk2⟶∞,n=\mathfrak{n}_{S}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{I}(S)}\tau_{k}g_{k}^{2}\longrightarrow\infty,

and suppose (55) holds. Then, for every fixed L>0L>0, there exist constants 0<c<C<∞0<c<C<\infty such that

cn−2α/(2α+d)≤inff^supf0∈Θα​(L)𝔼f0[∥f^−f0∥ℍ2]≤Cn−2α/(2α+d).cn^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d)}\leq\inf_{\widehat{f}}\sup_{f_{0}\in\Theta_{\alpha}(L)}\mathbb{E}_{f_{0}}\left[\|\widehat{f}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]\leq Cn^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d)}. (94)

Here, the infimum is taken over all measurable estimators based on the observations in the sequence experiment. The posterior mean associated with (88) attains the upper bound up to a constant factor.

The proof is provided in Appendix B.14.

Theorem 6 is a minimax result for the stated Gaussian shared-function experiment. It does not imply the same lower bound for an unrestricted heterogeneous reinforcement-learning model without an explicit reduction to this experiment. Related conjugate Gaussian sequence analyses are discussed by Knapik et al. (2011).

Let τ0\tau_{0} denote the target-only precision in the same Gaussian sequence experiment. Since the contraction radius has order n−aαn^{-a_{\alpha}}, where aα=α2​α+d,a_{\alpha}=\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha+d}, the nominal ratio between the pooled and target-only contraction scales is

𝔫S−aατ0−aα=(𝔫Sτ0)−aα.\frac{\mathfrak{n}_{S}^{-a_{\alpha}}}{\tau_{0}^{-a_{\alpha}}}=\left(\frac{\mathfrak{n}_{S}}{\tau_{0}}\right)^{-a_{\alpha}}.

Thus, if 𝔫Sτ0⟶ρ∈(1,∞),\frac{\mathfrak{n}_{S}}{\tau_{0}}\longrightarrow\rho\in(1,\infty), the limiting ratio is ρ−aα<1\rho^{-a_{\alpha}}<1, corresponding to a constant-factor improvement in the nominal contraction scale. If 𝔫Sτ0⟶∞,\frac{\mathfrak{n}_{S}}{\tau_{0}}\longrightarrow\infty, the ratio tends to zero. These comparisons concern contraction and minimax scales. They do not by themselves imply strict frequentist risk improvement for a fixed target truth. In the scalar sequence experiment (B.7), the posterior mean at precision nn is

θ^j,n=wj(n)(θ0​j⋆+n−1/2ξj).\widehat{\theta}_{j,n}=w_{j}(n)\left(\theta_{0j}^{\star}+n^{-1/2}\xi_{j}\right).

Its exact frequentist risk at a fixed f0f_{0} is therefore

ℛn​(f0):=𝔼f0​[‖f^n−f0‖ℍ2]=∑j≥1[(θ0​j⋆)2(1+n​λj)2+n​λj2(1+n​λj)2].\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{n}(f_{0}):=\mathbb{E}_{f_{0}}\left[\|\widehat{f}_{n}-f_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]=\sum_{j\geq 1}\left[\frac{(\theta_{0j}^{\star})^{2}}{(1+n\lambda_{j})^{2}}+\frac{n\lambda_{j}^{2}}{(1+n\lambda_{j})^{2}}\right]. (95)

Hence, for deterministic precisions n1>n0n_{1}>n_{0}, strict frequentist improvement at the fixed truth f0f_{0} occurs precisely when ℛn1​(f0)<ℛn0​(f0).\mathcal{R}_{n_{1}}(f_{0})<\mathcal{R}_{n_{0}}(f_{0}). This truth-specific comparison cannot be inferred from the minimax rate alone.

Proposition 2 (Exact Bayesian transfer gain from additional information).

Let FF be an ℍ\mathbb{H}-valued random element satisfying 𝔼​‖F‖ℍ2<∞,\mathbb{E}\|F\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}<\infty, and let 𝒟0⊆𝒟0​S\mathscr{D}_{0}\subseteq\mathscr{D}_{0S} be nested information sigma-fields. Define

m0=𝔼⁡[F∣𝒟0],m0​S=𝔼⁡[F∣𝒟0​S].m_{0}=\mathbb{E}\left[F\mid\mathscr{D}_{0}\right],\quad m_{0S}=\mathbb{E}\left[F\mid\mathscr{D}_{0S}\right].

Then

𝔼⁡[‖F−m0‖ℍ2]−𝔼⁡[‖F−m0​S‖ℍ2]=𝔼⁡[‖m0​S−m0‖ℍ2]≥0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|F-m_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\|F-m_{0S}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\|m_{0S}-m_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]\geq 0. (96)

The inequality is strict if and only if

ℙ⁡(m0​S≠m0)>0.\mathbb{P}\left(m_{0S}\neq m_{0}\right)>0.

If the two conditional laws are Gaussian with positive trace-class conditional covariance operators C0C_{0} and C0​SC_{0S}, then

𝔼⁡[‖F−m0‖ℍ2]−𝔼⁡[‖F−m0​S‖ℍ2]=𝔼⁡[tr⁡(C0−C0​S)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|F-m_{0}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\|F-m_{0S}\|_{\mathbb{H}}^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{tr}\left(C_{0}-C_{0S}\right)\right]. (97)

The proof is provided in Appendix B.15.

Proposition 2 is a prior-averaged statement under correct specification. It does not imply pointwise frequentist risk dominance for a fixed target truth. Such a conclusion requires a truth-specific comparison such as (95), rather than a minimax rate alone.
