Theorem 7 separates three sources of offline policy loss: restricted-action coverage, target Q-function estimation error, and pessimism. The coverage gap cβ(0)c_{\beta}^{(0)} and the concentrability coefficients Cβ(0)C_{\beta}^{(0)} and Cπ,β(0)C_{\pi,\beta}^{(0)} are population quantities. The theorem is pathwise in the posterior mean and uncertainty functions. No assumption is imposed on the realized sizes of ee,N(0)e_{e,N}^{(0)} or 𝔭e,N(0)\mathfrak{p}_{e,N}^{(0)}. Their statistical rates, when available from the preceding posterior analysis, may be substituted directly into (102). In particular, an L2​(PX(0))L^{2}(P_{X}^{(0)}) posterior-contraction result can support the average-performance bound only after the corresponding posterior-mean and posterior-uncertainty norms have been controlled. It does not by itself imply the uniform quantities appearing in (101). Likewise, cβ(0)≡0c_{\beta}^{(0)}\equiv 0 eliminates the restricted-action approximation error but does not by itself establish either estimation accuracy or concentrability.

The preceding results address distinct stages of the transfer-learning procedure. The source-selection theory controls posterior weight on predictively inferior subsets. Theorem 3 transfers verified oracle and Bellman-perturbation bounds to the target working posterior. Theorem 4 identifies the full-rank regime in which the target precision determines the contraction order, while Theorem 5 and Theorem 6 establish the pooled rate and its minimax optimality in the exact shared-function experiment. The offline result Theorem 7 adds support coverage and norm conversion to translate target Q-function accuracy into policy performance.

5 Experiments

We evaluate Bayesian transfer Gaussian-process Q-learning (BT-GP-OQL) in a unified synthetic benchmark designed to investigate the effects of task heterogeneity, imbalanced behavior coverage, Bellman bootstrapping, and target-aware source selection in offline reinforcement learning. By varying a common per-task sample size and evaluating all performance metrics within the same Monte Carlo replications, the experimental design enables systematic comparisons of source-selection accuracy, target Q-function estimation, negative-transfer behavior, uncertainty-aware pessimism, and offline policy quality. This unified setting also allows us to examine how these aspects of transfer learning evolve as the amount of available training data increases. The implementation retains the multi-task GP covariance structure and conservative target Bellman pseudo-responses specified in Algorithm 2, while incorporating practical procedures for predictive source scoring, numerical stabilization, and final transfer acceptance.

5.1 Common experimental setup

The state space is 𝒮=[0,1]2\mathcal{S}=[0,1]^{2}, and the action space is 𝒜={1,2,3,4}\mathcal{A}=\{1,2,3,4\}. Each GP input is represented by a state-action pair x=(s,a)x=(s,a), with state dependence modeled through a continuous kernel and action dependence captured by a discrete-action covariance. We consider one target task and five source tasks,

𝒯={M(0),M(1),M(2),M(3),M(4),M(5)},\mathcal{T}=\{M^{(0)},M^{(1)},M^{(2)},M^{(3)},M^{(4)},M^{(5)}\},

where the source tasks are labeled good1, good2, weak, bad1, and bad2, respectively. For each experimental configuration, all tasks have the same trajectory length:

n0=n1=⋯=n5=n,n∈{30,50,80,120,170}.n_{0}=n_{1}=\cdots=n_{5}=n,\qquad n\in\{30,50,80,120,170\}.

Combining the five sample sizes with 30 Monte Carlo seeds yields 150 offline task-family runs. For each seed, the underlying latent functions are held fixed across sample sizes, and trajectory generation uses random seeds independent of nn. As a result, shorter trajectories form prefixes of the corresponding longer trajectories. The final target evaluation states are also held fixed across sample sizes within each seed.

To construct the random spectral functions, we set d=2d=2, α=1.5\alpha=1.5, and M=80M=80. The nonzero frequency vectors in {0,…,8}2\{0,\ldots,8\}^{2} are ordered by increasing squared Euclidean norm, with ties resolved lexicographically, and denoted by m1,…,mMm_{1},\ldots,m_{M}. The corresponding basis functions are defined as

ϕj​(s)=∏ℓ=12{1,mj​ℓ=0,2​cos⁡(π​mj​ℓ​sℓ),mj​ℓ>0.\phi_{j}(s)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{2}\begin{cases}1,&m_{j\ell}=0,\\ \sqrt{2}\cos(\pi m_{j\ell}s_{\ell}),&m_{j\ell}>0.\end{cases}

For each component function and Monte Carlo seed, independent random signs ξj∈{−1,1}\xi_{j}\in\{-1,1\} and amplitudes uj∼Unif⁡(0.8,1.2)u_{j}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0.8,1.2) are used to generate the spectral coefficients:

θ~j=ξj​uj​j−(α/d+1/2),θj=R​θ~j(∑ℓ=1Mℓ2​α/d​θ~ℓ2)1/2,F⁡(s)=∑j=1Mθj​ϕj​(s).\widetilde{\theta}_{j}=\xi_{j}u_{j}j^{-(\alpha/d+1/2)},\qquad\theta_{j}=\frac{R\widetilde{\theta}_{j}}{\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{M}\ell^{2\alpha/d}\widetilde{\theta}_{\ell}^{2}\right)^{1/2}},\qquad F(s)=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\theta_{j}\phi_{j}(s).

This normalization ensures that ∑j=1Mj2​α/d​θj2=R2\sum_{j=1}^{M}j^{2\alpha/d}\theta_{j}^{2}=R^{2}. We set R=2R=2 for the shared state component F0F_{0} and the source-specific perturbation functions HkH_{k}, and R=1.5R=1.5 for the four action-dependent components FaF_{a}. This construction generates finite-dimensional random functions satisfying a Sobolev-type weighted coefficient constraint. Since the functions are finite cosine expansions, they are smooth and are not claimed to possess exact regularity α\alpha. Moreover, averaging estimation errors over this random function ensemble does not constitute an estimate of the worst-case Sobolev risk.

The target optimal action-value function is constructed as

Q⋆(0)​(s,a)=−0.35+0.10​F0​(s)+ba+0.035​Fa​(s),b=(0.13,0.10,0.07,−0.10).Q_{\star}^{(0)}(s,a)=-0.35+0.10F_{0}(s)+b_{a}+0.035F_{a}(s),\qquad b=(0.13,0.10,0.07,-0.10).

The action-specific offsets assign a lower baseline value to the fourth action, which is also sampled infrequently under the target behavior policy. To introduce varying degrees of task mismatch, the source optimal action-value functions are defined by

Q⋆(k)(s,a)=Q⋆(0)(s,a)+ckHk(s)+dk,a,k=1,…,5,Q_{\star}^{(k)}(s,a)=Q_{\star}^{(0)}(s,a)+c_{k}H_{k}(s)+d_{k,a},\qquad k=1,\ldots,5,

where the task-specific coefficients are given in Table 1. Sources 1 and 2 are designed to be closely related to the target task, whereas source 3 introduces a larger perturbation and remains eligible for inclusion in the empirical near-oracle reference class. Sources 4 and 5 are designated as potentially harmful because they combine substantial Q-function mismatch with action-specific offsets favoring the fourth action. These design-based classifications are distinguished from the empirical assessment of source usefulness through target prediction risk and policy performance.

For each task kk, the initial state is sampled uniformly from [0,1]2[0,1]^{2}, and subsequent states evolve according to

St+1(k)=clip[0,1]2⁡{0.55​St(k)+0.45​(1/2,1/2)+uAt(k)+vk+ζt},ζt∼N⁡(0,0.062​I2),S_{t+1}^{(k)}=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]^{2}}\left\{0.55S_{t}^{(k)}+0.45(1/2,1/2)+u_{A_{t}^{(k)}}+v_{k}+\zeta_{t}\right\},\qquad\zeta_{t}\sim N(0,0.06^{2}I_{2}), (103)

where u1=(−0.05,0)u_{1}=(-0.05,0), u2=(0.05,0)u_{2}=(0.05,0), u3=(0,−0.05)u_{3}=(0,-0.05), and u4=(0,0.05)u_{4}=(0,0.05) specify the action-dependent state shifts, while vkv_{k} represents the task-specific transition shift. The behavior policy selects actions independently of the current state, with action probabilities β0=(0.323,0.323,0.324,0.030)\beta_{0}=(0.323,0.323,0.324,0.030), βk=(0.315,0.315,0.320,0.050)\beta_{k}=(0.315,0.315,0.320,0.050), and ≥1\geq 1. With discount factor γ=0.95\gamma=0.95, the reward is constructed from the prescribed optimal Q-function as

rt(k)=Q⋆(k)​(St(k),At(k))−γ​maxa′​Q⋆(k)​(St+1(k),a′)+ϵt,ϵt∼N⁡(0,0.082).r_{t}^{(k)}=Q_{\star}^{(k)}(S_{t}^{(k)},A_{t}^{(k)})-\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}}Q_{\star}^{(k)}(S_{t+1}^{(k)},a^{\prime})+\epsilon_{t},\qquad\epsilon_{t}\sim N(0,0.08^{2}).

Taking conditional expectations verifies that Q⋆(k)Q_{\star}^{(k)} satisfies the Bellman optimality equation for the constructed task. These prespecified optimal Q-functions are used to generate rewards and evaluate estimation errors. During training, however, Bellman pseudo-responses are constructed using estimated continuation values rather than oracle Q⋆Q_{\star} labels. The implementation uses the known behavior probabilities with a support threshold of τβ=0.01\tau_{\beta}=0.01. Since all four actions have probabilities above this threshold, Cβ​(s)=𝒜C_{\beta}(s)=\mathcal{A} throughout the benchmark, despite the limited coverage of the fourth action. This setting allows the effect of uncertainty-aware pessimism to be evaluated without excluding the rarely sampled action from the admissible action set.

For the sample-size comparisons, we use the nominal reference scale Nnom=n0+n1+n2=3​n,N_{\mathrm{nom}}=n_{0}+n_{1}+n_{2}=3n, corresponding to the target task and the two core source tasks. This quantity represents the nominal number of observations rather than the effective information size appearing in the theoretical analysis. The final GP model based on the selected source subset uses n⁡(1+|S^|)n(1+|\widehat{S}|) observations, where S^\widehat{S} may include the weak source or be empty. To provide an additional diagnostic of temporal dependence, we estimate an autocorrelation-based effective sample size for each task. Specifically, effective sample sizes are computed for the two state coordinates s1s_{1} and s2s_{2}, the reward, and the indicator of selecting action 4, using an initial-positive- autocorrelation sum with at most min⁡(30,⌊n/4⌋)\min(30,\lfloor n/4\rfloor) lags. The median of these four estimates is recorded as the task-level diagnostic effective sample size. This quantity is used only for descriptive purposes and does not replace the mixing conditions or effective sample sizes required by the theoretical analysis.

5.2 Gaussian-process implementation and source selection

All fits use zero prior mean and a separable state-action kernel

kin((s,a),(s′,a′))=0.52(1+z)exp(−z)[𝟏{a=a′}+0.03𝟏{a≠a′}],z=3​‖s−s′‖20.30.k_{\mathrm{in}}((s,a),(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}))=0.5^{2}(1+z)\exp(-z)\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{a=a^{\prime}\}+0.03\mathbf{1}\{a\neq a^{\prime}\}\bigr],\quad z=\frac{\sqrt{3}\|s-s^{\prime}\|_{2}}{0.30}.

The state factor corresponds to a Matérn-3/23/2 kernel, with smoothness parameter ν=1.5\nu=1.5 and length scale ℓ=0.30\ell=0.30. For an active task set, the multi-task covariance is

kMT​((k,x),(ℓ,x′))=Ktask​(k,ℓ)​kin​(x,x′),Ktask=(1−ρ)​I+ρ​𝟏𝟏⊤.k_{\mathrm{MT}}((k,x),(\ell,x^{\prime}))=K_{\mathrm{task}}(k,\ell)k_{\mathrm{in}}(x,x^{\prime}),\qquad K_{\mathrm{task}}=(1-\rho)I+\rho\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}.

For source selection, we fit a separate two-task Gaussian process jointly to the target task and each candidate source, using a task-correlation parameter of ρ=0.88\rho=0.88. For the final multi-task GP fits, we set ρ=0.92\rho=0.92. The target-only baseline uses the corresponding single-task kernel, which is independent of ρ\rho. Posterior means and latent-function variances are computed using exact GP regression with Cholesky factorization and diagonal pseudo-observation noise covariance matrices. To improve numerical stability, an initial diagonal stabilization term of 10−810^{-8} is added to the GP covariance matrix before Cholesky factorization. All available training observations are retained without imposing a predefined sample-size cap. At the largest sample size, the all-source GP fit therefore uses 6×170=10206\times 170=1020 observations.

During the Bellman bootstrapping stage, a separate GP model is fitted for each task, with μe−1(k)\mu_{e-1}^{(k)} and σe−1(k)\sigma_{e-1}^{(k)} denoting the corresponding posterior mean and latent standard deviation, respectively. At epoch ee, the raw target and source responses are

zi,e(0)\displaystyle z_{i,e}^{(0)} =ri(0)+γ​maxa′∈Cβ​(si′)​{μe−1(0)​(si′,a′)−0.75​σe−1(0)​(si′,a′)},\displaystyle=r_{i}^{(0)}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in C_{\beta}(s_{i}^{\prime})}\left\{\mu^{(0)}_{e-1}(s_{i}^{\prime},a^{\prime})-0.75\sigma^{(0)}_{e-1}(s_{i}^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right\}, (104)
zi,e(k)\displaystyle z_{i,e}^{(k)} =ri(k)+γ​maxa′∈𝒜​μe−1(k)​(si′,a′),k≥1.\displaystyle=r_{i}^{(k)}+\gamma\max_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\mu^{(k)}_{e-1}(s_{i}^{\prime},a^{\prime}),\quad k\geq 1. (105)

In the first epoch, the continuation-value estimates are set to zero, yielding zi,1(k)=ri(k)z_{i,1}^{(k)}=r_{i}^{(k)}. To improve numerical stability during iterative Bellman bootstrapping, subsequent pseudo-responses are updated using the following relaxation scheme:

yi,1(k)=zi,1(k),yi,e(k)=0.55​yi,e−1(k)+0.45​zi,e(k),e≥2.y_{i,1}^{(k)}=z_{i,1}^{(k)},\qquad y_{i,e}^{(k)}=0.55y_{i,e-1}^{(k)}+0.45z_{i,e}^{(k)},\quad e\geq 2.

The target pseudo-observation variance follows the uncertainty weighting used in Algorithm 2,

vi,e(0)=0.082+[σe−1(0)​(si,ai)]2.v_{i,e}^{(0)}=0.08^{2}+\bigl[\sigma_{e-1}^{(0)}(s_{i},a_{i})\bigr]^{2}.

For source tasks the implementation additionally uses vi,e(k)=3​(0.082)+0.10​[σe−1(k)​(si,ai)]2v_{i,e}^{(k)}=3(0.08^{2})+0.10[\sigma_{e-1}^{(k)}(s_{i},a_{i})]^{2}. At initialization, the current-state variance is set to 0.520.5^{2}. Relaxation and the source variance rule are numerical choices of this simulation implementation, rather than extra theoretical guarantees.

To monitor the stability of the taskwise Bellman updates, we construct an auxiliary evaluation grid 𝒢\mathcal{G} by pairing 180 states sampled under the target behavior policy with all four actions. At epoch ee, the maximum change in posterior mean predictions across tasks and grid points is defined as

de=max0≤k≤5⁡maxx∈𝒢​|μe(k)​(x)−μe−1(k)​(x)|.d_{e}=\max_{0\leq k\leq 5}\max_{x\in\mathcal{G}}\left|\mu_{e}^{(k)}(x)-\mu_{e-1}^{(k)}(x)\right|. (106)

Each run performs between four and 20 epochs. After the minimum of four epochs, the procedure terminates when de≤0.015d_{e}\leq 0.015, or when ded_{e} exceeds 1.6 times the smallest change observed among eligible epochs for two consecutive epochs. The pseudo-responses and associated working variances are retained from the eligible epoch with the smallest ded_{e}, with rollback to an earlier epoch if necessary. This selection criterion relies exclusively on changes in fitted posterior means and does not require knowledge of the true optimal Q-functions Q⋆(k)Q_{\star}^{(k)}. Source selection is then performed using the retained pseudo-data, followed by a single final joint multi-task GP fit. The resulting implementation therefore adopts a staged approximation to the joint Bellman recursion, rather than updating source-selection decisions at every bootstrap epoch.

To assess the predictive contribution of each candidate source kk to the target task, we compare a target-only GP with a two-task GP fitted jointly to the target and source kk. The retained target pseudo-data are randomly partitioned into three folds. For each fold ff, μ−f,k\mu_{-f,k} and s−f,k2s^{2}_{-f,k} denote the target predictive mean and latent variance obtained by excluding the target observations in fold ff while retaining all observations from source kk. The subscript ∅\varnothing denotes the corresponding target-only fit. Using the retained target pseudo-observation variances vi(0)v_{i}^{(0)}, we define the cross-validated predictive score difference as

Lk=∑f=13∑i∈flog⁡φ⁡(yi(0),μ−f,k​(xi),s−f,k2​(xi)+vi(0))φ⁡(yi(0),μ−f,∅​(xi),s−f,∅2​(xi)+vi(0)),L_{k}=\sum_{f=1}^{3}\sum_{i\in f}\log\frac{\varphi(y_{i}^{(0)};\mu_{-f,k}(x_{i}),s^{2}_{-f,k}(x_{i})+v_{i}^{(0)})}{\varphi(y_{i}^{(0)};\mu_{-f,\varnothing}(x_{i}),s^{2}_{-f,\varnothing}(x_{i})+v_{i}^{(0)})}, (107)

where φ⁡(⋅,m,v)\varphi(\cdot;m,v) denotes the Gaussian density with mean mm and variance vv.

To account for distributional differences between the target and source tasks, we compute the squared maximum mean discrepancy MMD^k2\widehat{\mathrm{MMD}}_{k}^{2} using a Gaussian kernel on the normalized state-action representation (s1,s2,a/4)(s_{1},s_{2},a/4). The kernel bandwidth is set to the median positive pairwise distance among the combined target and source observations. We use the biased all-pairs MMD estimator, restricting this calculation to the first min⁡(n,120)\min(n,120) observations from each task. The resulting source inclusion score and preliminary selected subset are defined by

p^k=logit−1⁡{logit⁡(0.35)+0.60​Lk−0.08​n​MMD^k2},S^pre={k:p^k≥0.5}.\widehat{p}_{k}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left\{\operatorname{logit}(0.35)+0.60L_{k}-0.08n\widehat{\mathrm{MMD}}_{k}^{2}\right\},\qquad\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{pre}}=\{k:\widehat{p}_{k}\geq 0.5\}. (108)

Although the figures use the term “posterior inclusion probability” for consistency with the implementation, p^k\widehat{p}_{k} represents an empirical-Bayes-style inclusion weight based on tempered predictive scores, rather than an exact spike-and-slab posterior obtained by integrating over all source subsets. Furthermore, the Bellman pseudo-responses and their working variances are computed before the cross-validation folds are formed and remain fixed throughout the scoring procedure. The Bellman regression stage is not repeated within individual folds. Consequently, these scores serve as conditional predictive model-comparison diagnostics rather than independent validation of the complete adaptive learning procedure.

For a nonempty preliminary subset S^pre\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{pre}}, we perform an additional two-fold target-predictive comparison between the selected source subset and the target-only model. Let LgateL_{\mathrm{gate}} denote the corresponding aggregate predictive score difference, computed analogously to (107). Assigning equal prior weights to the two candidates, we define the final transfer acceptance score and selected source subset as

ptr=logit−1⁡(0.70​Lgate),S^={S^pre,ptr≥0.5,∅,ptr<0.5.p_{\mathrm{tr}}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(0.70L_{\mathrm{gate}}),\qquad\widehat{S}=\begin{cases}\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{pre}},&p_{\mathrm{tr}}\geq 0.5,\\ \varnothing,&p_{\mathrm{tr}}<0.5.\end{cases}

If S^pre=∅\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{pre}}=\varnothing, the final comparison is omitted, ptrp_{\mathrm{tr}} is recorded as missing, and the target-only model is retained. We report the frequencies of empty preliminary subsets, explicit transfer rejections, and overall target-only selection separately. This data-dependent acceptance rule provides a mechanism for reverting to target-only learning when the preliminary transfer model fails to improve the predictive score. However, it does not guarantee non-degradation of population target Q-function risk or policy performance in finite samples.

5.3 Evaluation protocol and connection to theory

We evaluate three GP-based estimators: Target-only (S=∅S=\varnothing), All-source (S={1,…,5}S=\{1,\ldots,5\}), and BT-GP-OQL (S=S^S=\widehat{S}). All three estimators use the same retained taskwise pseudo-responses for their respective active tasks. As a simulation-based benchmark, we additionally consider an Oracle-safe reference that evaluates all eight subsets of {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}, including the empty subset, and selects the one minimizing the empirical target Q-function risk on an independent set of 700 evaluation states. The selected oracle model is subsequently assessed on the common final test set, which is distinct from the states used for oracle selection. This benchmark provides a restricted finite-sample reference rather than the unrestricted population oracle considered in the theoretical analysis. For all methods except the no-pessimism ablation, the offline policy is obtained by maximizing the pessimistic posterior value estimate over the behavior-supported action set:

π^S​(s)=arg⁡maxa∈Cβ​(s)​{μS(0)​(s,a)−0.75​σS(0)​(s,a)}.\widehat{\pi}_{S}(s)=\arg\max_{a\in C_{\beta}(s)}\left\{\mu_{S}^{(0)}(s,a)-0.75\sigma_{S}^{(0)}(s,a)\right\}. (109)

The Selected-source, no pessimism ablation instead uses arg⁡maxa​μS^(0)​(s,a)\arg\max_{a}\mu_{\widehat{S}}^{(0)}(s,a), based on the same final selected GP posterior. This comparison isolates the effect of pessimism during policy extraction while retaining the conservative Bellman updates used during training.

For each Monte Carlo seed, we generate m=1600m=1600 evaluation states from a target-behavior trajectory following a burn-in period of 60 transitions. All four actions are evaluated at each state. For a fitted posterior mean Q^\widehat{Q}, the empirical target Q-function mean squared error is defined as

MSE^Q​(Q^)=14​m​∑j=1m∑a=14[Q^​(sj,a)−Q⋆(0)​(sj,a)]2,m=1600.\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}_{Q}(\widehat{Q})=\frac{1}{4m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{a=1}^{4}\left[\widehat{Q}(s_{j},a)-Q_{\star}^{(0)}(s_{j},a)\right]^{2},\qquad m=1600. (110)

This metric assigns equal weight to all four actions, regardless of their frequencies under the target behavior policy. To assess decision quality, we report the average optimal-Q score of the actions selected by a policy and the corresponding optimal-action Q gap:

J^​(π)\displaystyle\widehat{J}(\pi) =1m​∑j=1mQ⋆(0)​(sj,π⁡(sj)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}Q_{\star}^{(0)}(s_{j},\pi(s_{j})), (111)
G^Q​(π)\displaystyle\widehat{G}_{Q}(\pi) =1m​∑j=1m[maxa⁡Q⋆(0)​(sj,a)−Q⋆(0)​(sj,π⁡(sj))].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left[\max_{a}Q_{\star}^{(0)}(s_{j},a)-Q_{\star}^{(0)}(s_{j},\pi(s_{j}))\right].

The quantity G^Q​(π)\widehat{G}_{Q}(\pi) measures the average optimal-action Q gap at the evaluation states and should not be interpreted as the infinite-horizon policy value loss V⋆−VπV^{\star}-V^{\pi}. To complement this statewise comparison, we compute a separate rollout diagnostic G^80\widehat{G}_{80} based on 80-step discounted returns. The learned and true greedy policies are evaluated from 120 common initial states using identical transition-noise realizations. Reward noise is omitted during evaluation, and no terminal-value correction is applied to the truncated returns.

The designated harmful-source set is 𝒰={4,5}\mathcal{U}=\{4,5\}. We report the empirical frequency with which the final selected subset S^\widehat{S} contains at least one source in 𝒰\mathcal{U}, together with the frequency of retaining both core sources {1,2}\{1,2\}. To summarize the pre-gate inclusion scores, we also compute the factorized quantity

w𝒰=1−∏k∈𝒰(1−p^k).w_{\mathcal{U}}=1-\prod_{k\in\mathcal{U}}(1-\widehat{p}_{k}).

The complementary quantity 1−w𝒰1-w_{\mathcal{U}} is labeled “posterior no unsafe” in the figures. These quantities are constructed from the approximate marginal inclusion scores and do not represent posterior probabilities obtained from a joint source-subset model after the final transfer gate. To evaluate proximity to the restricted oracle reference, we define the empirical target-risk gap on the final test states as

ΔR=MSE^Q​(Q^BT)−MSE^Q​(Q^oracle).\Delta_{R}=\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}_{Q}(\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{BT}})-\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}_{Q}(\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{oracle}}).

A run is classified as near-oracle when

ΔR≤max⁡{0.010, 0.15​MSE^Q​(Q^oracle)}.\Delta_{R}\leq\max\left\{0.010,\;0.15\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}_{Q}(\widehat{Q}_{\mathrm{oracle}})\right\}. (112)

We report the continuous risk gap alongside this binary indicator, since the fixed absolute tolerance may be relatively permissive when the oracle estimation error is small. To assess negative transfer in policy quality, we compare each transfer policy with the target-only baseline using the paired difference

ΔJ​(S)=J^​(π^S)−J^​(π^∅).\Delta_{J}(S)=\widehat{J}(\widehat{\pi}_{S})-\widehat{J}(\widehat{\pi}_{\varnothing}).

We report both the frequency of negative transfer, defined by ΔJ<0\Delta_{J}<0, and the frequency of material degradation, defined by ΔJ<−0.010\Delta_{J}<-0.010. The latter threshold specifies a practical effect-size criterion and does not replace the zero-threshold definition of negative transfer.

At epoch ee, the continuation-value function used by the algorithm for task kk is denoted by Ve−1(k),algV_{e-1}^{(k),\mathrm{alg}}, including the pessimistic adjustment for the target task in Equations (104)– (105). The bootstrap discrepancy is measured by

Be=16​∑k=051n​∑i=1nγ2​[Ve−1(k),alg​(si′)−maxa⁡Q⋆(k)​(si′,a)]2.B_{e}=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{k=0}^{5}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma^{2}\left[V_{e-1}^{(k),\mathrm{alg}}(s_{i}^{\prime})-\max_{a}Q_{\star}^{(k)}(s_{i}^{\prime},a)\right]^{2}.

This quantity measures the squared discrepancy between the continuation values used by the algorithm and the corresponding optimal continuation values. On the monitoring grid consisting of 180 states and four actions, we approximate the algorithm- aligned, unrelaxed Bellman update using 12 fresh transitions for each state-action pair. The mean squared discrepancy between this Monte Carlo Bellman approximation and the fitted posterior mean μe(k)\mu_{e}^{(k)} is denoted by DeD_{e} and averaged across tasks. We additionally record the successive-iterate change ded_{e} defined in Equation (106) and the maximum grid-based Q-function error

Ue=maxk,x∈𝒢⁡|μe(k)​(x)−Q⋆(k)​(x)|.U_{e}=\max_{k,x\in\mathcal{G}}\left|\mu_{e}^{(k)}(x)-Q_{\star}^{(k)}(x)\right|.

These diagnostics characterize the taskwise Bellman bootstrapping stage rather than the final selected multi-task GP posterior. Moreover, the grid-based maxima and Monte Carlo Bellman approximations should not be identified with exact uniform-norm errors or population Bellman residuals.

To characterize empirical scaling over the simulated sample-size range, we fit the following log-linear model for each positive outcome Er,nE_{r,n} and Monte Carlo seed rr:

log⁡Er,n=cr−β​log⁡(3​n)+εr,n,\log E_{r,n}=c_{r}-\beta\log(3n)+\varepsilon_{r,n},

where crc_{r} denotes a seed-specific fixed effect. The quantity 3​n3n is the nominal combined sample size of the target task and the two core sources, rather than a theoretically established effective sample size. In addition to the primary seed-fixed-effect regressions, we report pooled estimates and descriptive fits restricted to runs without selected harmful sources or satisfying the near-oracle criterion. Since these restrictions depend on observed outcomes, the corresponding estimates are treated as supplementary descriptive summaries rather than the primary rate analysis. The theoretical reference exponents are 2​α/(2​α+d)=0.62\alpha/(2\alpha+d)=0.6 for squared estimation error and α/(2​α+d)=0.3\alpha/(2\alpha+d)=0.3 for root estimation error. The exponent 0.30.3 is also displayed as a reference for policy-related outcomes, without asserting that it provides an exact decay rate for the empirical optimal-action Q gap in Equation (111).

All reported means are computed over 30 Monte Carlo seeds at each sample size nn. Within each seed, method comparisons are based on common underlying trajectories and evaluation states. Error bars for source-inclusion scores and pessimism gains reproduce the implementation’s mean ±1.96\pm 1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors. The rate tables report nominal 95% confidence intervals obtained from ordinary linear regression with seed fixed effects. These intervals are neither seed-cluster-adjusted nor bootstrap-based, although the nested sample-size design induces dependence among observations from the same seed. The available experimental summaries provide standard errors for BT-GP-OQL Q-function estimation error, source-inclusion scores, and pessimism gains, but do not include paired standard errors for every comparison between methods. We therefore interpret the reported differences as empirical average improvements unless the available uncertainty estimates support a stronger statistical conclusion.

5.4 Simulation results

5.4.1 Target-aware source selection and the target-only gate

Table 2 and Figure 1 show increasing separation between similar and designated harmful sources. The mean inclusion score of good1 increases from 0.423 to 0.788, and that of good2 increases from 0.425 to 0.803. In contrast, the scores of bad1 and bad2 decrease from 0.201 and 0.101 to 0.055 and 0.025. The weak source remains competitive, with its mean score rising from 0.485 to 0.763. This behavior is consistent with selecting sources for their predictive contribution rather than imposing exact recovery of {1,2}\{1,2\}.

The frequency of selecting both core sources rises from 13.3% to 90.0%, whereas the final harmful-source selection frequencies are 3.3%, 10.0%, 6.7%, 0%, and 0% over the five sample sizes. Thus no harmful source is selected in the 30 runs at either n=120n=120 or n=170n=170, although this observed zero frequency is not a zero population probability. The mean factorized harmful-source score decreases from 0.285 to 0.079. Table 3 also shows that the near-oracle success frequency rises from 60.0% to 100%. More informatively, the mean continuous risk gap decreases from 0.01196 to 0.00045; the mean relative gap decreases from 45.8% to 12.4%. The 100% success rate should be read together with the tolerance in Equation (112), rather than as exact oracle recovery.

The final target-only comparison is summarized in Table 4 and Figure 2. At n=30n=30, seven runs have no preliminary transfer proposal and three additional runs reject a nonempty proposal, giving ten target-only runs in total. At n=50n=50 the corresponding numbers are two and one; at n=80n=80 there is one explicit rejection and no preliminary-empty run. At n=120n=120 and n=170n=170, all runs retain a transfer proposal. The mean final transfer score, conditional on gate evaluation, increases from 0.781 to 0.993. These observations document the fallback mechanism; they do not show that it guarantees policy safety, since its criterion is conditional predictive density rather than policy return.

5.4.2 Target-function estimation and transfer gain

The final target-function errors in Table 5 decrease with sample size for all four methods. Mean BT MSE decreases from 0.04550 at n=30n=30 to 0.00744 at n=170n=170, an 83.7% reduction over the simulated range. It is below the target-only mean at every sample size. The reductions relative to the target-only aggregate MSE are 17.8%, 21.4%, 20.2%, 12.4%, and 17.2%, respectively. The restricted oracle reference has the lowest mean error, and the BT–oracle gap becomes small at the largest sample size. All-source regression has higher mean MSE than target-only throughout this sequence. Figure 3 therefore displays a persistent average advantage for selective transfer over indiscriminate pooling. The supplied summaries do not establish a positive paired gain in every seed or provide paired uncertainty for each MSE contrast.

5.4.3 Negative-transfer safety and offline policy quality

Table 6 and Figure 4 show that all-source transfer can harm the target policy despite using more observations. Its mean safety gap is negative at all five sample sizes, reaching −0.05745-0.05745 at n=80n=80. BT reduces this average harm substantially, but does not eliminate it in every setting: its mean gaps at n=50n=50, 8080, and 120120 are −0.00913-0.00913, −0.01954-0.01954, and −0.00180-0.00180. In particular, lower average QQ-MSE does not ensure a positive policy-value gap, because the two metrics weight errors differently and policy extraction depends on action ranking and uncertainty. The material negative-transfer frequencies correspond to 18, 20, 21, 17, and 8 all-source failures out of 30 runs, compared with 3, 8, 8, 2, and 0 BT failures. These results support a reduction in the observed frequency and magnitude of material harm, not finite-sample non-degradation. At n=170n=170, the zero-threshold BT negative-transfer rate is still 16.7% even though no run crosses the material threshold −0.010-0.010; reporting both thresholds prevents small negative gaps from being hidden.

For completeness, Table 7 gives the policy-quality means themselves. The BT action gap decreases from 0.06509 to 0.00905, an 86.1% reduction, and the 80-step rollout gap decreases from 1.2449 to 0.1761. The two measures have the same overall direction, but different definitions and scales. Figure 5 provides descriptive support for improving target decision quality with additional data, without identifying the plotted QQ gap with the value-loss quantity in Theorem 5.

5.4.4 Contribution of uncertainty-aware pessimism

Table 8 reports the policy-extraction ablation on the same selected GP posterior. The mean gain from using μ−0.75​σ\mu-0.75\sigma rather than μ\mu is positive at every sample size and decreases from 0.05297 to 0.00381. The program’s nominal mean ±1.96\pm 1.96 SE intervals are above zero for all five displayed comparisons. These are unadjusted Monte Carlo intervals, not a simultaneous multiple-comparison statement. Figure 6 relates these gains to the action-4 selection frequencies. Without pessimism, the frequencies decrease from 49.17% to 2.02%; with pessimism, they decrease from 23.21% to 0.10%. Thus the conservative rule reduces the selection of the poorly covered fourth action, and its mean advantage becomes small when the action is rarely selected by either rule. This is evidence for the decision-stage contribution of uncertainty penalization in this benchmark. It does not isolate the effect of conservative pseudo-labels, which are shared by both policies.

5.4.5 Numerical Bellman stability and bootstrap error

Figure 7 shows that successive fitted-function changes decrease sharply from their initial values and reach approximately 0.020.02–0.030.03 near the end of the iterations. Table 9 reports the diagnostics at the retained epoch. The mean algorithm-aligned Bellman residual decreases from 0.0546 to 0.0191 as nn increases. The mean bootstrap discrepancy also decreases across sample sizes, from 0.3993 to 0.2149, although it generally increases with epoch within a fixed sample size. The corresponding pooled descriptive exponents are 0.560 (nominal interval [0.447,0.673][0.447,0.673]) for DeD_{e} and 0.297 ([0.100,0.493][0.100,0.493]) for BeB_{e}. These quantities must be distinguished. Small ded_{e} indicates small successive updates; it does not imply small error relative to Q⋆Q_{\star}. Here BeB_{e} includes target pessimism as well as function-estimation and bootstrap error, and the reported summaries do not separate these contributions. Moreover, only 20.0%–40.0% of runs meet the stopping tolerance. No run activates the growth guard, and one run at n=120n=120 retains an earlier epoch. The results support improved numerical behavior and smaller residuals with more data, but not verification that the bootstrap error converges to zero or that every fitted iteration satisfies the assumptions of Theorem 1.

5.4.6 Finite-range contraction slopes

Table 10 and Figure 8 summarize the seed-fixed-effect regressions. Over the nominal range Nnom=90N_{\mathrm{nom}}=90–510510, the estimated BT MSE exponent is 1.104, with a reported nominal interval of [0.948,1.260][0.948,1.260]. The restricted oracle exponent is 0.981 ([0.819,1.144][0.819,1.144]). The BT root-error exponent is exactly half the MSE exponent, 0.552 ([0.474,0.630][0.474,0.630]), because the corresponding run-level response is the square root of the same MSE. It is therefore not an independent rate confirmation. The action-gap exponent is 0.698 ([0.442,0.953][0.442,0.953]).

The slopes exceed the displayed nonparametric references over this finite range. This is not a test that the estimates equal the theoretical exponents. Theorem 3 concerns a posterior contraction guarantee under its assumptions, whereas the plotted curves measure the error of posterior means after finite, conservative bootstrapping. The truth ensemble has a fixed 80-term truncation and represents random functions rather than a worst-case class. In addition, the mean final selected source count rises from 1.2 to 2.9, so the information used by the estimator does not remain a constant multiple of the nominal core-source count across the finite grid. These features preclude interpreting the fitted exponent as an exact minimax exponent. The increased R2R^{2} of the fixed-effect fit also includes the seed intercepts; by itself it does not measure the quality of a universal power law. The result establishes a decreasing average estimation-error pattern in the reported range, not a separate proof of the posterior theorem.

5.5 Discussion of simulation results

The unified simulation benchmark provides empirical evidence for the benefits of target-aware Bayesian transfer in offline Q-learning with heterogeneous source tasks. As the available training data increase, the source-selection mechanism becomes more effective at distinguishing informative sources from those exhibiting substantial task mismatch. Closely related sources are increasingly retained, while the inclusion of designated harmful sources becomes less frequent. This improved source discrimination is accompanied by more accurate target Q-function estimation. Across all evaluated sample sizes, BT-GP-OQL achieves lower mean estimation error than both target-only learning and indiscriminate all-source transfer. Moreover, its estimation error progressively approaches that of the restricted oracle reference, suggesting that target-predictive source selection can exploit useful cross-task information while limiting the adverse effects of task heterogeneity.

The policy-level results further highlight the importance of combining source selection with uncertainty-aware pessimism. Compared with indiscriminate source sharing, BT-GP-OQL substantially reduces the observed frequency and magnitude of material negative transfer, although performance degradation relative to target-only learning is not eliminated in every finite-sample setting. The pessimistic policy-extraction rule also achieves higher average decision quality than its non-pessimistic counterpart when applied to the same fitted GP posterior. In particular, penalizing posterior uncertainty reduces the selection of the rarely observed fourth action, which is more susceptible to estimation uncertainty. Both the optimal-action Q gap and the truncated rollout gap decrease as the training sample size increases, indicating improved decision quality. These findings illustrate the complementary roles of target-aware source selection in controlling cross-task mismatch and posterior pessimism in addressing uncertainty associated with limited data coverage.

The experiments also reveal decreasing estimation errors and improved Bellman-update diagnostics as more data become available. The observed empirical decay rates are favorable over the investigated sample-size range, while the Bellman residual and bootstrap discrepancy generally decrease with increasing sample size. Nevertheless, these numerical patterns should be distinguished from the asymptotic guarantees established in the theoretical analysis. In particular, the empirical inclusion scores are approximate predictive weights rather than exact source-subset posterior probabilities, and the observed error-decay exponents are based on a finite-dimensional function ensemble and nominal sample sizes. They therefore do not directly verify posterior contraction or minimax optimality under the general assumptions of the theoretical framework. Furthermore, the finite-sample results do not establish unconditional protection against negative transfer. Taken together, the simulations support the practical value of integrating target-aware source selection, multi-task GP estimation, and uncertainty-aware conservative policy learning, while clarifying the statistical and empirical limitations of the proposed offline transfer framework.

6 Real data analysis

To complement the synthetic benchmark, we assess BT-GP-OQL using the human decision-making data released with Ben-Artzi et al. (2023a). We address two distinct empirical questions: whether cross-participant transfer improves decision quality relative to learning from target data alone, and whether target-aware selection identifies more useful sources than uniformly choosing the same number from a fixed candidate pool. The comparators are Target-only, BT-GP-OQL, and Random-mm, evaluated at γ∈{0,0.5,0.95}\gamma\in\{0,0.5,0.95\}. The actions and payoffs are genuine behavioral observations, although the reward schedules were generated by the experimental task rather than observed in a financial market. Accordingly, this application evaluates immediate action-selection quality on recorded histories; it does not identify the counterfactual long-horizon return of deploying a learned policy.

The original study analyzed 178 participants in a four-armed bandit experiment. Each participant completed four blocks of 50 trials, with two of four cards offered on each trial. Reward probabilities drifted over time, and feedback was available for the chosen card. Blocks alternated between gain and loss conditions, with recorded payoffs in {0,1}\{0,1\} and {−1,0}\{-1,0\}, respectively; different blocks used different cards (Ben-Artzi et al., 2023a). We start from the archived df_raw.csv, containing 40,600 trial records and 203 participant identifiers, rather than the processed subset used for the original behavioral comparisons (Ben-Artzi et al., 2023b). Thus, the raw-data count and the original study’s final analysis sample are different quantities. We check participant identifiers, trial order, offered and chosen cards, and condition-specific reward ranges. Invalid choices and missing rewards do not contribute fitting responses. For γ>0\gamma>0, nonterminal responses require consecutive valid observations within the same participant and block: missing trials and block boundaries are not bridged, and an unavailable successor is not treated as a terminal state. At γ=0\gamma=0, a valid immediate-reward observation can be used without a valid successor. These eligibility rules distinguish usable reward observations from usable transitions.

The preceding development protocol excluded 23 participants involved in exploratory screening and used a separate 24-participant cohort for calibration. The remaining 156 participants form the evaluation cohort. The configuration denoted C10 was locked using development data and is not recalibrated here. For each evaluation target ii, a frozen, outcome-independent assignment supplies seven distinct candidate source participants, CiC_{i}, from the other evaluation participants. The target never appears in its own source pool. The same assignments are used across methods and discounts; development and excluded participants are not reintroduced as sources. Each participant defines a constructed transfer task, with blocks retained as separate episodes. Local card identities are combined with block context without assuming that equally numbered cards have identical reward schedules across participants. Every comparison uses K=7K=7 candidate sources, even though 156 targets are evaluated. Sources can be shared between targets, so target-level analyses are not fully independent. The matched-size comparison and the additional γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 setting were introduced after the evaluation histories had been examined; they are therefore reported as post-hoc mechanism and sensitivity analyses, not as a new independent confirmation.

Within each block, using zero-based indices t=0,…,49t=0,\ldots,49, trials 0–29 are used for GP fitting, 30–34 for source screening and the final transfer gate, 35–38 for a later-validation diagnostic, and 40–49 for target evaluation. Trial 39 is not a fitting or validation-scoring response, but remains in the sequence and may supply the successor state for trial 38. Each participant contributes at most 120 fitting observations, so a joint fit with mm sources contains at most 120​(1+m)120(1+m) observations. Sources contribute only their fitting partitions. A fitting-partition boundary is not an episode terminal: the response at trial 29 can use the pre-choice state at trial 30, but not trial 30’s current reward. Only trial 49 is a true block terminal. Early and late validation use disjoint scoring responses, although their histories and successor states remain temporally related. Earlier recorded rewards may enter later pre-choice history summaries, but GP parameters remain frozen during evaluation. Test scores and the archived reward probabilities are excluded from fitting, screening, and gating.

For task kk, block bb, and trial tt, let 𝒪b,t(k)⊆{0,1,2,3}\mathcal{O}_{b,t}^{(k)}\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\} denote the offered pair. The working state is

sb,t(k)=(t49,cb(k),𝐞b,𝐨b,t(k),𝐧b,t(k)50,𝐫¯b,t(k)),s_{b,t}^{(k)}=\left(\frac{t}{49},\ c_{b}^{(k)},\ \mathbf{e}_{b},\ \mathbf{o}_{b,t}^{(k)},\ \frac{\mathbf{n}_{b,t}^{(k)}}{50},\ \overline{\mathbf{r}}_{b,t}^{(k)}\right),

where cb(k)c_{b}^{(k)} indicates the gain condition, 𝐞b\mathbf{e}_{b} encodes the block, 𝐨b,t(k)\mathbf{o}_{b,t}^{(k)} indicates available cards, and 𝐧b,t(k)\mathbf{n}_{b,t}^{(k)} and 𝐫¯b,t(k)\overline{\mathbf{r}}_{b,t}^{(k)} contain past selection counts and mean observed rewards. Histories reset at block boundaries. Unselected cards have count and mean initialized to zero, with the count distinguishing no experience from an observed zero mean. Only pre-choice information enters the state; this representation is not an assertion of a fully observed stationary Markov decision process. All maximizations are restricted to offered cards. A ridge-penalized choice model, fitted only to target training choices, retains offered actions whose estimated choice probability is at least 0.010.01. If thresholding removes both cards, the offered card with highest estimated probability is retained. All three target comparators use this same supported set, denoted 𝒞i​(s)\mathcal{C}_{i}(s). Sources use their offered pair without the target-specific support restriction. Random presentation of a pair is not interpreted as a uniform participant choice propensity.

Taskwise models, source scores, and selected subsets are recomputed separately for each γ∈{0,0.5,0.95}\gamma\in\{0,0.5,0.95\}. The unrelaxed Bellman response is

zb,t,e,γ(k)={rb,t(k),t=49,rb,t(k)+γ​maxa∈𝒞b,t+1(k)​{μe−1,γ(k)​(sb,t+1(k),a)−αk​σe−1,γ(k)​(sb,t+1(k),a)},t<49,z_{b,t,e,\gamma}^{(k)}=\begin{cases}r_{b,t}^{(k)},&t=49,\\[2.0pt] r_{b,t}^{(k)}+\gamma\displaystyle\max_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{b,t+1}^{(k)}}\left\{\mu_{e-1,\gamma}^{(k)}(s_{b,t+1}^{(k)},a)-\alpha_{k}\sigma_{e-1,\gamma}^{(k)}(s_{b,t+1}^{(k)},a)\right\},&t<49,\end{cases}

where 𝒞(0)\mathcal{C}^{(0)} is the supported target offer set, 𝒞(k)=𝒪(k)\mathcal{C}^{(k)}=\mathcal{O}^{(k)} for sources, α0=0.75\alpha_{0}=0.75, and αk=0\alpha_{k}=0 for k≥1k\geq 1. The nonterminal expression requires a valid successor, and continuation is initialized to zero. At γ=0\gamma=0, a single GP regression fits immediate rewards. Positive discounts use response relaxation with weight 0.450.45, at most 20 epochs, and the change-based stopping and rollback rules of the implementation. In particular, the γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 results arise from actual refitting, not interpolation between the other settings. The input kernel combines a Matérn-3/23/2 state kernel (length scale 0.300.30, signal standard deviation 0.500.50) with an action factor equal to one for matching actions and 0.030.03 otherwise. The joint task correlation matrix has unit diagonal and constant off-diagonal correlation: 0.880.88 for single-source screening and 0.920.92 for final joint fitting. Exact GP linear algebra is used. Target working variances are 0.25+σe−1,γ2​(s,a)0.25+\sigma_{e-1,\gamma}^{2}(s,a); source working variances are 0.75+0.10​σe−1,γ2​(s,a)0.75+0.10\sigma_{e-1,\gamma}^{2}(s,a). These are pseudo-response working variances, not a Gaussian generative model for binary payoffs. Final joint fits combine retained taskwise pseudo-responses and variances without adding validation or test responses to GP training.

For each target and discount, early-validation pseudo-responses and working variances are constructed from the training-only target continuation estimate and held fixed across candidates. Let ℓi,γ0\ell_{i,\gamma}^{0} be the summed univariate Gaussian log predictive density on trials 30–34 under Target-only, and ℓi​k,γpair\ell_{ik,\gamma}^{\mathrm{pair}} the corresponding score after including source kk with the screening task correlation. Write Δ​ℓi​k,γ=ℓi​k,γpair−ℓi,γ0\Delta\ell_{ik,\gamma}=\ell_{ik,\gamma}^{\mathrm{pair}}-\ell_{i,\gamma}^{0}. With ni,γfitn_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{fit}} usable target fitting responses, C10 uses

p~i​k,γ=logit−1⁡[logit⁡(0.50)+1.20​Δ​ℓi​k,γ−0.04​ni,γfit​D^i​k,γ],\widetilde{p}_{ik,\gamma}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\!\left[\operatorname{logit}(0.50)+1.20\,\Delta\ell_{ik,\gamma}-0.04\,n_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{fit}}\widehat{D}_{ik,\gamma}\right],

where D^i​k,γ\widehat{D}_{ik,\gamma} is the nonnegative empirical squared maximum mean discrepancy between target and source training inputs, using the radial-basis kernel and median bandwidth rule in the implementation. Sources with p~i​k,γ≥0.5\widetilde{p}_{ik,\gamma}\geq 0.5 form Si,γpreS_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{pre}}. This quantity is a tempered predictive inclusion score, not an exact full spike-and-slab subset posterior. For a nonempty preliminary subset, a final joint fit is compared with Target-only on the same early-validation responses:

qi,γ=logit−1⁡[logit⁡(0.50)+0.70​{ℓi,γjoint​(Si,γpre)−ℓi,γ0}].q_{i,\gamma}=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\!\left[\operatorname{logit}(0.50)+0.70\left\{\ell_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{joint}}(S_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{pre}})-\ell_{i,\gamma}^{0}\right\}\right].

The final subset S^i,γ\widehat{S}_{i,\gamma} equals Si,γpreS_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{pre}} when qi,γ≥0.5q_{i,\gamma}\geq 0.5 and is empty otherwise. An empty preliminary subset also yields Target-only, without computing a gate score. Screening and gating reuse early validation, so the gate is a model-selection rule, not independent evidence of finite-sample safety. C10 and all thresholds are fixed across discounts.

Target-only uses target fitting data; BT-GP-OQL additionally uses S^i,γ\widehat{S}_{i,\gamma}. To isolate the contribution of source identity at a matched source count, set mi,γ=|S^i,γ|m_{i,\gamma}=|\widehat{S}_{i,\gamma}| and let

𝔖i,γ={S⊆Ci:|S|=mi,γ},|𝔖i,γ|=(7mi,γ).\mathfrak{S}_{i,\gamma}=\{S\subseteq C_{i}:|S|=m_{i,\gamma}\},\qquad|\mathfrak{S}_{i,\gamma}|=\binom{7}{m_{i,\gamma}}.

Random-mm fits every subset in 𝔖i,γ\mathfrak{S}_{i,\gamma} as a separate policy, without an additional screening or gate step. All methods use identical target test records, GP settings, supported actions, and the decision rule

π^i,S,γ​(s)=arg⁡maxa∈𝒞i​(s)​{μ^i,S,γ​(s,a)−0.75​σ^i,S,γ​(s,a)}.\widehat{\pi}_{i,S,\gamma}(s)=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{i}(s)}\left\{\widehat{\mu}_{i,S,\gamma}(s,a)-0.75\widehat{\sigma}_{i,S,\gamma}(s,a)\right\}.

Thus, this design compares transfer and source identity selection; it does not separately identify the effect of decision-stage pessimism. Setting MECH_RANDOM_DRAWS = 35L permits complete enumeration because max0≤m≤7⁡(7m)=35\max_{0\leq m\leq 7}\binom{7}{m}=35. Actual subset counts and uniqueness are checked. Random-mm is the exact uniform mean of the separate subset-policy scores, not a posterior-mixture policy, majority vote, or test-selected best subset. It uses real source participants. When mi,γ=0m_{i,\gamma}=0, both BT-GP-OQL and Random-mm coincide with Target-only.

The archived prob1 and prob2 fields contain the favorable-outcome probabilities of the historically chosen and unchosen cards (Ben-Artzi et al., 2023b). They are mapped to the actual offered card identities and accessed only after the fitted model and its test actions have been frozen. They are reward probabilities, not behavior-policy propensities. For test record jj of target ii,

mi​j​(a)={pi​j​(a),gain condition,pi​j​(a)−1,loss condition,m_{ij}(a)=\begin{cases}p_{ij}(a),&\text{gain condition},\\ p_{ij}(a)-1,&\text{loss condition},\end{cases}

where the favorable loss outcome is zero. On the common evaluable test set ℐi\mathcal{I}_{i}, the expected immediate payoff and optimal-action gap are

J^i,γ​(π)=1|ℐi|​∑j∈ℐimi​j​(π⁡(si​j)),G^i,γ​(π)=1|ℐi|​∑j∈ℐi[maxa∈𝒪i​j⁡mi​j​(a)−mi​j​(π⁡(si​j))].\widehat{J}_{i,\gamma}(\pi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{i}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{i}}m_{ij}\!\left(\pi(s_{ij})\right),\qquad\widehat{G}_{i,\gamma}(\pi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{i}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{i}}\left[\max_{a\in\mathcal{O}_{ij}}m_{ij}(a)-m_{ij}\!\left(\pi(s_{ij})\right)\right].

The reference maximum uses the full offered pair, so the gap includes any loss caused by support restrictions. On identical test records, J^+G^\widehat{J}+\widehat{G} is the method-independent offered-pair oracle score. Payoff and gap are therefore complementary expressions of the same immediate action-selection quality, not independent confirmations. For Random-mm, define

J¯i,γrand=(7mi,γ)−1​∑S∈𝔖i,γJ^i,γ​(π^i,S,γ),\overline{J}_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{rand}}=\binom{7}{m_{i,\gamma}}^{-1}\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{S}_{i,\gamma}}\widehat{J}_{i,\gamma}(\widehat{\pi}_{i,S,\gamma}),

with an analogous gap. Subsets are averaged within target before targets receive equal weight. With Neval=156N_{\mathrm{eval}}=156, our principal contrasts are

Δ^transfer​(γ)=1Neval​∑i=1Neval(J^i,γBT−J^i,γtarget),Δ^selection​(γ)=1Neval​∑i=1Neval(J^i,γBT−J¯i,γrand).\widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{transfer}}(\gamma)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\left(\widehat{J}_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{BT}}-\widehat{J}_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{target}}\right),\qquad\widehat{\Delta}_{\mathrm{selection}}(\gamma)=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{eval}}}\left(\widehat{J}_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{BT}}-\overline{J}_{i,\gamma}^{\mathrm{rand}}\right).

The first measures transfer relative to target-only fitting; the second measures source identity selection conditional on the source count chosen by BT-GP-OQL. On trials 35–38, we evaluate single-source log predictive density (LPD) gains relative to Target-only, using frozen target-only continuation responses for each discount. Within each target, these per-trial gains are averaged separately over finally selected and excluded sources, and their difference is then averaged across eligible targets. Cases lacking either group are omitted from this diagnostic, not coded as zero; they remain in the main policy comparisons. This assesses prediction of working Bellman responses rather than accuracy against a known long-horizon value function. The early and later windows have disjoint scoring responses but retain temporal dependence. The intervals displayed in this section are 95% percentile intervals from 2,000 fixed-fit target-participant bootstrap draws. Subset scores are averaged within target before resampling, and each draw uses the same target indices across methods and discounts. These intervals are descriptive and conditional on the fitted models and frozen source assignments. They do not propagate all uncertainty from shared sources or model refitting, and the enumerated subsets are not treated as additional participants. Although the implementation also supports a separate participant-cohort resampling and joint-refitting procedure, those source-aware intervals are not the intervals shown in the present three-discount figures. In particular, no endpoint-discount interval is reused for γ=0.5\gamma=0.5.

The analysis covers 156 evaluation targets at each of the three discounts, yielding 468 target–discount groups before subset enumeration. Table 11 and Figure 9 show the same ordering of mean expected immediate payoff at every discount:

J¯BT​(γ)>J¯Random​-​m​(γ)>J¯Target−only​(γ),γ∈{0,0.5,0.95}.\overline{J}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\gamma)>\overline{J}_{\mathrm{Random}\text{-}m}(\gamma)>\overline{J}_{\mathrm{Target-only}}(\gamma),\qquad\gamma\in\{0,0.5,0.95\}. (113)

At γ=0\gamma=0, the corresponding means are 0.012160.01216, 0.008570.00857, and 0.003230.00323. At the added middle discount, they are 0.007970.00797, 0.003540.00354, and −0.00331-0.00331, respectively. At γ=0.95\gamma=0.95, they are 0.005620.00562, 0.001230.00123, and −0.00435-0.00435. Thus, the observed advantage is not restricted to the two previously examined endpoint settings.

Table 12 and Figure 10 isolate the first research question. The mean BT-GP-OQL gains over Target-only are 0.008930.00893, 0.011280.01128, and 0.009970.00997 at γ=0\gamma=0, 0.50.5, and 0.950.95, respectively. The displayed fixed-fit percentile intervals lie above zero in all three cases. These results provide descriptive support for positive average transfer gains under the frozen source assignments and fitted models. They do not imply that every participant benefits or that the transfer gate guarantees finite-sample safety.

The second contrast holds the candidate pool and the number of sources fixed within each target–discount group. BT-GP-OQL exceeds the exact uniform matched-size Random-mm mean by 0.003580.00358, 0.004430.00443, and 0.004390.00439 at the three respective discounts (Table 12). The descriptive intervals in Figure 11 also lie above zero. Thus, the selected source identities yield better cohort-average immediate payoff than uniform same-size selection in each examined setting. Because every matched-size subset is included, this result is not an artifact of drawing a particularly unfavorable Monte Carlo sample of random subsets. Nevertheless, it remains a post-hoc comparison on previously examined histories: exhaustive enumeration removes subset-sampling error, not participant dependence or selection of the analysis itself. The result concerns the mean over matched-size subsets, not the best subset for each participant.

The gap results in Table 11 and Figure 12 are consistent with the payoff ordering. BT-GP-OQL has the smallest mean gap at each discount: 0.070750.07075, 0.074940.07494, and 0.077290.07729, compared with 0.079680.07968, 0.086220.08622, and 0.087250.08725 for Target-only. Random-mm lies between them. As noted above, this gap reduction is the complementary expression of higher payoff on the same test records, not a statistically independent outcome. The middle discount preserves both positive mean contrasts, with a transfer gain of 0.011280.01128 and a matched-size selection gain of 0.004430.00443. It therefore extends the observed direction of the results to a setting between the original endpoints. It does not identify an optimal discount: BT-GP-OQL’s absolute mean immediate payoff is higher at γ=0\gamma=0 than at 0.50.5 or 0.950.95, while its largest observed gain relative to the discount-specific Target-only comparator occurs at γ=0.5\gamma=0.5. Absolute payoff and improvement over a moving baseline are different comparisons. No conclusion about the best long-horizon discount follows from these immediate-reward scores.

Table 13 and Figure 13 provide an auxiliary check on the source-selection mechanism. Selected sources exceed excluded sources in mean later-validation per-trial LPD gain by 0.009980.00998, 0.011100.01110, and 0.012350.01235 at γ=0\gamma=0, 0.50.5, and 0.950.95, respectively. The displayed descriptive intervals remain above zero. Thus, the ranking obtained from early validation also separates sources with stronger and weaker predictive compatibility in the later window, rather than reflecting only fit to the screening responses. This is supporting predictive evidence, not proof that excluded sources are harmful or that the inclusion-score construction dominates other ranking rules. The later responses concern working Bellman targets, and the two windows remain temporally dependent.

The three-discount results support two focused observations: cross-participant information sharing improves cohort-average immediate payoff relative to Target-only, and target-aware source choice improves upon the exact uniform matched-size comparator. The direction of both contrasts is preserved at the supplementary γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 setting, with no recalibration of C10. These are average, protocol-specific findings, not claims of improvement for every participant or subset-size stratum. They do not establish universal negative-transfer protection, computational savings, superiority to unreported methods, or a distinct benefit of decision-stage pessimism. The fixed-fit intervals are pointwise descriptive summaries, not simultaneous or source-aware coverage guarantees. Finally, because evaluation conditions on logged histories while fitted parameters remain frozen, it does not identify a counterfactual closed-loop policy return. Within these limits, the application supplies complementary behavioral evidence for transfer and target-adaptive source selection alongside the known-value synthetic experiments.

A.2 Proof of Lemma 2

Proof.

Stationarity identifies its mean with v⊤​Σk​vv^{\top}\Sigma_{k}v. Applying Lemma 1 at deviation level ν/4\nu/4 and taking a union bound over tasks and net points therefore yields

Let ℰD\mathcal{E}_{D} denote the complementary event. On ℰD\mathcal{E}_{D}, λmin​(Ak)≥N​ν/2\lambda_{\min}(A_{k})\geq N\nu/2 for every kk. Write ξk=(ξ1(k),…,ξN(k))⊤\xi_{k}=(\xi_{1}^{(k)},\ldots,\xi_{N}^{(k)})^{\top}. For a fixed unit vector vv, the coefficient v⊤​ψ​(Xt(k))v^{\top}\psi(X_{t}^{(k)}) is ℱt(k)\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}-measurable. The conditional noise assumption therefore implies

𝔼⁡[exp⁡(u​v⊤​ψ​(Xt(k))​ξt(k))∣ℱt(k)]≤exp⁡(u2​σ2​κ22).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\exp\!\left(uv^{\top}\psi(X_{t}^{(k)})\xi_{t}^{(k)}\right)\mid\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}\right]\leq\exp\!\left(\frac{u^{2}\sigma^{2}\kappa^{2}}{2}\right).

Repeated conditioning gives

Choose a 1/21/2-net 𝒰\mathcal{U} of the unit sphere with |𝒰|≤5m|\mathcal{U}|\leq 5^{m}, so that ‖z‖2≤2​maxv∈𝒰​|v⊤​z|\|z\|_{2}\leq 2\max_{v\in\mathcal{U}}|v^{\top}z|. ‖A−1‖b≤2N​ν,‖λN​A−1​Ω‖b≤2​λN​ΛNN​ν≤12.\|A^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{b}}\leq\frac{2}{N\nu},\quad\|\lambda_{N}A^{-1}\Omega\|_{\mathrm{b}}\leq\frac{2\lambda_{N}\Lambda_{N}}{N\nu}\leq\frac{1}{2}.

A.3 Proof of Lemma 3

Proof.

Fix a task kk and a deterministic q∈𝒬kq\in\mathcal{Q}_{k}. Write Vq​(s)=maxa∈𝒜(k)⁡q⁡(s,a)V_{q}(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}^{(k)}}q(s,a) and define

Conditional Cauchy–Schwarz therefore gives

𝔼⁡[eu​ξt(k)​(q)∣ℱt(k)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[e^{u\xi_{t}^{(k)}(q)}\mid\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}] ≤{𝔼⁡[e2​u​ϵt(k)∣ℱt(k)]}1/2​{𝔼⁡[e2​u​γ​ζt​(q)∣ℱt(k)]}1/2\displaystyle\leq\left\{\mathbb{E}[e^{2u\epsilon_{t}^{(k)}}\mid\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}]\right\}^{1/2}\left\{\mathbb{E}[e^{2u\gamma\zeta_{t}(q)}\mid\mathscr{F}_{t}^{(k)}]\right\}^{1/2}
≤exp⁡(u2​σ2+4​u2​γ2​B2)\displaystyle\leq\exp(u^{2}\sigma^{2}+4u^{2}\gamma^{2}B^{2})
=exp⁡(u2​σB22).\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(\frac{u^{2}\sigma_{B}^{2}}{2}\right).

No independence between the innovation and the continuation-value fluctuation is used.

≤aN+4​κν​{2​σB​κ​2​ℓNN+2​γ​κ​ε+κ​aN+λN​ΛN​RNN}\displaystyle\leq a_{N}+\frac{4\kappa}{\nu}\left\{2\sigma_{B}\kappa\sqrt{\frac{2\ell_{N}}{N}}+2\gamma\kappa\varepsilon+\kappa a_{N}+\frac{\lambda_{N}\Lambda_{N}R_{N}}{N}\right\}

A.5 Proof of Corollary 1

Proof.

It remains to establish the mean-square bound. Suppose that the fitted update is deterministically restricted to the supremum-norm ball of radius BB and that ‖Q∗(k)‖∞≤B\|Q_{*}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\leq B for every task. Then, for every realization,

≤maxk⁡{‖Q^e−1(k)‖∞+‖Q∗(k)‖∞}\displaystyle\leq\max_{k}\left\{\|\widehat{Q}_{e-1}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}+\|Q_{*}^{(k)}\|_{\infty}\right\}
≤2​B.\displaystyle\leq 2B.

Decomposing according to ℰN\mathcal{E}_{N} gives

𝔼⁡[De−1,N2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[D_{e-1,N}^{2}] =𝔼⁡[De−1,N2​𝟏ℰN]+𝔼⁡[De−1,N2​𝟏ℰNc]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\!\left[D_{e-1,N}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}_{N}}\right]+\mathbb{E}\!\left[D_{e-1,N}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}_{N}^{c}}\right]
≤re−1,N2​ℙ​(ℰN)+4​B2​ℙ​(ℰNc)\displaystyle\leq r_{e-1,N}^{2}\,\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{N})+4B^{2}\,\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{N}^{c})
≤re−1,N2+4​B2​δN.\displaystyle\leq r_{e-1,N}^{2}+4B^{2}\delta_{N}.

On the other hand, the pathwise inequality already proved implies

(bt,e(k))2≤γ2​De−1,N2.(b_{t,e}^{(k)})^{2}\leq\gamma^{2}D_{e-1,N}^{2}.

Taking expectations,

𝔼⁡[(bt,e(k))2]≤γ2​𝔼​[De−1,N2].\mathbb{E}\!\left[(b_{t,e}^{(k)})^{2}\right]\leq\gamma^{2}\mathbb{E}[D_{e-1,N}^{2}].

The right-hand side does not depend on kk or tt, so

supk,t𝔼⁡[(bt,e(k))2]≤γ2​𝔼​[De−1,N2]≤γ2​{re−1,N2+4​B2​δN}.\displaystyle\sup_{k,t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(b_{t,e}^{(k)})^{2}\right]\leq\gamma^{2}\mathbb{E}[D_{e-1,N}^{2}]\leq\gamma^{2}\left\{r_{e-1,N}^{2}+4B^{2}\delta_{N}\right\}.

This proves (27). Finally, if reN−1,N→0r_{e_{N}-1,N}\to 0 and δN→0\delta_{N}\to 0, then

γ2​{reN−1,N2+4​B2​δN}⟶0,\gamma^{2}\left\{r_{e_{N}-1,N}^{2}+4B^{2}\delta_{N}\right\}\longrightarrow 0,

and therefore

supk,t𝔼⁡[(bt,eN(k))2]⟶0.\sup_{k,t}\mathbb{E}\!\left[(b_{t,e_{N}}^{(k)})^{2}\right]\longrightarrow 0.

∎

A.6 Proof of Lemma 4

Proof.

Fix S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J}. Since the same predictive specification is used for the actual and oracle-response scores, the predictive covariance VSV_{S} is unchanged when 𝐘¯\overline{\mathbf{Y}} is replaced by 𝐘e=𝐘¯+𝐛e\mathbf{Y}_{e}=\overline{\mathbf{Y}}+\mathbf{b}_{e}. 𝐘e(0)−𝐚S−AS​𝐘e(S)=𝐘¯(0)+𝐛e(0)−𝐚S−AS​(𝐘¯(S)+𝐛e(S))=𝐫S∘+𝐝S,e.\displaystyle\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(0)}-\mathbf{a}_{S}-A_{S}\mathbf{Y}_{e}^{(S)}=\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(0)}+\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(0)}-\mathbf{a}_{S}-A_{S}\bigl(\overline{\mathbf{Y}}^{(S)}+\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(S)}\bigr)=\mathbf{r}_{S}^{\circ}+\mathbf{d}_{S,e}.

=−(𝐫S∘)⊤​VS−1​𝐝S,e−12​𝐝S,e⊤​VS−1​𝐝S,e.\displaystyle=-(\mathbf{r}_{S}^{\circ})^{\top}V_{S}^{-1}\mathbf{d}_{S,e}-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{d}_{S,e}^{\top}V_{S}^{-1}\mathbf{d}_{S,e}.

Since λmin​(VS)≥v¯N,\lambda_{\min}(V_{S})\geq\underline{v}_{N}, we have ‖VS−1‖op≤v¯N−1.\|V_{S}^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\underline{v}_{N}^{-1}. Therefore,

|ℓe,N​(S)−ℓN∘​(S)|≤1v¯N​{‖𝐫S∘‖2​‖𝐝S,e‖2+12​‖𝐝S,e‖22}≤ℛN​𝒟e,N+12​𝒟e,N2v¯N.\displaystyle\left|\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S)\right|\leq\frac{1}{\underline{v}_{N}}\left\{\|\mathbf{r}_{S}^{\circ}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{d}_{S,e}\|_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{d}_{S,e}\|_{2}^{2}\right\}\leq\frac{\mathcal{R}_{N}\mathcal{D}_{e,N}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{D}_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{v}_{N}}.

Recall that

ue,N​(S)={ℓe,N​(S)−ℓN∘​(S)}−{ℓe,N​(SN⋆)−ℓN∘​(SN⋆)}.\displaystyle u_{e,N}(S)=\bigl\{\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S)\bigr\}-\bigl\{\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})-\ell_{N}^{\circ}(S_{N}^{\star})\bigr\}.

The triangle inequality thus yields

|ue,N​(S)|≤2​ℛN​𝒟e,N+𝒟e,N2v¯N.|u_{e,N}(S)|\leq\frac{2\mathcal{R}_{N}\mathcal{D}_{e,N}+\mathcal{D}_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{v}_{N}}.

Taking the maximum over S∈𝒮JS\in\mathcal{S}_{J} proves (28).
Next,

‖𝐝S,e‖2=‖𝐛e(0)−AS​𝐛e(S)‖2≤‖𝐛e(0)‖2+‖AS‖op​‖𝐛e(S)‖2≤(1+LA,N)​‖𝐛e‖2.\displaystyle\|\mathbf{d}_{S,e}\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(0)}-A_{S}\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(S)}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(0)}\|_{2}+\|A_{S}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\mathbf{b}_{e}^{(S)}\|_{2}\leq(1+L_{A,N})\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}.

Taking the maximum over SS proves (29). Substitution into (28) yields (30). ∎

A.7 Proof of Corollary 2

Proof.

Set te,N=ntot​βe,N,t_{e,N}=\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{tot}}}\,\beta_{e,N}, and define the deterministic rate

ρe,Nbt=(1+LA,N)​sN​te,N+(1+LA,N)2​te,N2v¯N.\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}=\frac{(1+L_{A,N})s_{N}t_{e,N}+(1+L_{A,N})^{2}t_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{v}_{N}}.

It is enough to show that 𝔅e,N=Oℙ⋆​(ρe,Nbt).\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=O_{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}\bigl(\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\bigr). 𝔼⋆​‖𝐛e‖22=∑k=0J∑t=1nk𝔼⋆​[(bt,e(k))2]≤ntot​βe,N2=te,N2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\star}\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{J}\sum_{t=1}^{n_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[(b_{t,e}^{(k)})^{2}\right]\leq n_{\mathrm{tot}}\beta_{e,N}^{2}=t_{e,N}^{2}.

In this case, Lemma 4 gives 𝔅e,N=0\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=0 almost surely, so the conclusion is immediate. We therefore consider te,N>0t_{e,N}>0. For any constant M≥1M\geq 1, Markov’s inequality gives

ℙ⋆​(‖𝐛e‖2>M​te,N)=ℙ⋆​(‖𝐛e‖22>M2​te,N2)≤𝔼⋆​‖𝐛e‖22M2​te,N2≤M−2.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}>Mt_{e,N}\right)=\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}^{2}>M^{2}t_{e,N}^{2}\right)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\star}\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}^{2}}{M^{2}t_{e,N}^{2}}\leq M^{-2}. (A.4)

By assumption, ℙ⋆​(ℛN>sN)≤ηR,N.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathcal{R}_{N}>s_{N}\right)\leq\eta_{R,N}. Define ℰN(M)={ℛN≤sN}∩{∥𝐛e∥2≤Mte,N}.\mathcal{E}_{N}(M)=\left\{\mathcal{R}_{N}\leq s_{N}\right\}\cap\left\{\|\mathbf{b}_{e}\|_{2}\leq Mt_{e,N}\right\}. The union bound and (A.4) imply ℙ⋆​(ℰN​(M)c)≤ηR,N+M−2.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\bigl(\mathcal{E}_{N}(M)^{c}\bigr)\leq\eta_{R,N}+M^{-2}. On ℰN​(M)\mathcal{E}_{N}(M), the pathwise bound (30) yields

𝔅e,N≤1v¯N​{2​M​(1+LA,N)​sN​te,N+M2​(1+LA,N)2​te,N2}.\displaystyle\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}\leq\frac{1}{\underline{v}_{N}}\Bigl\{2M(1+L_{A,N})s_{N}t_{e,N}+M^{2}(1+L_{A,N})^{2}t_{e,N}^{2}\Bigr\}.

Since M≥1M\geq 1, 2​M​a+M2​b≤3​M2​(a+b),a,b≥0.2Ma+M^{2}b\leq 3M^{2}(a+b),~a,b\geq 0. Therefore, 𝔅e,N≤3​M2​ρe,Nbt​on ​ℰN​(M).\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}\leq 3M^{2}\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}~\text{on }\mathcal{E}_{N}(M). Consequently,

ℙ⋆​(𝔅e,N>3​M2​ρe,Nbt)≤ηR,N+M−2.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}>3M^{2}\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\right)\leq\eta_{R,N}+M^{-2}. (A.5)

Now fix ε>0\varepsilon>0. Choose M≥1M\geq 1 sufficiently large that M−2<ε2.M^{-2}<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}. Hence, 𝔅e,N=Oℙ⋆​(ρe,Nbt).\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=O_{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}\bigl(\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\bigr). Substituting te,N=ntot​βe,Nt_{e,N}=\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{tot}}}\beta_{e,N} into the definition of ρe,Nbt\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}} gives

𝔅e,N=Oℙ⋆​[(1+LA,N)​sN​ntot​βe,N+(1+LA,N)2​ntot​βe,N2v¯N],\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=O_{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}\left[\frac{(1+L_{A,N})s_{N}\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{tot}}}\,\beta_{e,N}+(1+L_{A,N})^{2}n_{\mathrm{tot}}\beta_{e,N}^{2}}{\underline{v}_{N}}\right],

A.8 Proof of Lemma 5

Proof.

By the definition of the working subset posterior,

Πe,N​(ℬ∣𝐘e,X)\displaystyle\Pi_{e,N}(\mathcal{B}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X) =∑S∈ℬΠN​(S)​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(S)}∑U∈𝒮JΠN​(U)​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(U)}.\displaystyle=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathcal{B}}\Pi_{N}(S)\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(S)\}}{\displaystyle\sum_{U\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\Pi_{N}(U)\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(U)\}}.

The denominator is bounded below by the contribution of the reference subset:

∑U∈𝒮JΠN​(U)​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(U)}≥πN⋆​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(SN⋆)}.\sum_{U\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\Pi_{N}(U)\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(U)\}\geq\pi_{N}^{\star}\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\}.

Therefore,

Πe,N​(ℬ∣𝐘e,X)\displaystyle\Pi_{e,N}(\mathcal{B}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X) ≤∑S∈ℬΠN​(S)πN⋆​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)}\displaystyle\leq\sum_{S\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{\Pi_{N}(S)}{\pi_{N}^{\star}}\exp\left\{\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\right\}
≤|ℬ|​exp⁡(qN+maxS∈ℬ⁡{ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)}).\displaystyle\leq|\mathcal{B}|\exp\Bigg(q_{N}+\max_{S\in\mathcal{B}}\bigl\{\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\bigr\}\Bigg).

Since posterior mass is at most one, (33) follows. For each S∈ℬS\in\mathcal{B},

Πe,N​(S∣𝐘e,X)Πe,N​(SN⋆∣𝐘e,X)=ΠN​(S)πN⋆​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)}.\frac{\Pi_{e,N}(S\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X)}{\Pi_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X)}=\frac{\Pi_{N}(S)}{\pi_{N}^{\star}}\exp\left\{\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\right\}.

Using log⁡ΠN​(S)πN⋆≤qN\log\frac{\Pi_{N}(S)}{\pi_{N}^{\star}}\leq q_{N} and taking the maximum over S∈ℬS\in\mathcal{B} proves (34). ∎

A.9 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

If ℬN=∅\mathcal{B}_{N}=\varnothing, all conclusions are immediate. Hence consider NN for which ℬN≠∅\mathcal{B}_{N}\neq\varnothing. Define ℰ1,N={maxS∈ℬNZN(S)≤aN}.\mathcal{E}_{1,N}=\left\{\max_{S\in\mathcal{B}_{N}}Z_{N}(S)\leq a_{N}\right\}. By (35), ℙ⋆​(ℰ1,Nc)=ΞN+​(aN,dN)⟶0.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathcal{E}_{1,N}^{c}\right)=\Xi_{N}^{+}(a_{N};d_{N})\longrightarrow 0. Since κN→∞\kappa_{N}\to\infty, we have κN>0\kappa_{N}>0 for all sufficiently large NN. Define ℰ2,N={𝔅e,N≤κN2}.\mathcal{E}_{2,N}=\left\{\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}\leq\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2}\right\}. Corollary 2 gives 𝔅e,N=Oℙ⋆​(ρe,Nbt).\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=O_{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}\left(\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\right). Together with ρe,Nbt=o⁡(κN)\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}=o(\kappa_{N}), this implies

𝔅e,NκN→ℙ⋆0.\frac{\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}}{\kappa_{N}}\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}0.

To verify this implication explicitly, fix ε>0\varepsilon>0. By 𝔅e,N=Oℙ⋆​(ρe,Nbt)\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}=O_{\mathbb{P}_{\star}}(\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}), there exists Cε<∞C_{\varepsilon}<\infty such that, for all sufficiently large NN,

ℙ⋆​(𝔅e,N>Cε​ρe,Nbt)<ε.\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}>C_{\varepsilon}\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\right)<\varepsilon.

Since ρe,NbtκN⟶0,\frac{\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}}{\kappa_{N}}\longrightarrow 0, we have Cε​ρe,Nbt<κN2C_{\varepsilon}\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}<\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2} for all sufficiently large NN. Consequently,

ℙ⋆​(ℰ2,Nc)=ℙ⋆​(𝔅e,N>κN2)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\star}(\mathcal{E}_{2,N}^{c})=\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}>\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2}\right) ≤ℙ⋆​(𝔅e,N>Cε​ρe,Nbt)<ε.\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}>C_{\varepsilon}\rho_{e,N}^{\mathrm{bt}}\right)<\varepsilon.

Because ε>0\varepsilon>0 is arbitrary, ℙ⋆​(ℰ2,Nc)⟶0.\mathbb{P}_{\star}(\mathcal{E}_{2,N}^{c})\longrightarrow 0. Let ℰN=ℰ1,N∩ℰ2,N.\mathcal{E}_{N}=\mathcal{E}_{1,N}\cap\mathcal{E}_{2,N}. The union bound gives

ℙ⋆​(ℰNc)≤ΞN+​(aN,dN)+ℙ⋆​(𝔅e,N>κN2)⟶0.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\star}(\mathcal{E}_{N}^{c})\leq\Xi_{N}^{+}(a_{N};d_{N})+\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}>\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2}\right)\longrightarrow 0.

Now fix S∈ℬNS\in\mathcal{B}_{N}. By definition of ℬNpred​(dN)\mathcal{B}_{N}^{\mathrm{pred}}(d_{N}),

ℒN∗−ℒN∘​(S)≥dN.\mathcal{L}_{N}^{*}-\mathcal{L}_{N}^{\circ}(S)\geq d_{N}. (A.6)

The exact score decomposition (3.2) gives

ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)\displaystyle\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star}) =−{ℒN∗−ℒN∘​(S)}+ZN​(S)+ue,N​(S).\displaystyle=-\left\{\mathcal{L}_{N}^{*}-\mathcal{L}_{N}^{\circ}(S)\right\}+Z_{N}(S)+u_{e,N}(S).

On ℰN\mathcal{E}_{N}, ZN​(S)≤aNZ_{N}(S)\leq a_{N} and ue,N​(S)≤|ue,N​(S)|≤𝔅e,N≤κN2.u_{e,N}(S)\leq|u_{e,N}(S)|\leq\mathfrak{B}_{e,N}\leq\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2}. Combining these inequalities with (A.6) yields, simultaneously for all S∈ℬNS\in\mathcal{B}_{N},

ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)≤−dN+aN+κN2.\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\leq-d_{N}+a_{N}+\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2}.

We next bound the posterior mass of ℬN\mathcal{B}_{N} directly. From (3.2),

Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)=∑S∈ℬNΠN​(S)​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(S)}∑U∈𝒮JΠN​(U)​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(U)}.\displaystyle\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathcal{B}_{N}}\Pi_{N}(S)\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(S)\}}{\displaystyle\sum_{U\in\mathcal{S}_{J}}\Pi_{N}(U)\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(U)\}}.

The denominator is at least πN⋆​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(SN⋆)}.\pi_{N}^{\star}\exp\{\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\}. Therefore, on ℰN\mathcal{E}_{N},

Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)≤ΠN​(ℬN)πN⋆​exp⁡{−dN+aN+κN2}.\displaystyle\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\leq\frac{\Pi_{N}(\mathcal{B}_{N})}{\pi_{N}^{\star}}\exp\left\{-d_{N}+a_{N}+\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2}\right\}.

By the definition of ΛN​(dN)\Lambda_{N}(d_{N}), ΠN​(ℬN)πN⋆≤exp⁡{ΛN​(dN)}.\frac{\Pi_{N}(\mathcal{B}_{N})}{\pi_{N}^{\star}}\leq\exp\{\Lambda_{N}(d_{N})\}. Hence

Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)≤exp⁡{ΛN​(dN)−dN+aN+κN2}.\displaystyle\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\leq\exp\left\{\Lambda_{N}(d_{N})-d_{N}+a_{N}+\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2}\right\}.

Since κN=dN−aN−ΛN​(dN),\kappa_{N}=d_{N}-a_{N}-\Lambda_{N}(d_{N}), the exponent equals −κN/2-\kappa_{N}/2. Thus,

Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)≤exp⁡(−κN2)on ​ℰN.\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\kappa_{N}}{2}\right)\quad\text{on }\mathcal{E}_{N}. (A.7)

Because κN→∞\kappa_{N}\to\infty, exp(−κN/2)⟶0.\exp(-\kappa_{N}/2)\longrightarrow 0. For any fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0, the right-hand side of (A.7) is smaller than ε\varepsilon for all sufficiently large NN. Therefore,

ℙ⋆{Πe,N(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)>ε}≤ℙ⋆(ℰNc)⟶0,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left\{\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)>\varepsilon\right\}\leq\mathbb{P}_{\star}(\mathcal{E}_{N}^{c})\longrightarrow 0,

which proves (36). Since posterior mass is bounded by one,

𝔼⋆​[Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\right]
=𝔼⋆​[Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)​𝟏ℰN]+𝔼⋆​[Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)​𝟏ℰNc]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}_{N}}\right]+\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{E}_{N}^{c}}\right]
≤exp(−κN/2)+ℙ⋆(ℰNc)⟶0.\displaystyle\leq\exp(-\kappa_{N}/2)+\mathbb{P}_{\star}(\mathcal{E}_{N}^{c})\longrightarrow 0.

This proves (37).
Suppose next that S^\widehat{S} is drawn from the working subset posterior. Conditional on (𝐘e,X)(\mathbf{Y}_{e},X),

ℙ⁡(S^∈ℬN∣𝐘e,X)=Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X).\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{S}\in\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)=\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right).

Taking expectation over the data and auxiliary posterior-sampling randomness gives

ℙ⋆​(S^∈ℬN)=𝔼⋆​[Πe,N​(ℬN∣𝐘e,X)]⟶0.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\star}\left(\widehat{S}\in\mathcal{B}_{N}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\star}\left[\Pi_{e,N}\left(\mathcal{B}_{N}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X\right)\right]\longrightarrow 0.

This proves (38).
Finally, let S^MAP\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{MAP}} be any maximum-a-posteriori subset. For every S∈ℬNS\in\mathcal{B}_{N},

Πe,N​(S∣𝐘e,X)Πe,N​(SN⋆∣𝐘e,X)\displaystyle\frac{\Pi_{e,N}(S\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X)}{\Pi_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star}\mid\mathbf{Y}_{e},X)} =ΠN​(S)πN⋆​exp⁡{ℓe,N​(S)−ℓe,N​(SN⋆)}.\displaystyle=\frac{\Pi_{N}(S)}{\pi_{N}^{\star}}\exp\left\{\ell_{e,N}(S)-\ell_{e,N}(S_{N}^{\star})\right\}.

Since ΠN​(S)≤ΠN​(ℬN),\Pi_{N}(S)\leq\Pi_{N}(\mathcal{B}_{N}), on ℰN\mathcal{E}_{N},

B.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

Var⁡(θ0​j∣𝐙j,S)=λj​B00−λj2​B0​S​(λj​BS​S+DS,src−1)−1​BS​0=cj,S.\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\left(\theta_{0j}\mid\mathbf{Z}_{j,S}\right)=\lambda_{j}B_{00}-\lambda_{j}^{2}B_{0S}\left(\lambda_{j}B_{SS}+D_{S,\mathrm{src}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}B_{S0}=c_{j,S}.

For S=∅S=\varnothing, this conditional variance is simply λj​B00\lambda_{j}B_{00}, agreeing with the stated convention. Conditional on the source observations, the target observation is Z0​j=θ0​j+τ0−1/2ξ0​j.Z_{0j}=\theta_{0j}+\tau_{0}^{-1/2}\xi_{0j}. Thus the source-conditioned Gaussian prior for θ0​j\theta_{0j} has variance cj,Sc_{j,S}, while the target observation contributes precision τ0\tau_{0}. Gaussian conjugacy gives

Var⁡(θ0​j∣𝐙j)=(cj,S−1+τ0)−1,\operatorname{Var}\left(\theta_{0j}\mid\mathbf{Z}_{j}\right)=\left(c_{j,S}^{-1}+\tau_{0}\right)^{-1},

which proves (48).
Suppose next that BS≻0B_{S}\succ 0. Its principal source block BS​SB_{SS} is then positive definite, and the Schur complement of BS​SB_{SS} in BSB_{S} satisfies χS=B00−B0​S​BS​S−1​BS​0>0.\chi_{S}=B_{00}-B_{0S}B_{SS}^{-1}B_{S0}>0. Since λj​BS​S+DS,src−1⪰λj​BS​S,\lambda_{j}B_{SS}+D_{S,\mathrm{src}}^{-1}\succeq\lambda_{j}B_{SS}, the order-reversing property of matrix inversion yields

(λj​BS​S+DS,src−1)−1⪯λj−1​BS​S−1.\left(\lambda_{j}B_{SS}+D_{S,\mathrm{src}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}\preceq\lambda_{j}^{-1}B_{SS}^{-1}.

Hence

cj,S=λj​B00−λj2​B0​S​(λj​BS​S+DS,src−1)−1​BS​0≥λj​B00−λj​B0​S​BS​S−1​BS​0\displaystyle c_{j,S}=\lambda_{j}B_{00}-\lambda_{j}^{2}B_{0S}\left(\lambda_{j}B_{SS}+D_{S,\mathrm{src}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}B_{S0}\geq\lambda_{j}B_{00}-\lambda_{j}B_{0S}B_{SS}^{-1}B_{S0} =λj​χS,\displaystyle=\lambda_{j}\chi_{S},

proving (49).
Because the map c⟼(τ0+c−1)−1c\longmapsto(\tau_{0}+c^{-1})^{-1} is increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty), (49) implies

v0​j​(S)≥{τ0+(λj​χS)−1}−1,v_{0j}(S)\geq\left\{\tau_{0}+(\lambda_{j}\chi_{S})^{-1}\right\}^{-1},

which proves (50).
If mink∈S⁡τk→∞\min_{k\in S}\tau_{k}\to\infty, then DS,src−1⟶0D_{S,\mathrm{src}}^{-1}\longrightarrow 0 in operator norm. Continuity of matrix inversion on the positive definite cone gives

Substituting this limit into (47) yields cj,S⟶λj​χS,c_{j,S}\longrightarrow\lambda_{j}\chi_{S}, and continuity of the scalar posterior-variance map proves (51).
For the two-task covariance matrix, B00=1,BS​S=1,B0​S=BS​0=ϱ,B_{00}=1,~B_{SS}=1,~B_{0S}=B_{S0}=\varrho, therefore,

χS=1−ϱ2.\chi_{S}=1-\varrho^{2}.

Equation (52) follows immediately.
The variance floor also gives a direct obstruction to target posterior contraction from source information alone. Fix any frequency j0j_{0} with λj0>0\lambda_{j_{0}}>0 and keep τ0\tau_{0} fixed. By (50),

v0​j0​(S)≥v∗={τ0+(λj0​χS)−1}−1>0,v_{0j_{0}}(S)\geq v_{*}=\left\{\tau_{0}+(\lambda_{j_{0}}\chi_{S})^{-1}\right\}^{-1}>0,
